For \(\kappa=10\) the shape parameters are \(a=4\) and \(b=6\) and the variance is \(0.4(0.6)/11\approx 0.0218\), so the standard deviation is approximately \(0.148\). For \(\kappa=50\) the shape parameters are \(a=20\) and \(b=30\) and the variance is \(0.4(0.6)/51\approx 0.0047\), so the standard deviation is approximately \(0.069\). The model with \(\kappa=50\) is narrower, because a larger precision concentrates the probability around the mean.

title: Distributions
text:
3.11 Weibull distribution
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \texttt{dweibull, pweibull, qweibull, rweibull} \\
\text{Type}: &\quad \text{Continuous} \\
\text{Range}: &\quad x \geq 0 \\
\text{Density}: &\quad
\frac{k}{\lambda}\left(\frac{x}{\lambda}\right)^{k-1}
\exp\left[-\left(\frac{x}{\lambda}\right)^k\right] \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad k\;(\texttt{shape})>0;\quad
\lambda\;(\texttt{scale})>0 \\
\text{Mean}: &\quad E[X] = \lambda\Gamma(1+1/k) \\
\text{Variance}: &\quad
\operatorname{Var}(X) = \lambda^2\left[\Gamma(1+2/k)-\Gamma(1+1/k)^2\right] \\
\text{Inverse}: &\quad
\lambda = \frac{\mu}{\Gamma(1+1/k)}
\end{aligned}
\]
The Weibull distribution is a model for the waiting time until a single event happens when the rate at which the event occurs changes with time. It is often used for lifespans and survival times. It has a shape parameter \(k>0\) and a scale parameter \(\lambda>0\), where the scale has the same units as the waiting time. The shape determines how the rate changes: for \(k<1\) the rate decreases with time (e.g., when mortality is highest in young individuals), for \(k>1\) it increases with time (e.g., when mortality increases with age) and for \(k=1\) it is constant, in which case we recover the Exponential distribution with rate \(1/\lambda\).
Its probability density function is
\[
f_X(x)=\frac{k}{\lambda}\left(\frac{x}{\lambda}\right)^{k-1}
\exp\left[-\left(\frac{x}{\lambda}\right)^k\right], \qquad x \geq 0.
\]
The probability that the event has not yet happened at time \(x\) has a simple formula:
\[
P(X>x)=\exp\left[-\left(\frac{x}{\lambda}\right)^k\right].
\]
The mean and variance are:
\[
\mu=E[X]=\lambda\,\Gamma\left(1+\frac{1}{k}\right)
\]
and
\[
\operatorname{Var}(X)=\lambda^2\left[\Gamma\left(1+\frac{2}{k}\right)-
\Gamma\left(1+\frac{1}{k}\right)^2\right],
\]
where \(\Gamma\) is the gamma function (gamma() in R). I show below how to parameterise from the mean and shape.

3.11.1 Example: leaf lifespan
Suppose the lifespan of a leaf has a mean of 2 years and follows a Weibull distribution with shape \(k=1.5\). The scale is
\[
\lambda=\frac{2}{\Gamma(1+1/1.5)}\approx\frac{2}{0.9027}\approx 2.215 \text{ years}.
\]
The probability that a leaf lives longer than 3 years is
\[
P(X>3)=\exp\left[-\left(\frac{3}{2.215}\right)^{1.5}\right]
\approx e^{-1.576}\approx 0.207.
\]
We can verify our math with R:

# Calculate the scale from the mean lifespan (in years) and the shape.
mean_lifespan = 2
lifespan_shape = 1.5
lifespan_scale = mean_lifespan / gamma(1 + 1 / lifespan_shape)
lifespan_scale

[1] 2.215464

# Use the upper tail for the probability of living longer than three years.
pweibull(q = 3, shape = lifespan_shape, scale = lifespan_scale, lower.tail = FALSE)

[1] 0.2068543







Weibull probability density for the lifespan of a leaf.










ImportantPractice: seedling survival time



Suppose the survival time of a seedling follows a Weibull distribution with shape \(k=0.8\) and scale \(\lambda=2\) years. Does the mortality rate increase or decrease with age? Calculate the probability that a seedling survives its first year and the mean survival time.






TipSolution





The shape is smaller than one, so the mortality rate decreases with age. The probability of surviving the first year is \(\exp[-(1/2)^{0.8}]\approx 0.563\) and the mean survival time is \(2\,\Gamma(1+1/0.8)\approx 2.27\) years:

# Calculate the probability of surviving beyond one year and the mean survival time.
pweibull(q = 1, shape = 0.8, scale = 2, lower.tail = FALSE)

[1] 0.5630712

2 * gamma(1 + 1 / 0.8)

[1] 2.266006

title: Distributions
text:
4.1 Multinomial distribution
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \texttt{dmultinom, rmultinom} \\
\text{Type}: &\quad \text{Discrete, multivariate} \\
\text{Range}: &\quad x_i \in \{0,1,\ldots,n\},\quad \sum_{i=1}^K x_i=n \\
\text{Probability}: &\quad
\frac{n!}{\prod_{i=1}^K x_i!}\prod_{i=1}^K p_i^{x_i} \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad n\;(\texttt{size}) = \text{number of trials};\quad
p_i\;(\texttt{prob}) = \text{probability of category }i,\quad \sum_i p_i=1 \\
\text{Mean}: &\quad \mu_i = np_i \\
\text{Variance}: &\quad \operatorname{Var}(X_i)=np_i(1-p_i) \\
\text{Covariance}: &\quad \operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j)=-np_ip_j,\quad i\ne j \\
\text{Inverse}: &\quad p_i = \mu_i/n,\quad \sum_i\mu_i=n
\end{aligned}
\]
The Multinomial distribution generalises the Binomial distribution to events that have more than two possible outcomes. Each of \(n\) independent events falls into one of \(K\) categories, where category \(i\) has probability \(p_i\) and the probabilities add up to one. The random variables \(X_1, \ldots, X_K\) are the number of events in each category, so they always add up to \(n\).
The probability mass function is
\[
P(X_1=x_1,\ldots,X_K=x_K)=\frac{n!}{x_1!\cdots x_K!}\,p_1^{x_1}\cdots p_K^{x_K},
\]
where the first factor counts the number of ways in which the \(n\) events can be assigned to the categories. The mean and variance of each count are:
\[
E[X_i]=np_i
\]
and
\[
\operatorname{Var}(X_i)=np_i(1-p_i).
\]
These are the mean and variance of a Binomial distribution. In fact, each count on its own follows a Binomial distribution with \(n\) trials and probability \(p_i\). However, the counts are not independent of each other. Because the total is fixed, a higher count in one category leaves fewer events for the others, which results in a negative covariance:
\[
\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j)=-np_ip_j, \qquad i \neq j.
\]

4.1.1 Example: species in a sample
Suppose we capture 20 individuals and each of them belongs to one of three species with probabilities \(0.25\), \(0.4\) and \(0.35\). The expected counts are \(20(0.25)=5\), \(20(0.4)=8\) and \(20(0.35)=7\). The probability of capturing exactly those numbers is
\[
P(X_1=5,X_2=8,X_3=7)
=
\frac{20!}{5!\,8!\,7!}(0.25)^5(0.4)^8(0.35)^7
\approx 0.0411,
\]
and the covariance between the counts of the first two species is \(-20(0.25)(0.4)=-2\). We can verify the probability in R:

# Set the number of captured individuals and the probability of each species.
captured_count = 20
species_probability = c(0.25, 0.4, 0.35)

# Probability of one particular combination of counts.
dmultinom(x = c(5, 8, 7), size = captured_count, prob = species_probability)

[1] 0.04108172


We can check the means and the covariance by simulating many samples. Note that rmultinom() returns a matrix with one row per category and one column per sample:

# Simulate 5000 samples of 20 individuals.
set.seed(2026)
species_counts = rmultinom(n = 5000, size = captured_count, prob = species_probability)

# Every sample adds up to the total number of individuals.
range(colSums(species_counts))

[1] 20 20

# Average count per species and covariance between the first two species.
rowMeans(species_counts)

[1] 4.9834 7.9938 7.0228

cov(species_counts[1, ], species_counts[2, ])

[1] -1.878479


The averages and the covariance of the simulated samples are close to the values of the model.





Probability mass for the number of individuals of the first species in a sample of 20, which is a Binomial distribution.










ImportantPractice: habitat use



An animal is observed on 10 independent occasions and on each occasion it is in one of three habitats with probabilities \(0.5\), \(0.3\) and \(0.2\). Calculate the probability of observing it 5, 3 and 2 times in each habitat, respectively. What is the covariance between the counts in the first two habitats?






TipSolution





The probability is
\[
\frac{10!}{5!\,3!\,2!}(0.5)^5(0.3)^3(0.2)^2 = 2520 \times 0.00003375 \approx 0.085,
\]
and the covariance is \(-10(0.5)(0.3)=-1.5\). In R:

# Probability of one particular combination of counts across the three habitats.
dmultinom(x = c(5, 3, 2), size = 10, prob = c(0.5, 0.3, 0.2))

[1] 0.08505

title: Distributions
text:
4.2 Multivariate Normal distribution
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \texttt{dmvnorm};\quad \texttt{MASS::mvrnorm} \\
\text{Type}: &\quad \text{Continuous, multivariate} \\
\text{Range}: &\quad \mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^K \\
\text{Density}: &\quad
\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{K/2}|\boldsymbol{\Sigma}|^{1/2}}
\exp\left[
-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^\mathsf{T}
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})
\right] \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad
\boldsymbol{\mu}\;(\texttt{mu}) = \text{mean vector};\quad
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\;(\texttt{Sigma}) = \text{covariance matrix} \\
\text{Mean}: &\quad \operatorname{E}[\mathbf{X}]=\boldsymbol{\mu} \\
\text{Covariance}: &\quad
\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf{X})=\boldsymbol{\Sigma} \\
\text{Inverse}: &\quad
\Sigma_{ii}=\sigma_i^2;\quad
\Sigma_{ij}=\rho_{ij}\sigma_i \sigma_j\quad(i\ne j)
\end{aligned}
\]
The Multivariate Normal distribution generalises the Normal distribution to \(K\) continuous random variables that are correlated with each other. It has two parameters: a vector \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) with the mean of each variable and a covariance matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) with \(K\) rows and \(K\) columns. The diagonal of the covariance matrix contains the variance of each variable and the other elements contain the covariance between each pair of variables.
Its probability density function is
\[
f_{\mathbf{X}}(\mathbf{x})=
\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{K/2}|\boldsymbol{\Sigma}|^{1/2}}
\exp\left[
-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^\mathsf{T}
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})
\right],
\]
where \(|\boldsymbol{\Sigma}|\) is the determinant of the covariance matrix and \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\) is its inverse.
It is usually easier to think in terms of standard deviations and correlations than in terms of covariances. If \(\sigma_i\) is the standard deviation of variable \(i\) and \(\rho_{ij}\) is the correlation between variables \(i\) and \(j\), the elements of the covariance matrix are:
\[
\Sigma_{ii}=\sigma_i^2
\]
and
\[
\Sigma_{ij}=\rho_{ij}\sigma_i\sigma_j, \qquad i \neq j.
\]
Each variable on its own follows a Normal distribution with mean \(\mu_i\) and variance \(\sigma_i^2\). When all the correlations are zero, the variables are independent.

4.2.1 Example: length and width of mussel shells
Suppose the length and the width of the shell of a mussel follow a Multivariate Normal distribution. The length has a mean of 60 mm and a standard deviation of 5 mm, the width has a mean of 30 mm and a standard deviation of 3 mm, and the correlation between them is \(0.6\). The covariance between length and width is
\[
\Sigma_{12}=0.6(5)(3)=9,
\]
so the covariance matrix is
\[
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=
\begin{pmatrix}
5^2 & 9 \\
9 & 3^2
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
25 & 9 \\
9 & 9
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
We can construct this matrix in R from the standard deviations and the correlation matrix:

# Set the means, standard deviations and correlation matrix of shell length and width.
shell_means = c(length = 60, width = 30)
shell_sds = c(5, 3)
shell_correlation = matrix(c(1, 0.6,
                            0.6, 1), nrow = 2)

# diag() creates a matrix with the standard deviations on its diagonal and
# %*% is matrix multiplication.
Sigma = diag(shell_sds) %*% shell_correlation %*% diag(shell_sds)
Sigma

     [,1] [,2]
[1,]   25    9
[2,]    9    9


The density function is dmvnorm() of RTMB. At the means, the exponent of the density is zero, and the determinant of this covariance matrix is \(25(9)-9(9)=144\), so the density is \(1/(2\pi\sqrt{144})\approx 0.0133\)/mm\(^2\):

# Density at the mean length and width.
dmvnorm(x = c(60, 30), mu = shell_means, Sigma = Sigma)

[1] 0.01326291


RTMB has no random number generator for this distribution, but we can generate random samples with the function mvrnorm() from the MASS package:

library(MASS) # Install it first

# Simulate 5000 mussels. Each row is a mussel and each column a variable.
set.seed(2026)
shell_draws = mvrnorm(n = 5000, mu = shell_means, Sigma = Sigma)

# The means and covariances of the sample are close to those of the model.
colMeans(shell_draws)

  length    width 
60.05366 29.98649 

cov(shell_draws)

          length    width
length 24.820913 8.670962
width   8.670962 8.860767







Length and width of the shells of 500 mussels simulated from a Multivariate Normal distribution with a correlation of 0.6.










ImportantPractice: a covariance matrix for two traits



Suppose the wing length of a bird has a standard deviation of 2 mm, its body mass has a standard deviation of 3 g and the correlation between the two traits is \(0.8\). Write down the covariance matrix. What would the covariance matrix be if the two traits were independent?






TipSolution





The variances are \(2^2=4\) and \(3^2=9\) and the covariance is \(0.8(2)(3)=4.8\), so
\[
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=
\begin{pmatrix}
4 & 4.8 \\
4.8 & 9
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
If the traits were independent the correlation would be zero, so the covariance would also be zero and only the variances on the diagonal would remain.

title: Distributions
text:
4.3 Dirichlet distribution
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \texttt{ddirichlet, rdirichlet} \\
\text{Type}: &\quad \text{Continuous, multivariate} \\
\text{Range}: &\quad x_i>0,\quad \sum_{i=1}^K x_i=1 \\
\text{Density}: &\quad
\frac{\Gamma(\alpha_0)}{\prod_{i=1}^K\Gamma(\alpha_i)}
\prod_{i=1}^K x_i^{\alpha_i-1},
\quad \alpha_0=\sum_{i=1}^K\alpha_i \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad \alpha_i>0\;(\texttt{alpha}) = \text{shape parameters} \\
\text{Mean}: &\quad \mu_i=\alpha_i/\alpha_0 \\
\text{Variance}: &\quad
\operatorname{Var}(X_i)=\frac{\mu_i(1-\mu_i)}{\alpha_0+1} \\
\text{Covariance}: &\quad
\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j)=\frac{-\mu_i\mu_j}{\alpha_0+1},\quad i\ne j \\
\text{Inverse}: &\quad
\alpha_0=\kappa;\quad \alpha_i=\kappa\mu_i
\end{aligned}
\]
The Dirichlet distribution generalises the Beta distribution to \(K\) continuous random variables that are each between \(0\) and \(1\) and that always add up to one. It is therefore a model for how a total is divided among several components, such as the fractions of sand, silt and clay in a soil. It has one shape parameter \(\alpha_i>0\) per component and for \(K=2\) it reduces to the Beta distribution.
Its probability density function is
\[
f_{\mathbf{X}}(\mathbf{x})=
\frac{\Gamma(\alpha_0)}{\prod_{i=1}^K\Gamma(\alpha_i)}
\prod_{i=1}^K x_i^{\alpha_i-1},
\qquad \alpha_0=\sum_{i=1}^K\alpha_i,
\]
where \(\Gamma\) is the gamma function. The sum of the shape parameters, \(\alpha_0\), plays the role of a precision (the larger it is, the less the fractions vary). The mean and variance of each fraction are:
\[
\mu_i=E[X_i]=\frac{\alpha_i}{\alpha_0}
\]
and
\[
\operatorname{Var}(X_i)=\frac{\mu_i(1-\mu_i)}{\alpha_0+1}.
\]
As in the Multinomial distribution, the fractions are not independent. Because they add up to one, a larger fraction for one component leaves less for the others, which results in a negative covariance:
\[
\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j)=\frac{-\mu_i\mu_j}{\alpha_0+1}, \qquad i \neq j.
\]
As with the Beta distribution, it is convenient to parameterise the Dirichlet distribution from the mean fractions and a precision \(\kappa=\alpha_0\), so that \(\alpha_i=\kappa\mu_i\).
RTMBdist provides the density, ddirichlet(), and a random number generator, rdirichlet(), which is enough for this course.

4.3.1 Example: biomass partitioning
Suppose a plant allocates on average 20% of its biomass to leaves, 30% to stems and 50% to roots, and that these fractions vary among plants according to a Dirichlet distribution with precision \(\kappa=12\). The shape parameters are
\[
\alpha_1=12(0.2)=2.4, \qquad \alpha_2=12(0.3)=3.6, \qquad \alpha_3=12(0.5)=6.
\]
The variance of the fraction allocated to roots is
\[
\operatorname{Var}(X_3)=\frac{0.5(1-0.5)}{12+1}\approx 0.0192,
\]
which corresponds to a standard deviation of approximately \(0.139\). We can check these values by simulating many plants:

# Convert the mean fractions and the precision into the shape parameters.
fraction_means = c(leaves = 0.2, stems = 0.3, roots = 0.5)
fraction_precision = 12
alpha = fraction_precision * fraction_means

# Simulate 5000 plants. Each row is a plant and each column a fraction.
set.seed(2026)
biomass_draws = rdirichlet(n = 5000, alpha = alpha)

# The fractions of every plant add up to one.
range(rowSums(biomass_draws))

[1] 1 1

# Average fraction per component and variance of the fraction allocated to roots.
colMeans(biomass_draws)

[1] 0.1991646 0.3016528 0.4991826

var(biomass_draws[, 3])

[1] 0.01903802







Fractions of biomass allocated to leaves and roots in 500 plants simulated from a Dirichlet distribution.










ImportantPractice: soil texture



Suppose the mean fractions of sand, silt and clay in the soils of a region are \(0.6\), \(0.3\) and \(0.1\), and that they vary among sites according to a Dirichlet distribution with precision \(\kappa=50\). Calculate the shape parameters and the standard deviation of the clay fraction.






TipSolution





The shape parameters are \(50(0.6)=30\), \(50(0.3)=15\) and \(50(0.1)=5\). The variance of the clay fraction is \(0.1(0.9)/51\approx 0.00176\), so its standard deviation is approximately \(0.042\).

title: Distributions
text:
5.1 Zero-inflated distributions in RTMBdist
RTMBdist implements zero-inflated versions of several distributions: dzipois(), dzibinom(), dzinbinom(), dzinbinom2(), dzigamma(), dzilnorm() and dziweibull(), among others. In all of them the argument zeroprob is \(p_{0}\), and the other arguments are those of the original distribution. For example, for a zero-inflated Negative Binomial distribution with mean 8, shape \(k=2\) and \(p_{0}=0.25\):

# Parameters of the zero-inflated Negative Binomial distribution.
mu = 8
size = 2
prob = size / (size + mu)
pzero = 0.25

# Probability mass of zero to three counts; zeroprob is the probability p0.
dzinbinom(x = 0:3, size = size, prob = prob, zeroprob = pzero)

[1] 0.28000 0.04800 0.05760 0.06144


Several of these distributions also have a function for the cumulative probability (e.g., pzipois()) and for random numbers (e.g., rzipois()), named like the functions of the original distributions, with zi after the letter d, p or r.
For a distribution without a zero-inflated version in RTMBdist, the function zero_inflate() constructs one from its probability mass or density function. It takes two arguments:

dist: the mass or density function of the original distribution (e.g., dcompois2, with no brackets because we pass the function itself).
discrete: TRUE if dist is a probability mass function and FALSE if it is a density. This decides whether the probability of zero in the original distribution is added to \(p_{0}\), as in the first formula above, or not, as in the second one. RTMBdist recognises a few mass functions of base R by their names (dpois, dbinom, dnbinom, dgeom, dmultinom and dhyper) and sets the value itself; for any other function we set it explicitly.

The new function takes the values, zeroprob and then the arguments of the original function. For example, for the Conway-Maxwell-Poisson distribution (see Section 2.4):

# Construct a zero-inflated Conway-Maxwell-Poisson probability mass function.
# discrete = TRUE says that the original distribution is a probability mass function.
dzicompois2 = zero_inflate(dcompois2, discrete = TRUE)

# Probability mass of zero to three eggs, with p0 = 0.25 and the arguments of dcompois2().
dzicompois2(x = 0:3, zeroprob = 0.25, mean = 2.5, nu = 2)

[1] 0.2671151 0.1307921 0.2498753 0.2121694


Applied to dnbinom, zero_inflate() gives the same probabilities as dzinbinom() above:

# Zero-inflated version of the Negative Binomial mass function of base R.
dzinbinom_made = zero_inflate(dnbinom, discrete = TRUE)
dzinbinom_made(x = 0:3, zeroprob = pzero, size = size, prob = prob)

[1] 0.28000 0.04800 0.05760 0.06144


The function that zero_inflate() returns calculates the probability mass or density and nothing else. Unlike the functions of RTMBdist that are written for a specific distribution, it has no argument log: to obtain the log probability for a negative log-likelihood, take the logarithm of the result, as in log(dzicompois2(...)). Setting log = TRUE passes that argument on to the original function without an error, but the result is not the log probability of the zero-inflated distribution. The function also creates no cumulative probability, quantile or random number functions. If you need those, or if the distribution that you want to inflate cannot be handled this way, write the functions yourself.

title: Distributions
text:
5.2 Writing your own zero-inflated distribution
Writing the functions yourself is the option for a zero-inflated distribution that zero_inflate() cannot construct: when you need the cumulative probability, quantile and random number functions as well as the mass function, or when the distribution to inflate is not available in RTMBdist and has to be written first. It is also what you do when you prefer not to depend on RTMBdist. Below is an example of how to define the dpqr functions for a discrete distribution, the zero-inflated Negative Binomial, using the same parameters as above. Their names start with my_ so that they do not replace the functions of RTMBdist.

# The mass/density function you will use for the likelihood, including log
my_dzinbinom = function(x, size, ..., pzero, log = FALSE) {
  baseline = dnbinom(x, size = size, ..., log = FALSE)
  result = (1 - pzero) * baseline
  result = ifelse(x == 0, pzero + result, result)
  if (log) log(result) else result
}

# The random number generator for sampling
my_rzinbinom = function(n, size, ..., pzero) {
  # Original distribution
  result = rnbinom(n, size = size, ...)
  # Bernoulli distribution
  result[runif(length(result)) < pzero] = 0
  result
}

# Cumulative probability for tail probabilities and p-values
my_pzinbinom = function(q, size, ..., pzero,
                         lower.tail = TRUE, log.p = FALSE) {
  baseline = pnbinom(q, size = size, ...,
                      lower.tail = TRUE, log.p = FALSE)
  result = ifelse(q < 0, 0, pzero + (1 - pzero) * baseline)
  if (!lower.tail) result = 1 - result
  if (log.p) log(result) else result
}

# Quantile function (assuming 0 < pzero < 1)
my_qzinbinom = function(p, size, ..., pzero, lower.tail = TRUE) {
  # Switch between lower or upper tail
  if (!lower.tail) p = 1 - p

  # Quantile in the original distribution
  baseline_p = (p - pzero) / (1 - pzero)
  baseline_q = qnbinom(baseline_p, size = size, ...)

  # Adjust for zero inflation
  cdf_at_zero = pzero + (1 - pzero)*pnbinom(0, size = size, ..., lower.tail = TRUE)
  ifelse(p <= cdf_at_zero, 0, baseline_q)
}

# Example, with the objects size, prob and pzero defined in the previous section
x = 0:my_qzinbinom(0.999, size = size, prob = prob, pzero = pzero)
plot(x, my_dzinbinom(x, size = size, prob = prob, pzero = pzero),
     type = "h", xlab = "Count", ylab = "Probability")







my_pzinbinom(0:10, size = size, prob = prob, pzero = pzero)

 [1] 0.2800000 0.3280000 0.3856000 0.4470400 0.5084800 0.5674624 0.6225126
 [8] 0.6728443 0.7181428 0.7584081 0.7938416

my_qzinbinom(c(0.5, 0.9), size = size, prob = prob, pzero = pzero)

[1]  4 15

my_rzinbinom(10, size = size, prob = prob, pzero = pzero)

 [1]  2  9  6  7  6 16  7  1  9  3


The function of RTMBdist gives the same probabilities as ours, which is a useful check of any function that you write:

# Compare our probability mass function with dzinbinom() of RTMBdist.
my_dzinbinom(0:3, size = size, prob = prob, pzero = pzero)

[1] 0.28000 0.04800 0.05760 0.06144

dzinbinom(x = 0:3, size = size, prob = prob, zeroprob = pzero)

[1] 0.28000 0.04800 0.05760 0.06144








NoteUsing your own distribution in a negative log-likelihood



A mass or density function that you write yourself can be used as the likelihood of a model fitted with MakeADFun(), as long as RTMB is able to differentiate it automatically (the gradient that optim() receives as obj$gr; see Chapter 6). The functions above meet this requirement because they only use arithmetic and dnbinom(), which RTMB knows how to differentiate, and because the condition of their ifelse() depends on the data (x == 0) and not on a parameter. A function that branches on a parameter, calls a function of another package that RTMB does not know, or calls a function with its package prefix (such as stats::dnbinom(), which forces the version that cannot be differentiated) may need additional steps. The same holds for the functions that simulate from the model with obj$simulate() or calculate residuals, which need extra code in your function. The article Adding a distribution of the RTMBdist documentation explains these steps, among them how to write conditions with arithmetic indicators such as smaller() and greater() instead of if and ifelse(), how to keep a function stable when it is evaluated at the boundary of its support, and how to test its gradient. The article is written for those who add a distribution to the package, and the functions of this section do not follow all its recommendations.

title: Distributions
text:
Footnotes


RTMB also has dcompois(), whose argument mode is \(\lambda^{1/\nu}\).↩︎

title: Chapter 8: Numerical optimisation
text:
The exercises take three fits that go wrong: the growth curve of loblolly pines with complete pooling (Exercise 1, from Exercise 1 of the Chapter 7 practical), a Gamma model of the body masses of Adelie penguins (Exercise 2) and the REML fits of a simulation of the variance among sites (Exercise 3, from Exercise 5 of the Chapter 7 practical). Each exercise is a full diagnosis in four steps: the symptom, a fit from plausible starting values that reports convergence code 0; the diagnosis, with the checks of the theory; the remedy; and the confirmation that the remedy found the maximum. All three exercises are the core of the practical. Work through the first exercise, which is worked in full on this page, before trying the other two. The ideas and tools are introduced in the Chapter 8 theory.
As in the theory, every model is written and fitted with the packages RTMB and RTMBdist. Exercise 1 also uses the package DEoptim for differential evolution, which you need to install once with install.packages("DEoptim"); we call its functions with the prefix DEoptim::, without attaching the package. Load RTMB first and RTMBdist second:
# Load RTMB first and RTMBdist second.
library(RTMB)
library(RTMBdist)

title: Chapter 8: Numerical optimisation
text:
1.1 Solution

1.1.1 Question 1
We load the data and keep the age and the height of each measurement; this model does not need the tree. The NLL is the one of Chapter 7:

# Loblolly pines (see ?Loblolly), as an ordinary data frame.
data(Loblolly, package = "datasets")
pines = as.data.frame(Loblolly)

# List of data: the age (years) and the height (ft) of each measurement.
pine_data = list(age = pines$age, height = pines$height)

# Negative log-likelihood with one growth curve for all the trees (complete pooling).
pooled_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  A = exp(log_A)
  k = exp(log_k)
  sd_obs = exp(log_sd_obs)
  # Expected height at the age of each measurement.
  mu = A * (1 - exp(-k * (age - t0)))
  -sum(dnorm(x = height, mean = mu, sd = sd_obs, log = TRUE))
}

We process the NLL with the starting values of Chapter 7 and fit it. The second fit uses the same object, with its starting values on the optimised scales given to optim():

# Connect a likelihood to a data set.
cmb = function(f, d) function(p) f(p, d)

# Process the NLL with the starting values of Chapter 7, and fit it.
pine_start = list(log_A = log(80), log_k = log(0.05), t0 = 2, log_sd_obs = log(2))
pooled_obj = MakeADFun(cmb(pooled_nll, pine_data), pine_start, silent = TRUE)
pooled_fit = optim(
  par = pooled_obj$par,
  fn = pooled_obj$fn,
  gr = pooled_obj$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)

# The same starting values with k = 0.1/year, on the optimised scales.
fast_start = c(log_A = log(80), log_k = log(0.1), t0 = 2, log_sd_obs = log(2))
fast_fit = optim(par = fast_start, fn = pooled_obj$fn, gr = pooled_obj$gr, method = "BFGS")

A small function returns the estimates of a fit on the original scale, so that we can compare the two fits in one table:

# Estimates on the original scale: A and sd_obs in ft, k in 1/year, t0 in years.
pine_estimates = function(fit) {
  c(
    A = exp(fit$par[["log_A"]]),
    k = exp(fit$par[["log_k"]]),
    t0 = fit$par[["t0"]],
    sd_obs = exp(fit$par[["log_sd_obs"]])
  )
}

# Convergence code, minimum of the NLL and estimates of the two fits.
signif(rbind(
  chapter_7 = c(convergence = pooled_fit$convergence, nll = pooled_fit$value,
                pine_estimates(pooled_fit)),
  fast_rate = c(convergence = fast_fit$convergence, nll = fast_fit$value,
                pine_estimates(fast_fit))
), 4)

          convergence   nll         A         k    t0 sd_obs
chapter_7           0 162.8 1.023e+02 3.892e-02 2.059  1.681
fast_rate           0 425.5 1.546e-08 3.583e-06 3.242 38.340

# Root mean square of the heights (ft).
sqrt(mean(pine_data$height^2))

[1] 38.33751


Both fits report convergence code 0. The first reaches the estimates of Chapter 7, with a minimum of the NLL of 162.82. The second stops at 425.49, 263 units higher, with an asymptote of about \(1.5\times10^{-8}\) ft and a rate of about \(3.6\times10^{-6}\)/year. Its curve is practically zero at every age, and its standard deviation, 38.3 ft, is the root mean square of the heights: the spread of the 84 heights around a curve of zero. This is the curve at zero that the CO₂ model of the theory reached from a high asymptote. The plot shows the two curves (Figure 1):

# Growth curve: asymptote A, rate k and age t0 at which the height is zero.
growth = function(t, A = 1, k = 1, t0 = 0) {
  A * (1 - exp(-k * (t - t0)))
}

# Measurements, and the curves of the two fits.
chapter_7_est = pine_estimates(pooled_fit)
fast_est = pine_estimates(fast_fit)
plot(height ~ age, data = pine_data, ylim = c(0, 65), xlab = "Age (years)",
     ylab = "Height (ft)")
curve(growth(x, A = chapter_7_est[["A"]], k = chapter_7_est[["k"]], t0 = chapter_7_est[["t0"]]),
      add = TRUE, col = "#D55E00")
curve(growth(x, A = fast_est[["A"]], k = fast_est[["k"]], t0 = fast_est[["t0"]]),
      add = TRUE, lty = 2)
legend("topleft", legend = c("Starting values of Chapter 7", "Start with k = 0.1/year"),
       col = c("#D55E00", "black"), lty = c(1, 2), bty = "n")







Figure 1: Height of 14 loblolly pines against age, with the curve of the fit from the starting values of Chapter 7 (solid line) and of the fit from the start with k = 0.1/year (dashed line, at zero).







1.1.2 Question 2
We look at the solution on the optimised scales, the gradient there and sdreport(). The object has been evaluated at many points, so we pass the values of this fit to sdreport() with par.fixed, as in the theory:

# The solution on the optimised scales, and the gradient there.
fast_fit$par

     log_A      log_k         t0 log_sd_obs 
-17.985311 -12.539391   3.241657   3.646429 

pooled_obj$gr(fast_fit$par)

              [,1]          [,2]         [,3]         [,4]
[1,] -1.504959e-12 -1.504912e-12 1.024158e-13 4.716017e-06

# sdreport() at the values of this fit.
fast_sd = sdreport(pooled_obj, par.fixed = fast_fit$par)
fast_sd

sdreport(.) result
             Estimate Std. Error
log_A      -17.985311        NaN
log_k      -12.539391        NaN
t0           3.241657        NaN
log_sd_obs   3.646429        NaN
Warning:
Hessian of fixed effects was not positive definite.
Maximum gradient component: 4.716017e-06 


On the optimised scales, \(\log(A)\) is about \(-18\) and \(\log(k)\) about \(-12.5\): both parameters ran towards zero, which lies at \(-\infty\) on the log scale. The gradient is tiny (its largest element, for \(\log(\sigma_{\mathrm{obs}})\), is about \(5\times10^{-6}\)), so the gradient alone does not reveal the problem. sdreport() does: the Hessian is not positive definite and no standard error can be calculated.
The slice fixes the other three parameters where each fit stopped and varies the rate between 0.02 and 0.08/year, with a for loop over pooled_obj$fn(). We draw each slice relative to the log-likelihood where its fit stopped:

# Slices along log(k) through the two fits: the other parameters stay where each fit stopped.
log_k_grid = seq(from = log(0.02), to = log(0.08), length.out = 301)
slice_chapter_7 = rep(NA, times = length(log_k_grid))
slice_fast = rep(NA, times = length(log_k_grid))
for (i in seq_along(log_k_grid)) {
  par_chapter_7 = pooled_fit$par
  par_chapter_7[["log_k"]] = log_k_grid[i]
  par_fast = fast_fit$par
  par_fast[["log_k"]] = log_k_grid[i]
  # Relative log-likelihood: the difference from the log-likelihood where the fit stopped.
  slice_chapter_7[i] = -pooled_obj$fn(par_chapter_7) + pooled_fit$value
  slice_fast[i] = -pooled_obj$fn(par_fast) + fast_fit$value
}

# Both slices against the rate, on a logarithmic axis.
plot(exp(log_k_grid), slice_chapter_7, type = "l", log = "x", ylim = c(-20, 2),
     col = "#D55E00", xlab = "Rate, k (1/year)", ylab = "Relative log-likelihood")
lines(exp(log_k_grid), slice_fast, lty = 2)
legend("bottomleft", legend = c("Starting values of Chapter 7", "Start with k = 0.1/year"),
       col = c("#D55E00", "black"), lty = c(1, 2), bty = "n")







Figure 2: Slices of the relative log-likelihood along the rate k, through the fit from the starting values of Chapter 7 (solid line) and through the fit from the start with k = 0.1/year (dashed line); the other parameters are fixed where each fit stopped.





The slice through the first fit has a sharp peak at the estimate of the rate, 0.039/year (sharp because the asymptote and \(t_0\) stay fixed, so a small change of the rate moves the whole curve away from the data). The slice through the second fit is flat: when the asymptote is practically zero, the curve stays at zero whatever the rate, so the NLL does not depend on \(k\). The same holds for \(t_0\), and for the asymptote itself over many orders of magnitude, because a curve of \(10^{-8}\) ft and one of \(10^{-2}\) ft are both zero compared with the heights. These flat directions are why the Hessian is not positive definite. So the estimates on the optimised scales, sdreport() and the slice reveal the problem, and the gradient and the convergence code do not.
How did the search get there? The gradient at the starting values of the second fit is:

# Gradient at the starting values with k = 0.1/year.
pooled_obj$gr(fast_start)

         [,1]     [,2]     [,3]      [,4]
[1,] 13533.96 6194.055 -751.298 -3754.323


Its elements are in the thousands. With \(k=0.1\)/year the curve lies well above the heights of the middle ages, and with a standard deviation of 2 ft every such difference weighs heavily in the NLL. The first step of BFGS goes along the negative gradient (theory), so it starts with a change of thousands of units in \(\log(A)\). The line search shortens the step until the NLL falls, and the first point where it falls already has an asymptote of practically zero: a curve of zero with a large standard deviation describes the heights better than the starting curve with \(\sigma_{\mathrm{obs}}=2\) ft. From there no slope leads back.


1.1.3 Question 3
The box is given on the optimised scales, in the order of the parameters of pooled_obj. The loop draws one set of starting values with runif() in each repetition, fits the model from it and stores the minimum of the NLL, the convergence code and the estimates on the optimised scales; the seed is set once, before the loop:

# Box of plausible starting values on the optimised scales: log asymptote, log rate,
# age at zero height and log standard deviation.
start_lower = c(log(30), log(0.005), -5, log(0.5))
start_upper = c(log(300), log(0.5), 5, log(20))

# 20 fits from random starting values within the box.
n_starts = 20
multi_results = data.frame(
  nll = rep(NA, n_starts),
  convergence = NA,
  log_A = NA, log_k = NA, t0 = NA, log_sd_obs = NA
)
set.seed(811)
for (i in 1:n_starts) {
  start = runif(4, min = start_lower, max = start_upper)
  names(start) = names(pooled_obj$par)
  fit = optim(par = start, fn = pooled_obj$fn, gr = pooled_obj$gr, method = "BFGS")
  multi_results[i, ] = c(fit$value, fit$convergence, fit$par)
}

# Where the 20 fits ended: minimum of the NLL (rounded) against the convergence code.
table(nll = round(multi_results$nll, 1), convergence = multi_results$convergence)

       convergence
nll      0
  162.8  5
  373.1  2
  425.5 12
  551.2  1


All 20 fits report code 0, but only 5 reach the lowest NLL, 162.8. The others end in three places. Twelve stop at the curve at zero of question 1 (425.5). Two stop at 373.1, with the rate run towards infinity, which makes the curve a constant; the estimates on the optimised scales show that its asymptote is the mean of the heights:

# Estimates of the fits that ended at 373.1, and the mean of the heights (ft).
multi_results[round(multi_results$nll, 1) == 373.1, ]

       nll convergence    log_A    log_k        t0 log_sd_obs
3 373.1119           0 3.477059 22.10266 0.6810957    3.02287
7 373.1119           0 3.477059 21.80525 1.1916336    3.02287

mean(pine_data$height)

[1] 32.3644


The asymptote of these fits is \(e^{3.477}\approx32.4\) ft, the mean of the 84 heights, and \(\log(k)\) is about 22. The last fit (551.2) ran far away. These are the failures of the theory again: the curve at zero, the constant curve and a search that runs away. We restart BFGS from the best of the 20 fits:

# Restart BFGS from the best of the 20 fits.
best = which.min(multi_results$nll)
best_start = unlist(multi_results[best, names(pooled_obj$par)])
best_fit = optim(par = best_start, fn = pooled_obj$fn, gr = pooled_obj$gr, method = "BFGS")
c(convergence = best_fit$convergence, nll = best_fit$value)

convergence         nll 
      0.000     162.817 


The restart stays at 162.82, the minimum of the first fit of question 1. Five of 20 starts is a quarter, so in this model a single fit from random starting values in this box fails more often than not; the agreement of five fits on the same minimum, with nothing lower, is evidence that it is the global minimum.


1.1.4 Question 4
nlminb() takes the starting values, the NLL and the gradient of the same object:

# nlminb() from the start with k = 0.1/year.
fast_nlminb = nlminb(start = fast_start, objective = pooled_obj$fn, gradient = pooled_obj$gr)
fast_nlminb[c("objective", "convergence", "message", "evaluations")]

$objective
[1] 162.817

$convergence
[1] 0

$message
[1] "relative convergence (4)"

$evaluations
function gradient 
      33       23 


From the starting values at which BFGS stopped at the curve of zero, nlminb() reaches the minimum of 162.82, because it controls the length of its steps differently and does not make the long first step of BFGS. Differential evolution needs no starting values, only the box:

# Differential evolution within the box of question 3.
set.seed(812)
pine_de = DEoptim::DEoptim(
  fn = pooled_obj$fn,
  lower = start_lower,
  upper = start_upper,
  control = DEoptim::DEoptim.control(NP = 40, itermax = 200, trace = FALSE)
)
c(nll = pine_de$optim$bestval, evaluations = pine_de$optim$nfeval)

        nll evaluations 
    162.817    8040.000 


Its best member reaches the minimum as well, after 8,040 evaluations of the NLL. We refine it with BFGS, giving the elements of the best member the names of the parameters:

# Refine the best member with BFGS.
de_start = pine_de$optim$bestmem
names(de_start) = names(pooled_obj$par)
pine_de_fit = optim(par = de_start, fn = pooled_obj$fn, gr = pooled_obj$gr, method = "BFGS")
c(convergence = pine_de_fit$convergence, nll = pine_de_fit$value)

convergence         nll 
      0.000     162.817 


BFGS stops at once at 162.82. Multiple starts, nlminb() and differential evolution all reach the same minimum, which none of the searches has gone below.


1.1.5 Question 5
We diagnose the restart of question 3 as in the theory and compare its estimates with those of Chapter 7:

# Largest absolute gradient and sdreport() at the best fit.
max(abs(pooled_obj$gr(best_fit$par)))

[1] 1.196019e-05

best_sd = sdreport(pooled_obj, par.fixed = best_fit$par)
best_sd$pdHess

[1] TRUE

summary(best_sd)

             Estimate Std. Error
log_A       4.6275393 0.05172560
log_k      -3.2461303 0.07948142
t0          2.0589563 0.11578222
log_sd_obs  0.5193593 0.07715165

# Estimates on the original scale: the best fit and the fit from the start of Chapter 7.
rbind(best = pine_estimates(best_fit), chapter_7 = pine_estimates(pooled_fit))

                 A          k       t0  sd_obs
best      102.2621 0.03892454 2.058956 1.68095
chapter_7 102.2621 0.03892454 2.058956 1.68095


The gradient is close to zero, the Hessian is positive definite and the standard errors are small, so the best fit passes every check. Its estimates agree with those of Chapter 7: an asymptote of 102 ft, a rate of 0.039/year, \(t_0=2.06\) years and a standard deviation of 1.68 ft. The fit of Chapter 7 had found the maximum; the second start of question 1 had not.
In a report we give the estimates of the best fit with their standard errors, and say how we know that it is the maximum: BFGS from one plausible start stopped at a curve of zero with code 0, 5 of 20 random starts reached the same minimum and none went lower, and nlminb() and differential evolution confirmed it.

title: Chapter 7: Grouped ecological response curves — solutions
text:
The fully worked first exercise is on the student practical page. These solutions use the same data, tasks and seeds as Exercises 2–5 on that page. Exercises 1 to 4 are the core of the practical and Exercise 5 is extra practice.
As on that page, we load RTMB first and RTMBdist second, and define the helper cmb() that connects a likelihood to a data set:
# Load RTMB first and RTMBdist second.
library(RTMB)
library(RTMBdist)

# Connect a likelihood to a data set.
cmb = function(f, d) function(p) f(p, d)

title: Chapter 7: Grouped ecological response curves — solutions
text:
1.1 Solution

1.1.1 Question 1
For a given deviation \(u\), the number of survivors of tank \(i\) is Binomial with the probability \(p_i(u)=1/\left(1+e^{-(\beta_0+\beta_{\mathrm{pred}}P_i+u)}\right)\), the inverse logit of the linear predictor. The deviation is not observed, so the marginal probability of the count averages the Binomial probability over the Normal distribution of the deviations:
\[
P(X_i=x_i)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
\binom{n_i}{x_i}p_i(u)^{x_i}\left(1-p_i(u)\right)^{n_i-x_i}
f(u\mid\sigma_{\mathrm{tank}})\,du,
\]
where \(f(u\mid\sigma_{\mathrm{tank}})\) is the Normal density with mean zero and standard deviation \(\sigma_{\mathrm{tank}}\). This integral has no closed form, so RTMB approximates it with the Laplace approximation.
Each tank gives one count, but the count is made of \(n_i\) tadpoles whose fates are independent for a given probability. For a given probability the Binomial distribution fixes how much the count can vary, so any variation among tanks of the same treatment beyond that is variation in the probability of survival among tanks, and that is what the random effect describes: the conditions that the tadpoles of a tank share and that other tanks do not. The Beta distribution of a Beta-Binomial model describes the same thing, so the two models answer the same question. They differ in three ways. The probabilities of the tanks follow a Normal distribution on the logit scale in one model and a Beta distribution on the probability scale in the other, which are different shapes. The integral of the Beta-Binomial model has a closed form, whereas that of the mixed model is approximated. And \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_{\mathrm{pred}}\) do not mean the same thing: in the mixed model they give the probability of a typical tank, with \(u_i=0\), whereas in the Beta-Binomial model they give the mean probability of the tanks (question 4).


1.1.2 Question 2
The list of data holds the number of survivors and of tadpoles of each tank and an indicator of predators. The joint NLL has the density of the deviations first, as in the theory:

# Load the reed frog data and put the survivors, the initial number of tadpoles and an
# indicator of predators (1 with predators, 0 without) in a list of data.
data(ReedfrogPred, package = "emdbook")
tank_data = list(
  survivors = ReedfrogPred$surv,
  tadpoles = ReedfrogPred$density,
  predators = as.numeric(ReedfrogPred$pred == "pred")
)

# Joint NLL of the Binomial model with a random effect for each tank on the logit scale.
tank_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  sd_tank = exp(log_sd_tank)
  # Minus the log density of the deviations of the tanks, before they are used.
  nll = -sum(dnorm(x = u, mean = 0, sd = sd_tank, log = TRUE))
  # Probability of survival in each tank, and minus the log probability of its survivors.
  p = plogis(beta_0 + beta_pred * predators + u)
  nll - sum(dbinom(x = survivors, size = tadpoles, prob = p, log = TRUE))
}

We start from a probability of 0.5 in both treatments (logit 0), a standard deviation among tanks of 0.5 on the logit scale and one deviation of zero for each of the 48 tanks:

# Process the joint NLL, integrating out the deviations of the tanks, and fit it.
tank_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(tank_nll, tank_data),
  list(beta_0 = 0, beta_pred = 0, log_sd_tank = log(0.5), u = rep(0, 48)),
  random = "u",
  silent = TRUE
)
tank_fit = optim(
  par = tank_obj$par,
  fn = tank_obj$fn,
  gr = tank_obj$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)
tank_fit$convergence

[1] 0

# Standard errors on the optimised scales, and the standard deviation among tanks.
tank_sd = sdreport(tank_obj)
summary(tank_sd, select = "fixed")

              Estimate Std. Error
beta_0       2.6980077  0.2422542
beta_pred   -2.6778992  0.3043952
log_sd_tank -0.2537464  0.1721570

exp(tank_fit$par[["log_sd_tank"]])

[1] 0.7758885


The fit converged. Predators lower the logit of the probability of survival of a typical tank by 2.68 (standard error 0.30), and the tanks vary around their typical value with a standard deviation of 0.78 on the logit scale.
In the Beta-Binomial model of Chapter 6, the probability \(p_i\) is the mean of a Beta distribution with precision \(\kappa\), whose shape parameters are \(\kappa p_i\) and \(\kappa(1-p_i)\). We give \(p_i\) the same linear predictor on the logit scale, without the deviations:

# NLL of the Beta-Binomial model: the logit of the mean probability depends on predators.
betabinomial_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  p = plogis(beta_0 + beta_pred * predators)
  kappa = exp(log_kappa)
  -sum(dbetabinom(
    x = survivors, size = tadpoles, shape1 = kappa * p, shape2 = kappa * (1 - p), log = TRUE
  ))
}

# Process the NLL, starting from logit 0 and a precision of 10, and fit it.
betabinomial_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(betabinomial_nll, tank_data),
  list(beta_0 = 0, beta_pred = 0, log_kappa = log(10)),
  silent = TRUE
)
betabinomial_fit = optim(
  par = betabinomial_obj$par,
  fn = betabinomial_obj$fn,
  gr = betabinomial_obj$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)
betabinomial_fit$convergence

[1] 0

# Estimates: the logits, and the precision on the original scale.
betabinomial_fit$par

   beta_0 beta_pred log_kappa 
 2.213874 -2.207554  2.257509 

exp(betabinomial_fit$par[["log_kappa"]])

[1] 9.559244


This fit converged too. The effect of predators on the logit scale is smaller (\(-2.21\)), and the precision is about 9.6, which allows much variation among tanks (Chapter 6 found \(\hat\kappa\approx26\) for the tanks of the functional response experiment).


1.1.3 Question 3
Both models have \(K=3\) parameters: \(\beta_0\), \(\beta_{\mathrm{pred}}\) and either \(\sigma_{\mathrm{tank}}\) or \(\kappa\). The minimum of each NLL is minus a maximum log-likelihood:

# AIC of the two models, with K = 3 parameters each.
K_tanks = c(mixed = length(tank_fit$par), betabinomial = length(betabinomial_fit$par))
nll_tanks = c(mixed = tank_fit$value, betabinomial = betabinomial_fit$value)
2 * K_tanks + 2 * nll_tanks

       mixed betabinomial 
    225.7998     233.9377 


AIC prefers the model with Normal tank deviations on the logit scale by about 8 units. AIC can compare the two models because both likelihoods are probabilities of the same thing: the counts of the 48 tanks, each with the variation of its probability integrated out. In the Beta-Binomial model the integral is done exactly, and in the mixed model by the Laplace approximation, but both are marginal likelihoods of a tank whose probability is not known. Neither model is a special case of the other at the boundary of a parameter, so the problem of the comparison of a mixed model with complete pooling does not arise. The difference does carry the error of the Laplace approximation, which the theory says is less accurate for counts near their bounds, as in the tanks without predators where nearly every tadpole survived.


1.1.4 Question 4
The probability of survival of a typical tank is the inverse logit of the linear predictor with \(u_i=0\). The mean probability over tanks averages the inverse logit over the distribution of the deviations, which we approximate by the average over one million simulated deviations:

# Probability of survival of a typical tank, without and with predators.
logit_typical = c(
  no = tank_fit$par[["beta_0"]],
  pred = tank_fit$par[["beta_0"]] + tank_fit$par[["beta_pred"]]
)
plogis(logit_typical)

      no     pred 
0.936909 0.505027 

# Mean probability of survival over tanks, from one million simulated tank deviations.
set.seed(seed = 721)
tank_deviations = rnorm(n = 1e6, mean = 0, sd = exp(tank_fit$par[["log_sd_tank"]]))
c(
  no = mean(plogis(logit_typical[["no"]] + tank_deviations)),
  pred = mean(plogis(logit_typical[["pred"]] + tank_deviations))
)

       no      pred 
0.9211021 0.5048173 

# Mean probability of survival under the Beta-Binomial model.
plogis(c(
  no = betabinomial_fit$par[["beta_0"]],
  pred = betabinomial_fit$par[["beta_0"]] + betabinomial_fit$par[["beta_pred"]]
))

       no      pred 
0.9014885 0.5015801 


Without predators, a typical tank has a probability of survival of 0.937, but the mean over tanks is 0.921. With predators both are about 0.505. The inverse logit is a curve: it is almost a straight line around a probability of 0.5, where deviations of the same size above and below the typical value change the probability by about the same amount, so they average out. Near one it flattens, so a tank with a negative deviation loses more probability than a tank with an equal positive deviation gains, and the mean lies below the typical value. This is Jensen’s inequality (see the box in Chapter 4), as for the median and the mean asymptote of the theory. The typical tank answers the question of what happens in a tank of median conditions; the mean answers the question of what fraction of the tadpoles in many tanks of equal size is expected to survive. The Beta-Binomial model gives mean probabilities of 0.901 and 0.502: it agrees with the mixed model with predators, and without predators it gives a lower mean, because its Beta distribution of the tank probabilities has another shape than the Normal distribution on the logit scale.


1.1.5 Question 5
The predicted tank effects are the rows of summary() with select = "random", one row for each tank, with their standard errors:

# Predicted tank effects and the range of their standard errors.
tank_effects = summary(tank_sd, select = "random")
range(tank_effects[, "Std. Error"])

[1] 0.3484849 0.6924917


With the effects in tank_effects, the code given with the questions draws the plot, and tapply() calculates the mean predicted effect of each combination:

# Combination of predators and size of each tank, its symbol and a small shift along x.
combination = paste(ReedfrogPred$pred, ReedfrogPred$size)
combination_names = c("no small", "no big", "pred small", "pred big")
combination_number = match(combination, combination_names)
shift = c(-1.2, -0.4, 0.4, 1.2)
symbols = c(1, 2, 16, 17)

# Predicted effects against the shifted densities; ylim leaves room for the legend above
# the points.
plot(ReedfrogPred$density + shift[combination_number], tank_effects[, "Estimate"],
     pch = symbols[combination_number], ylim = c(-1.6, 2.4),
     xlab = "Initial density (tadpoles per tank)", ylab = "Predicted tank effect (logit)")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
legend("top", legend = c("No predators, small", "No predators, big",
                         "Predators, small", "Predators, big"),
       pch = symbols, ncol = 2, bty = "n")

# Mean predicted effect for each combination of predators and size.
tapply(tank_effects[, "Estimate"], list(ReedfrogPred$size, ReedfrogPred$pred), mean)

               no       pred
small -0.09486863  0.3197643
big   -0.02280317 -0.3243567








Figure 1: Predicted effect of each of the 48 tanks on the logit scale of the probability of survival, against the initial density of tadpoles, for the four combinations of predators and size of the tadpoles (shifted slightly along the axis to avoid overlap).





Without predators the predicted effects scatter around zero, with no difference between the two sizes. With predators, the tanks with small tadpoles tend to have positive effects (a mean of 0.32 on the logit scale) and those with big tadpoles negative ones (a mean of \(-0.32\)), most clearly at densities of 25 and 35 tadpoles, whereas at a density of 10 most tanks with predators have positive effects, whatever the size. So the size of the tadpoles, and perhaps the density, seem to explain part of the variation among the tanks with predators. They could enter the model as group-level predictors on the logit scale, with their interactions with predators, as origin and chilling did in the theory, and the models could then be compared with this one by AIC. The plot suggests this, but it does not show it: the predicted effects are shrunk towards zero and have standard errors between 0.35 and 0.69, so a pattern among them is only a lead to follow with a model.

title: Chapter 7: Grouped ecological response curves — solutions
text:
2.1 Solution

2.1.1 Question 1
The observational unit is one visit of a parent to a nest, and the group is the nest: the visits to a nest share its brood, its site and its parents. The levels of Nest are the names of the nests in alphabetical order, so as.numeric() gives the position of the nest of each visit among them, a number from 1 to 27, and levels(Owls$Nest) gives the names in the same order. We put the calls, an indicator of satiated broods, the time of arrival and the nest in a list of data. table() of the index of the nests counts the visits of each nest, and table() of the index and the indicator of satiated broods counts the visits of each nest under each treatment, so a zero in it would be a nest without visits under one of the treatments:

# Load the owl data and put the calls, the food treatment (1 satiated, 0 deprived), the
# time of arrival (hours) and the nest of each visit in a list of data.
data(Owls, package = "glmmTMB")
nest_names = levels(Owls$Nest)
owl_data = list(
  calls = Owls$SiblingNegotiation,
  satiated = as.numeric(Owls$FoodTreatment == "Satiated"),
  time = Owls$ArrivalTime,
  nest = as.numeric(Owls$Nest)
)

# Number of visits of each nest.
n_visits = as.numeric(table(owl_data$nest))
range(n_visits)

[1]  4 52

# Visits of each nest (rows) under each food treatment (columns 0 deprived, 1 satiated),
# and the number of zeros in this table.
nest_food = table(owl_data$nest, owl_data$satiated)
sum(nest_food == 0)

[1] 0


The table has no zeros, so every nest has visits under both treatments: the food treatment changes within a nest and is measured on the visits, as the time of arrival is. The number of nestlings is measured on the nests: it is the same at every visit to a nest. The nests have between 4 and 52 visits, so they contribute very different amounts of information.

# Calls against the time of arrival, with a filled symbol for satiated broods.
plot(calls ~ time, data = owl_data, pch = ifelse(owl_data$satiated == 1, 16, 1),
     xlab = "Time of arrival (hours)", ylab = "Number of calls")
legend("topright", legend = c("Deprived", "Satiated"), pch = c(1, 16), bty = "n")







Figure 2: Number of calls of barn owl nestlings at 599 visits of a parent, against the time of arrival of the parent, for deprived (open circles) and satiated broods (filled circles).





The counts vary widely at every time, from zero to more than 30 calls, and many visits have no calls at all. Satiated broods tend to call less, and the calls seem to become fewer later in the night.


2.1.2 Question 2
The model without nest deviations is a Negative Binomial model with the log mean as a linear function of the two predictors, with the time measured from midnight so that \(\mu_0\) is the expected number at midnight. dnbinom2() takes the mean and the shape:

# NLL of the Negative Binomial model without nest deviations.
owl_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  mu = exp(log_mu0 + beta_sat * satiated + beta_time * (time - 24))
  -sum(dnbinom2(x = calls, mu = mu, size = exp(log_k), log = TRUE))
}

# Joint NLL with a random effect for each nest on the log scale of the mean.
nest_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  sd_nest = exp(log_sd_nest)
  # Minus the log density of the deviations of the nests, before they are used.
  nll = -sum(dnorm(x = u, mean = 0, sd = sd_nest, log = TRUE))
  # u[nest] is the deviation of the nest of each visit.
  mu = exp(log_mu0 + beta_sat * satiated + beta_time * (time - 24) + u[nest])
  nll - sum(dnbinom2(x = calls, mu = mu, size = exp(log_k), log = TRUE))
}

We start from a mean of 5 calls, no effects, a shape of 1 and, for the mixed model, a standard deviation among nests of 0.5 on the log scale:

# Starting values shared by the two models.
owl_start = list(log_mu0 = log(5), beta_sat = 0, beta_time = 0, log_k = 0)

# Fit the model without nest deviations.
owl_obj = MakeADFun(cmb(owl_nll, owl_data), owl_start, silent = TRUE)
owl_fit = optim(par = owl_obj$par, fn = owl_obj$fn, gr = owl_obj$gr, method = "BFGS")

# Fit the model with nest deviations, integrating them out.
nest_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(nest_nll, owl_data),
  c(owl_start, list(log_sd_nest = log(0.5), u = rep(0, 27))),
  random = "u",
  silent = TRUE
)
nest_fit = optim(par = nest_obj$par, fn = nest_obj$fn, gr = nest_obj$gr, method = "BFGS")
c(owl = owl_fit$convergence, nest = nest_fit$convergence)

 owl nest 
   0    0 


Both fits converged. The effects are on the log scale of the mean, so their exponentials are the factors by which they multiply the expected number of calls, and we calculate their Wald intervals on the log scale and transform the endpoints back:

# Estimates and standard errors of the model with nest deviations.
nest_sd = sdreport(nest_obj)
nest_summary = summary(nest_sd, select = "fixed")

# Factors of food and of one hour of time, with 95% Wald intervals from the log scale.
critical_value = qnorm(p = 0.975)
effect_rows = c("beta_sat", "beta_time")
exp(cbind(
  factor = nest_summary[effect_rows, "Estimate"],
  lower = nest_summary[effect_rows, "Estimate"] -
    critical_value * nest_summary[effect_rows, "Std. Error"],
  upper = nest_summary[effect_rows, "Estimate"] +
    critical_value * nest_summary[effect_rows, "Std. Error"]
))

             factor     lower     upper
beta_sat  0.5003787 0.4057774 0.6170349
beta_time 0.8910049 0.8479723 0.9362214

# Typical mean at midnight (deprived), the two factors and the shape k, without and with
# nest deviations: the exponentials of the estimates.
owl_rows = c("log_mu0", "beta_sat", "beta_time", "log_k")
owl_compare = exp(rbind(without = owl_fit$par[owl_rows], with = nest_fit$par[owl_rows]))
colnames(owl_compare) = c("mu0", "food_factor", "time_factor", "k")
owl_compare

             mu0 food_factor time_factor         k
without 8.737602   0.6153939   0.8851365 0.7691247
with    8.504022   0.5003787   0.8910049 0.8894070

# Standard deviation among nests (log scale of the mean).
exp(nest_fit$par[["log_sd_nest"]])

[1] 0.4164909

# AIC of the two models.
K_owls = c(owl = length(owl_fit$par), nest = length(nest_fit$par))
nll_owls = c(owl = owl_fit$value, nest = nest_fit$value)
2 * K_owls + 2 * nll_owls

     owl     nest 
3502.633 3478.379 


In a typical nest, satiated broods make half as many calls as deprived broods (a factor of 0.50, with a 95% Wald interval from 0.41 to 0.62), and each hour later in the night the expected number of calls falls by about 11% (a factor of 0.89 for each hour, from 0.85 to 0.94). A deprived brood in a typical nest makes about 8.5 calls at a visit at midnight. The model with nest deviations has an AIC about 24 units lower; as in Exercise 1, the model without them is the special case \(\sigma_{\mathrm{nest}}=0\) at the boundary, so the difference is an approximate guide, but a large one. Without nest deviations the effect of food is weaker (a factor of 0.62 against 0.50) and the shape \(k\) is smaller (0.77 against 0.89), whereas the effect of time hardly changes: part of the variation among nests was counted as variation among visits, and part of it was attributed to the food treatment.
\(\hat\sigma_{\mathrm{nest}}\approx0.42\) is a standard deviation on the log scale of the mean. It is not small, so it is no longer close to a coefficient of variation. A nest deviation multiplies the expected number of calls, so in 95% of new nests the expected number lies between the typical value multiplied by \(e^{-1.96\,\hat\sigma_{\mathrm{nest}}}\) and by \(e^{1.96\,\hat\sigma_{\mathrm{nest}}}\). For a deprived brood at midnight the typical value is \(\hat\mu_0\):

# Factors that give the range of 95% of new nests, and the range of the expected number
# of calls at midnight of a deprived brood.
new_nest_factor = exp(qnorm(p = c(0.025, 0.975)) * exp(nest_fit$par[["log_sd_nest"]]))
new_nest_factor

[1] 0.4420611 2.2621309

exp(nest_fit$par[["log_mu0"]]) * new_nest_factor

[1]  3.759297 19.237211


In 95% of nests the expected number of calls lies between 0.44 and 2.3 times that of the typical nest: at midnight, between about 4 and 19 calls for a deprived brood. So a nest near the upper end of this range has about five times as many calls as one near the lower end, in the same conditions, which is a larger difference than that between satiated and deprived broods. The range describes the variation among nests at the estimates and leaves out the uncertainty of the estimates themselves.


2.1.3 Question 3
Without pooling, log_mu0 is a vector with one log mean for each nest, and log_mu0[nest] selects the value of the nest of each visit; the effects of food and time and the shape are shared by all the nests:

# NLL with one log mean for each nest (no pooling).
separate_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  mu = exp(log_mu0[nest] + beta_sat * satiated + beta_time * (time - 24))
  -sum(dnbinom2(x = calls, mu = mu, size = exp(log_k), log = TRUE))
}

# Process the NLL with the same starting values, one log mean per nest, and fit it.
separate_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(separate_nll, owl_data),
  list(log_mu0 = rep(log(5), 27), beta_sat = 0, beta_time = 0, log_k = 0),
  silent = TRUE
)
separate_fit = optim(
  par = separate_obj$par,
  fn = separate_obj$fn,
  gr = separate_obj$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)
separate_fit$convergence

[1] 0


The fit converged. The predicted log mean of a nest under the mixed model is \(\log(\hat\mu_0)+\hat u_j\), from the rows of summary() with select = "random". We plot both log means against the number of visits, so the two values of a nest lie above each other:

# Log means without pooling and predicted by the mixed model.
log_mu0_separate = separate_fit$par[names(separate_fit$par) == "log_mu0"]
log_mu0_typical = nest_fit$par[["log_mu0"]]
log_mu0_predicted = log_mu0_typical + summary(nest_sd, select = "random")[, "Estimate"]

plot(n_visits, log_mu0_separate, xlab = "Number of visits",
     ylab = "Log mean number of calls at midnight (deprived)")
points(n_visits, log_mu0_predicted, pch = 16)
abline(h = log_mu0_typical, lty = 2)
legend("bottomright", legend = c("No pooling", "Mixed model"), pch = c(1, 16), bty = "n")

# The two nests with the fewest visits, relative to the typical value.
few_visits = n_visits == min(n_visits)
data.frame(
  nest = nest_names[few_visits],
  separate = log_mu0_separate[few_visits] - log_mu0_typical,
  predicted = log_mu0_predicted[few_visits] - log_mu0_typical
)

   nest    separate   predicted
1 Forel -3.12010430 -0.45675308
2 Sevaz -0.08998133 -0.04912727








Figure 3: Log mean number of calls at midnight of a deprived brood in each of 27 barn owl nests, against the number of visits of the nest: without pooling (open circles) and predicted by the model with nest deviations (filled circles). The dashed line is the typical value of the mixed model.





Every predicted log mean lies between the log mean of the nest without pooling and the typical value: each nest is pulled towards the typical nest. Nests with many visits keep most of their distance from the typical value, and the nests with few visits tend to be pulled further. The clearest case is Forel, one of the two nests with four visits: without pooling its log mean lies 3.1 below the typical value, an expected number of calls about 20 times smaller, and the mixed model predicts a value only 0.46 below it. Four visits with few calls are weak evidence that a nest is that unusual, so the distribution of nests, which says that most nests lie much closer to the typical value, counts for much. The other nest with four visits, Sevaz, moves little, because its own log mean is already close to the typical value. So the size of the pull depends on how far a nest lies from the typical value as well as on its number of visits, and among the nests with 10 to 30 visits the pattern is irregular: their counts are very variable (\(\hat k\approx0.89\)), so the number of visits is only a rough measure of how much a nest tells about itself.

title: Chapter 7: Grouped ecological response curves — solutions
text:
3.1 Solution

3.1.1 Question 1
The site is the group, and both predictors are properties of the sites, so, as in the theory, the list of data holds them as vectors with one value for each site, in the order of the integer index of the sites. site is an ordered factor, so we build the index with match(), numbering the sites in the order in which they first appear, and take the predictors of each site from its first count:

# Spring salamander counts, the index (1 to 23) of the site of each count, and the row of
# the first count of each site.
data(Salamanders, package = "glmmTMB")
spring = Salamanders[Salamanders$spp == "GP", ]
site_names = unique(as.character(spring$site))
site = match(as.character(spring$site), site_names)
first_row = match(seq_along(site_names), site)

# List of data: the counts and their sites, and for each site an indicator of mining
# (1 mined, 0 not mined) and its cover.
salamander_data = list(
  count = spring$count,
  site = site,
  mined = as.numeric(spring$mined[first_row] == "yes"),
  cover = spring$cover[first_row]
)

# Mean count at mined and unmined sites.
tapply(spring$count, spring$mined, mean)

       yes         no 
0.04545455 2.20833333 


The 44 counts at mined sites have a mean of 0.045 salamanders per visit, two salamanders in total, against 2.2 per visit at unmined sites. The NLL calculates the mean of each site and selects it for each count with lambda[site]. We mark the counts with OBS() to simulate from the model:

# NLL of the Poisson model with the effects of mining and cover, without site deviations.
poisson_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  count = OBS(count)
  # Mean count of each site.
  lambda = exp(log_lambda0 + beta_mined * mined + beta_cover * cover)
  -sum(dpois(x = count, lambda = lambda[site], log = TRUE))
}

# Process the NLL, starting from a mean of one and no effects, and fit it.
poisson_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(poisson_nll, salamander_data),
  list(log_lambda0 = 0, beta_mined = 0, beta_cover = 0),
  silent = TRUE
)
poisson_fit = optim(
  par = poisson_obj$par,
  fn = poisson_obj$fn,
  gr = poisson_obj$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)
poisson_fit$convergence

[1] 0


The fit converged. We simulate 1,000 hypothetical samples, calculate the residuals of the counts with the mean of each site as the expected value and integerResponse = TRUE because the counts are whole numbers, and then one residual per site:

# 1,000 hypothetical samples of the 92 counts at the estimates.
n_sim = 1000
poisson_simulations = matrix(NA, nrow = length(salamander_data$count), ncol = n_sim)
set.seed(seed = 741)
for (j in seq_len(n_sim)) {
  poisson_simulations[, j] = poisson_obj$simulate(poisson_fit$par)$count
}

# Expected count of each visit: the mean of its site.
poisson_lambda = exp(
  poisson_fit$par[["log_lambda0"]] +
    poisson_fit$par[["beta_mined"]] * salamander_data$mined +
    poisson_fit$par[["beta_cover"]] * salamander_data$cover
)
poisson_residuals = DHARMa::createDHARMa(
  simulatedResponse = poisson_simulations,
  observedResponse = salamander_data$count,
  fittedPredictedResponse = poisson_lambda[salamander_data$site],
  integerResponse = TRUE
)

# Dispersion statistic, and one residual per site.
DHARMa::testDispersion(poisson_residuals, plot = FALSE)$statistic

dispersion 
  2.246096 

poisson_site_scaled = residuals(
  DHARMa::recalculateResiduals(poisson_residuals, group = salamander_data$site)
)
names(poisson_site_scaled) = site_names
round(poisson_site_scaled, 3)

 VF-1  VF-2  VF-3   R-1   R-2   R-3   R-4   R-5   R-6   R-7  VF-4   R-8   R-9 
0.240 0.995 0.337 0.882 0.893 0.662 0.279 0.729 0.966 0.000 0.388 0.030 0.008 
 R-10  R-11  VF-5  VF-6  R-12  VF-7  VF-9  VF-8 VF-10 VF-11 
0.937 0.402 0.087 0.756 0.816 0.034 0.272 0.795 0.741 0.583 


The counts vary around the means of their sites about 2.2 times as much (as a variance) as in the simulations: the Poisson model with these two predictors leaves much variation unexplained. The residuals of the sites show where it is. Four sites have residuals below 0.05 (R-7, R-8, R-9 and VF-7), and two have residuals above 0.95 (VF-2 and R-6): their counts are lower or higher than in almost all the simulated samples. Among 23 sites we expect about one below 0.05 and one above 0.95. So the sites differ more than mining and cover explain, and treating the four visits to a site as independent hides this: it is the dependence of grouped observations that the theory describes.


3.1.2 Question 2
The joint NLL adds a deviation for each site on the log scale of the mean, with its density first:

# Joint NLL of the Poisson model with a random effect for each site.
site_poisson_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  count = OBS(count)
  sd_site = exp(log_sd_site)
  # Minus the log density of the deviations of the sites, before they are used.
  nll = -sum(dnorm(x = u, mean = 0, sd = sd_site, log = TRUE))
  lambda = exp(log_lambda0 + beta_mined * mined + beta_cover * cover + u)
  nll - sum(dpois(x = count, lambda = lambda[site], log = TRUE))
}

# Process the joint NLL, integrating out the deviations of the sites, and fit it.
site_poisson_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(site_poisson_nll, salamander_data),
  list(log_lambda0 = 0, beta_mined = 0, beta_cover = 0, log_sd_site = log(0.5),
       u = rep(0, 23)),
  random = "u",
  silent = TRUE
)
site_poisson_fit = optim(
  par = site_poisson_obj$par,
  fn = site_poisson_obj$fn,
  gr = site_poisson_obj$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)
site_poisson_fit$convergence

[1] 0


The fit converged. The effects of mining and cover are on the log scale of the mean, so we transform their estimates and the endpoints of their Wald intervals with exp():

# Estimates and standard errors on the optimised scales.
site_poisson_sd = sdreport(site_poisson_obj)
site_poisson_summary = summary(site_poisson_sd, select = "fixed")
site_poisson_summary

              Estimate Std. Error
log_lambda0  0.6326079  0.2041167
beta_mined  -3.7426861  0.7660337
beta_cover   0.1327551  0.1915960
log_sd_site -0.8505659  0.4245552

# Factors of mining and of one unit of cover, with 95% Wald intervals from the log scale
# (critical_value from Exercise 3).
effect_rows = c("beta_mined", "beta_cover")
exp(cbind(
  factor = site_poisson_summary[effect_rows, "Estimate"],
  lower = site_poisson_summary[effect_rows, "Estimate"] -
    critical_value * site_poisson_summary[effect_rows, "Std. Error"],
  upper = site_poisson_summary[effect_rows, "Estimate"] +
    critical_value * site_poisson_summary[effect_rows, "Std. Error"]
))

               factor       lower     upper
beta_mined 0.02369038 0.005278652 0.1063215
beta_cover 1.14197028 0.784454956 1.6624232

# Typical mean at an unmined site of average cover, and the standard deviation among sites.
exp(site_poisson_fit$par[c("log_lambda0", "log_sd_site")])

log_lambda0 log_sd_site 
  1.8825137   0.4271731 

# AIC of the two models.
K_salamanders = c(poisson = length(poisson_fit$par), site = length(site_poisson_fit$par))
nll_salamanders = c(poisson = poisson_fit$value, site = site_poisson_fit$value)
2 * K_salamanders + 2 * nll_salamanders

 poisson     site 
229.1860 226.2415 


A typical unmined site with average cover is expected to give about 1.9 spring salamanders per visit. At a mined site with the same cover the expected count is about 2% of that (a factor of 0.024, with a 95% Wald interval from 0.005 to 0.11). The interval is wide because the effect rests on 44 counts that are almost all zero. One standard deviation more cover multiplies the expected count by about 1.14, but the interval runs from 0.78 to 1.66, so the data say little about the effect of cover. The sites vary around their typical value with a standard deviation of 0.43 on the log scale. The deviations of the mined sites are hardly determined by their counts, which are zeros whatever the deviation, so the variance among sites is informed mostly by the 12 unmined sites. These are observational data, so the effect of mining is an association between mining and the counts, which other differences between the sites could also produce.
The model with site deviations has an AIC about 3 units lower than the model without them. As in Exercise 1, this comparison is at the boundary \(\sigma_{\mathrm{site}}=0\) and only an approximate guide; the residuals of question 1 are a second reason to keep the site deviations.


3.1.3 Question 3
The simulations of the mixed model draw new deviations for the 23 sites and then new counts, and the expected value of a count is the typical mean (\(u_j=0\)) of its site:

# 1,000 hypothetical samples: new site deviations, then new counts for them.
site_poisson_simulations = matrix(NA, nrow = length(salamander_data$count), ncol = n_sim)
set.seed(seed = 742)
for (j in seq_len(n_sim)) {
  site_poisson_simulations[, j] = site_poisson_obj$simulate(site_poisson_fit$par)$count
}

# Expected count of each visit: the typical mean (u = 0) of its site.
site_poisson_lambda = exp(
  site_poisson_fit$par[["log_lambda0"]] +
    site_poisson_fit$par[["beta_mined"]] * salamander_data$mined +
    site_poisson_fit$par[["beta_cover"]] * salamander_data$cover
)
site_poisson_residuals = DHARMa::createDHARMa(
  simulatedResponse = site_poisson_simulations,
  observedResponse = salamander_data$count,
  fittedPredictedResponse = site_poisson_lambda[salamander_data$site],
  integerResponse = TRUE
)

# Dispersion statistic, and one residual per site.
DHARMa::testDispersion(site_poisson_residuals, plot = FALSE)$statistic

dispersion 
  1.544881 

site_scaled = residuals(
  DHARMa::recalculateResiduals(site_poisson_residuals, group = salamander_data$site)
)
names(site_scaled) = site_names
round(site_scaled, 3)

The dispersion statistic falls from 2.2 to 1.5, because the simulations now include the variation among sites. The residuals of the sites are less extreme than in question 1: two sites have residuals below 0.05 (R-7 and R-9) and one above 0.95 (VF-2), close to what we expect among 23 sites. A dispersion statistic above one still suggests that the counts of the visits to one site vary somewhat more than a Poisson distribution allows. The visits differed in conditions that this model leaves out (the data set also records, for example, the days since the last rain and the water temperature of each visit), so predictors measured on the visits, or a Negative Binomial distribution for a given site deviation, are candidates to compare with this model. As always, we read the residuals and the dispersion statistic as exploratory evidence.


3.1.4 Question 4
glmmTMB() fits the same model from a formula: mined + cover are the fixed effects on the log scale of the mean, (1 | site) is a random intercept for each site, and the Poisson family has a log link (see the glmmTMB supplement). It also uses TMB and the Laplace approximation:

# The same model with glmmTMB, called with the prefix so that the package is not attached.
salamander_glmmtmb = glmmTMB::glmmTMB(

  family = poisson,

)

c(glmmtmb = as.numeric(logLik(salamander_glmmtmb)), rtmb = -site_poisson_fit$value)
