title: Introduction to R (solutions)
section: 16.1 Example 1: Deal with warnings and errors
text:
16.1 Example 1: Deal with warnings and errors
Imagine we are adding two vectors and we are getting a warning

a = c(1,2,3)
b = c(4, 5)
a + b

You can safely ignore warnings if you understand what they mean. Otherwise treat them as errors. Assuming you don’t what this is, let’s ask an AI. I type this prompt to the AI:






NotePrompt





I am learning how to program in R. I just had an exercise with code that looks like this:

a = c(1,2,3)
b = c(4, 5)
a + b

And I got this warning: “In a + b : longer object length is not a multiple of shorter object length”
I am not sure what it means and why it was generated. I suspect I did something wrong and I am not getting the result that I want to (even though the code runs). Could you help me understand:

Why was the warning triggered.
How can I fix it.

Note that I do not just care about the solution to the problem but I want to understand why it happens and learn any R related concept that is relevant so that I can be a better programmer.
Please be concise in your answer.



Notice several things:

I include code within fenced quotes (the “```”) which tells the AI that what I type inside those quotes is code.
I also quote the warning message to make sure it understand this is a literal quote.
I give it context (I am student, I am learning R).
I do not just ask for a solution to my problem but explain why it is happening so that I can actually learn.
I am very explicit about what I want to get back (in bullet points).
Finally I ask the AI to be concise. You may or may not need to do this depending on which AI you are using and your own preferences. I find they all tend to talk too much…

This turns my interaction with the AI into an opportunity to learn. An AI can be an amazing personalized tutor (especially at this level). The answer that it give is actually very good, I do not think I could do much better!






NoteAnswer





Yes — this is an important R concept called vector recycling.
1. Why did the warning occur?
In R, + operates element-by-element:

a + b

means roughly:
a:  1  2  3
b:  4  5
    ↓  ↓  ↓
    5  7  ?
But b only has two elements. R therefore recycles b:
a:  1  2  3
b:  4  5  4
    ↓  ↓  ↓
    5  7  7
So R actually returns:

[1] 5 7 7

The warning occurs because the lengths are not compatible for clean recycling:

length(a)  # 3
length(b)  # 2

R’s recycling rule is:

If the longer vector’s length is a multiple of the shorter vector’s length, recycling happens without a warning.

For example:

c(1, 2, 3, 4) + c(10, 20)

[1] 11 22 13 24


gives:
11 22 13 24
because 4 is a multiple of 2.
But 3 is not a multiple of 2, so R warns you that it is doing something potentially unintended.
2. How do you fix it?
That depends on what you intended.
If you wanted to add only corresponding elements, make the vectors the same length:

a = c(1, 2)
b = c(4, 5)

a + b
# 5 7

If you intended b to repeat, make that explicit:

a + rep(b, length.out = length(a))
# 5 7 7

The important R concept
R is vectorized. Operations such as +, -, *, /, and many functions operate on whole vectors rather than requiring loops:

c(1, 2, 3) * 10
# 10 20 30

And when vector lengths differ, R uses recycling. This is very convenient, but it can also silently produce results you didn’t intend.
A good programming habit is therefore: when you see a recycling warning, don’t just suppress it — check whether you actually intended the recycling.

title: Introduction to R (solutions)
text:
16.2 Example 2: Learning a new feature
We have learned how to make scatterplots with ggplot2:

ggplot(iris, aes(x = Petal.Length, y = Sepal.Length, color = Species, shape = Species)) +
  geom_point()

I can see that there are fairly linear responses between Sepal Length and Petal Length. I would like to add some trendlines to the plot describing those linear trends. I have no idea how. I could search online, read some blog or book, or I can ask AI.






NotePrompt





I am a student learning R and I am interesting in becoming better at using ggplot2. I have produced a scatterplot of Sepal Length vs Petal Length for different species. Here is my current code:

ggplot(iris, aes(x = Petal.Length, y = Sepal.Length, color = Species, shape = Species)) +
  geom_point()

I can see three clear clusters of data (one per species) and also a strong linear relationship between the two variables for each cluster. I would like to add a linear trendline for each cluster to visualize better this relationship. I would like to know:

What is the procedure to add linear trends to an existing scatter plot in ggplot2 with differents groups? Is there a layer to do that or do I need to fit a model first?
How would it apply to my example

Note that my intent is to learn how to do this by myself in the future, I do not want just a solution specific to this problem.
Please be concise in your answer.



We use a similar strategy to before but notice that here I am also using my basic knowledge of ggplot2. Because of how this package works, I suspect (or rather hope) that there is a layer (like geom_point) that actually does the job. Something like geom_trendline or so. I also specify that I would rather not fit a model just to show the trendline. The rest is as before, I want to make sure that the answer I get is not “AI does my homework” but rather “I am going to learn something new”.






NotePrompt





Yes—ggplot2 has a layer specifically for this, so you do not need to fit the models yourself first.
1. General procedure
The layer is:

geom_smooth(method = "lm")

geom_smooth() fits a model and draws the fitted line. The important idea for grouped data is:

If you map a grouping variable to an aesthetic such as color, ggplot2 fits a separate model for each group.

So the general pattern is:

ggplot(data, aes(x = x_variable, y = y_variable, color = group)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")

You can think of this as:
data → points → group-wise model fitting → fitted lines
2. Your example
You already have Species mapped to color, so simply add the layer:

ggplot(iris, aes(x = Petal.Length,
                 y = Sepal.Length,
                 color = Species,
                 shape = Species)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")

ggplot2 will fit three separate linear models, one for each species, and draw the corresponding lines.
A useful thing to experiment with is:

geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE)

Here se = FALSE removes the shaded confidence interval, which can make the three trendlines easier to see.
Key principle to remember: geom_smooth() does the model fitting for you, and the grouping comes from your aesthetic mappings (here, color = Species).

title: Introduction to R (solutions)
section: 16.3 Example 3: Why the human still matters
text:
16.3 Example 3: Why the human still matters
As an example of why the human still matters, I did a little test. I gave the same AI as in previous exercises the seedpred dataset and simply ask “Can you tell which species was predated the most? And the least?”.
AI has advanced so much that it actually loaded the data, wrote a little Python script to analyze the data, generated a table of results and interpreted the results correctly, saying that cd experience the highes predation and uva the least.
I check the numbers and realized that what the AI had done is add up the number of seeds taken for each species (it did not explain it to me, I had to check the numbers). But is that we meant? If you look at the earlier exercise, we also calculated the proportion of instances when at least one seed was taken and the results are different.
It turns that predation data is a bit more complicated as it usually involves two processes: (i) the predator visits the location with seeds and (ii) the predator consumes the seeds. So what do we mean when we ask “most predated”? Also, is it enough to just do a simple calculation from the data? Are we going to get the same result if we repeat the experiment? What kind of statistics is relevant here?
Turning an ecological question into an acceptable scientific answer requires understanding ecology, statistics and often it also requires figuring out what we really want to know. AI understands nothing and generally does not ask, it just assumes and runs with it. We still matter :).

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
text:
Parameters, estimators and estimates
\[
X_i \sim \operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda)
\]
\(\lambda\): the expected number of seedlings per quadrat.
\(X_i\): the number of seedlings in quadrat \(i\)

Parameter: fixed and unknown; it defines the model.


Estimator: a rule to estimate a parameter from a random sample of a model.


Estimate: the number that the rule gives for one particular sample (\(\hat\lambda\)).

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
text:
The method of moments

Estimator for expectations equate expectations of model and empirical distribution.
One parameter: mean model = mean sample.
Two parameters: mean and variance model = mean and variance sample.
Three+ parameters: other expectations (kurtosis, skewness, etc.).


\[
\hat\lambda = \overline X
\]
50 fir quadrats: \(\hat\lambda = 2.14\) seedlings per quadrat.


Maximum likelihood in Chapter 4; next slides apply to any estimator.

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
text:
Discussion: parameter, estimator or estimate?

The expected number of seedlings per quadrat, \(\lambda\).
“Add the counts and divide by the number of quadrats.”
2.14 seedlings per quadrat for the 50 fir quadrats that were measured.
The mean of the 50 quadrats that a colleague will count next year.


Parameter · Estimator · Estimate

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
text:
The sampling distribution

Sampling distribution: the distribution of the estimates across repeated hypothetical samples with the same design and sample size.






Within a sample: quadrats vary (\(X_i\)).
Between samples: estimates vary (\(\hat\lambda\)).
Data: treated as a random sample from the model.
Sampling distributions are simulated, never measured

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
text:
Hypothetical samples in R

# Parameter of the model, quadrats per sample and number of hypothetical samples.
set.seed(seed = 401)
true_lambda = 2.14
n_quadrats = 50
n_samples = 2000

# Each run simulates one sample of 50 quadrats and returns its estimate of lambda.
lambda_estimates = replicate(
  n = n_samples,
  expr = mean(rpois(n = n_quadrats, lambda = true_lambda))
)

# Mean and standard deviation of the 2,000 estimates (one per hypothetical sample).
mean(lambda_estimates)
sd(lambda_estimates)


replicate(): evaluates expr n times and collects the results.

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
text:
A simulated sampling distribution





Properties of an estimator (bias, var, MSE).
Uncertainty (std error, conf intervals).
Plug-in estimates Replace \(\lambda\) with \(\hat \lambda\).
It has a mean (2.14) and variance (0.042).
We do not (always) know its “formula”.



Grey: 2,000 simulated estimates (\(\hat \lambda\)). Vermillion: the “true” parameter value (\(\lambda\)).

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
text:
Bias and variance
\[
\operatorname{Bias}(\hat\theta) = E[\hat\theta] - \theta
\]

Unbiased: the mean of a sample, intercepts and slopes, (sometimes) variances.
Biased in finite samples: most estimators, bias reduced with larger samples
Variance of the estimator: decreases with larger samples.


Simulation: bias about 0.001; variance 0.0419 against \(2.14/50 = 0.0428\).


Two studies of 50 quadrats report 1.9 and 2.3 seedlings per quadrat. What varies? Is the estimator biased?

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
text:
Mean squared error
\[
\operatorname{MSE}(\hat\theta) = \operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta) +
\operatorname{Bias}(\hat\theta)^2
\]

Mean squared error (MSE): the expected squared distance between estimates and the “true” value.
Use: compare estimators of the same parameter.
Trade-off: a biased estimator can have a smaller MSE.

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
text:
Standard errors

Standard error (SE): the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of an estimator
Plug-in estimate: Use \(\hat\theta\) instead of \(\theta\)


\[
\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\hat\lambda) = \sqrt{\frac{\hat\lambda}{n}}
\]


50 fir quadrats: about 0.21 seedlings per quadrat.

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
section: Discussion: standard deviation or standard error?
text:
Discussion: standard deviation or standard error?

How much the counts differ across the 50 quadrats.
How much the mean of 50 quadrats would differ among hypothetical repetitions.
The spread of the histogram on slide 19.
How much the count for one quadrat varies under the model.


Standard deviation · Standard error


1 minute: decide with a neighbour.

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
text:
Confidence intervals

Confidence interval: a range estimate (lower-upper) for a parameter with a given confidence level.


Confidence level: the fraction of hypothetical samples in which the interval would contain the parameter.


There are different confidence interval estimators.
Wald (confidence) interval: assumes sampling distribution is Normal.


\[
\hat\theta \pm z_{0.975}\,\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\hat\theta),
\qquad z_{0.975} \approx 1.96
\]

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
text:
Wald interval in R

# Estimate of lambda and number of quadrats in the sample.
lambda_hat = mean(seedling_counts)
n_counts = length(seedling_counts)
# Plug the estimate into the formula of the standard error.
estimated_se = sqrt(lambda_hat / n_counts)

# 0.975 quantile of the standard Normal distribution.
critical_value = qnorm(p = 0.975)
# Lower and upper endpoints of the interval: about 1.73 and 2.55.
interval = lambda_hat + c(-1, 1) * critical_value * estimated_se
interval


An interval estimate of the mean (\(\lambda\)), not for the count of single quadrats (\(X_i\)).

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
section: The dance of the confidence intervals
text:
The dance of the confidence intervals





Parameter: fixed (dashed line).
Interval: changes from sample to sample.
95%: describes the procedure.



Top: the simulated sampling distribution. Below: 20 hypothetical samples; vermillion: the one interval that misses the parameter.


The interval from a sample either contains \(\lambda\) or it does not.

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
text:
Coverage checked by simulation

Coverage: the fraction of hypothetical samples in which the interval actually contains the parameter.


2,000 samples of 50 quadrats: coverage 0.9525.


Small samples: Lower coverage; the lower endpoint can be negative.


A study reports a 95% confidence interval (1.5 - 2.9 seedlings per quadrat). What does the 95% refer to?

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
text:
Estimation of two parameters

Flipper lengths: \(X_i \sim \operatorname{Normal}(\mu, \sigma^2)\).

\[
\widehat{\sigma^2}_{\mathrm{MM}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(X_i - \overline X)^2
\]

\(\hat\mu \approx 217.2\) mm. \(\widehat{\sigma^2}_{\mathrm{MM}} \approx 41.7\) mm².


Variance estimator \(1/n\): biased. \(1/(n - 1)\): unbiased.

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
text:
Consistency

Consistent estimator: The sample-based estimate converges (in probability) to the “true” value as the sample size increases.


As for relative frequencies (slide 8): a trend, not true for a given sample.
Bias decreases: As sample grows, bias decreases towards 0.
Variance decreases: As sample grows, variance decreases towards 0.
All relevant statistical estimators are consistent.


20 quadrats give 2.1 and 100 quadrats give 2.3; the model mean is 2.14. Does this contradict consistency?

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
text:
Asymptotic normality


Grey: 2,000 simulated means. Vermillion: the Normal approximation.



\[
\hat\lambda \overset{\mathrm{approx}}{\sim} \operatorname{Normal}\left(\lambda,
\frac{\lambda}{n}\right)
\]


Asymptotic normality: Sampling distributions become approximately Normal as sample size grows.
5 quadrats: skewed, long tail.
100 quadrats: close to Normal.



It justifies the Wald interval; how large \(n\) must be depends on the model and estimator.

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
section: Recap: the steps of a fit
text:
Recap: the steps of a fit

Write the model: the random variable, its distribution, the assumptions.
Write the NLL: two lists, getAll(), log = TRUE, transformations.
Connect and process it: cmb() and MakeADFun().
Minimise it: optim(), and check convergence.
Transform back: and compare with the data.


Fir seedlings, 50 quadrats: \(\hat\lambda=2.14\) seedlings per quadrat. Owls: \(\hat\mu\approx4.75\) calls per visit, \(\hat k\approx0.33\).


Today: how uncertain, why it works, which model.

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
text:
Uncertainty from the likelihood


Wald interval
The curvature of the log-likelihood at its maximum, and asymptotic normality. Fast; what software usually reports.

Likelihood profile interval
The whole shape around the maximum. The reference method; it needs many fits.


Both work for any model fitted with optim(), without a formula for the variance.

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
text:
Asymptotic normality of the MLE
\[
\hat\theta \overset{\mathrm{approx}}{\sim}
\operatorname{Normal}\left(\theta,\operatorname{SE}(\hat\theta)^2\right)
\quad\text{for sufficiently large }n
\]

Several parameters: a multivariate Normal (Chapter 2), with a covariance matrix.
Wald interval: \(\hat\theta\pm1.96\,\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\hat\theta)\), as in Chapter 3.
Conditions: not on the boundary of its range; support independent of the parameter; smooth log-likelihood; number of parameters does not grow with \(n\).


Poisson mean: \(\operatorname{Normal}(\lambda,\lambda/n)\), the result of Chapter 3.

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
text:
Curvature and standard errors
\[
\ell(\theta)-\ell(\hat\theta)\approx
-\frac{(\theta-\hat\theta)^2}{2\,\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\hat\theta)^2}
\]





Large sample: near its maximum, the log-likelihood is close to a parabola.
Falls slowly: low curvature, many values supported, large standard error.
One parameter: standard error = \(1/\sqrt{\text{curvature}}\).
Several: the curvatures give the covariance matrix.


Standard error of \(\hat\lambda\): ten quadrats, 0.47; 50 quadrats, 0.207 seedlings per quadrat.



Relative log-likelihood of the same Poisson model. Solid: the first ten quadrats. Dotted: all 50.

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
text:
sdreport(): standard errors and correlations



sdreport(obj): after the fit; the curvature at the estimates.
summary(): a row per parameter, with Estimate and Std. Error, on the optimised scale.
cov.fixed: the covariance matrix; cov2cor() gives the correlations.
Tilted contours: correlated estimates.



# Standard errors after the fit of the owl model.
owl_sd = sdreport(owl_obj)
summary(owl_sd)
#        Estimate Std. Error
# log_mu    1.559      0.164
# log_k    -1.116      0.165

# Correlation between the two estimates.
cov2cor(owl_sd$cov.fixed)  # about 0



Correlation of the estimates: \(\log(\mu)\) and \(\log(k)\), about 0; \(\log(k)\) and \(\operatorname{logit}(p)\), 0.71, the tilt of the surface in Lecture 1.

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
text:
Back-transforming a standard error
sdreport() gives the standard error on the scale that was optimised.


A non-linear function and an average
For a non-linear \(g\): \(E[g(X)]\neq g(E[X])\).
A variance is an average and a standard error its square root, so applying \(g\) to them gives no standard error. Estimates and endpoints are values: they transform.

The delta method
Treats \(g\) as a straight line near the estimate: an approximation (Chapter 6).
ADREPORT(k) in the NLL: sdreport() adds a row with the standard error of \(k\).


Ten quadrats: 0.213 on the log scale; exp(0.213) gives 1.24, but the standard error of \(\hat\lambda\) is 0.47. Owls: \(\hat k=0.327\), standard error 0.054.


Transform estimates and endpoints; for a standard error on the new scale, use ADREPORT().

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
section: A Wald interval depends on the scale
text:
A Wald interval depends on the scale





Wald interval: replaces the log-likelihood by a parabola.
Optimised scale: an unconstrained parameter is closer to Normal; calculate it there.
Endpoints: an increasing transformation keeps the coverage.
Positive parameter: stays positive, and asymmetry is captured.


Ten quadrats: 1.28 to 3.12 on the original scale; 1.45 to 3.34 from the log scale. Owls, \(k\): 0.221 to 0.434; 0.237 to 0.453.



Solid: the log-likelihood. Dashed and dotted: parabolas on the original and the log scale. Grey line: \(-1.92\).

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
section: Practice 3: an interval from the log scale
text:
Practice 3: an interval from the log scale

2 minutes: R as a calculator.
A fit on the log scale returned par = 0.92 for the logarithm of the mean number of ticks per lizard, and sdreport() reports a standard error of 0.141.

Calculate a 95% Wald interval for the mean number of ticks per lizard.
Why is it not symmetric around the estimate?

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
text:
Likelihood profile intervals

Likelihood profile interval: all the values whose relative profile log-likelihood is within 1.92 units of the maximum; the other parameters are re-estimated for each value.


1.92: half the 0.95 quantile of a chi-squared distribution with one degree of freedom (3.84, the square of 1.96).
Wilks’ theorem: twice the drop at the generating value behaves like the square of a standard Normal variable.
So: about 95% of hypothetical samples fall within the cutoff.


qchisq(p = 0.95, df = 1) / 2  # 1.92

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
text:
Reading a likelihood profile interval





Shape: the interval follows the curve, so it need not be symmetric.
Scale: it does not depend on it.
Inner fits: move the parameter, re-estimate the others, record the NLL, find the two crossings of the cutoff.
Larger sample: closer to a parabola, so the intervals agree.


Ten quadrats: profile 1.40 to 3.25. With all 50 the three intervals nearly coincide.



95% intervals: Wald on the original scale, 1.28 to 3.12; Wald from the log scale, 1.45 to 3.34; profile, 1.40 to 3.25.

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
text:
tmbprofile() and confint()

TMB::tmbprofile(obj, name, trace = FALSE): profiles one parameter, named as in the list of parameters; returns a data frame.
confint(): finds the two crossings of the cutoff.
Both on the optimised scale: transform the endpoints back.


# Ten quadrats: 1.40 to 3.25 seedlings per quadrat.
fir_ten_profile = TMB::tmbprofile(fir_ten_obj, name = "log_lambda", trace = FALSE)
exp(confint(fir_ten_profile))

# Owls: k from 0.235 to 0.451.
owl_profile_k = TMB::tmbprofile(owl_obj, name = "log_k", trace = FALSE)
exp(confint(owl_profile_k))

text:
Profile intervals with several parameters

Each parameter: its own profile, with the others re-estimated.
Wald, optimised scale: can come close.
Wald, original scale: may miss the asymmetry.
The reference: the likelihood profile interval.

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
text:
Joint confidence regions

Joint confidence region: the combinations whose relative log-likelihood is above a cutoff; 3.00 for two parameters (half the 0.95 quantile with two degrees of freedom).






The region: lies inside one contour of the surface.
Beyond each interval: it extends further than either.
The rectangle of two intervals is not a 95% region.
Use: an interval for one parameter, a region for a combination.



The owl model. Vermillion contour: the region. Segments on the axes: the two profile intervals.

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
text:
Simulating from a fitted model

OBS() in the NLL: marks the data as observations.
obj$simulate(): draws a hypothetical sample of the size of the data, for parameters on the optimised scale.
Placeholder data of another length: give another sample size.


# The complete NLL of the Negative Binomial model.
nb_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  # Mark the data as observations, so that they can be simulated.
  calls = OBS(calls)
  mu = exp(log_mu)
  k = exp(log_k)
  ADREPORT(k)
  -sum(dnbinom2(x = calls, mu = mu, size = k, log = TRUE))
}
# After processing and fitting: the first 20 counts of one hypothetical sample.
owl_obj$simulate(owl_fit$par)$calls[1:20]

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
section: Coverage of Wald and profile intervals
text:
Coverage of Wald and profile intervals




Dashed line: the nominal level. Likelihood: the likelihood profile interval. Poisson: Wald on the original scale. Negative Binomial: Wald from the log scale.



Simulate from known parameters: does each interval contain them?
Wald, original scale: fails where the log-likelihood is far from a parabola.
Wald, suitable scale: can match the profile, with one fit.
Simulated coverage: has its own noise.



Wald 0.878 and profile 0.924 (Poisson); 0.945 and 0.942 (Negative Binomial).


Profile intervals: closer to 95% in small samples, at the cost of many fits. Wald on the log scale: the fast approximation.

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
text:
Discussion: Wald or profile?

Uses the curvature at the maximum.
Gives the same interval on any scale.
Needs a single fit.
Can include negative values for a positive parameter.


Wald · Profile


1 minute: decide with a neighbour.

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
text:
Consistency and asymptotic normality

Consistent estimator: the chance of missing the parameter by more than any given margin becomes small as the sample grows.


An MLE is an estimator: it has a sampling distribution, a bias and a variance.
MLEs are consistent: when the observations are i.i.d. from the model; a statement about probabilities, not about every sample.
Normal approximation: how large \(n\) must be depends on the model and the parameter.
Large \(n\): the standard error of one fit describes the spread across samples.


Missing \(k\) by 0.1 or more: 45% with 20 visits, 7% with 122, none with 500. With 122: standard deviation of \(\log(\hat k)\) 0.162, standard error 0.165.

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
text:
Efficiency

More efficient: estimates vary less across hypothetical samples.


Maximum likelihood: uses the probability of each observation; the method of moments only the mean and the variance.
Asymptotically efficient: in large samples no other regular estimator is more precise.
The limit: the variance from the curvature of the log-likelihood is the smallest that such an estimator can have.


Standard deviation of \(\hat k\): 122 visits, 0.055 against 0.086; 500 visits, 0.024 against 0.042. The method of moments would need about 2.5 times as many visits.


The reason to use maximum likelihood whenever the likelihood can be written.

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
text:
Bias in finite samples

MLEs: in general biased in finite samples.
The bias: shrinks as the sample grows, faster than the standard error.
Small sample: these properties are approximations.
Check by simulation: simulate hypothetical samples from the fit, refit each, and compare the mean of the estimates with the value used to simulate.


Relative bias of \(\hat k\): 21%, 2.6% and 0.6% for 20, 122 and 500 visits.

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
text:
Live demo: properties by simulation

One hypothetical sample: obj$simulate() at the estimates, fitted like the data.
Many samples: placeholder data set the sample size; keep every estimate.
Sampling distributions: a histogram of the estimates for each sample size.
Properties: consistency, the standard error, efficiency and bias from the estimates.


Script: demo-properties.R, sections 1 to 4 (the owl model; section 3 runs for about a minute).

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
text:
Misspecified models

Misspecified: the model does not contain the distribution of the data generating process, for any parameter values.


The MLE: converges to the values that bring the model closest to that process (the Kullback–Leibler divergence).
The fit: the best approximation that the model offers.
Standard errors and intervals: become approximations.

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
text:
The Akaike information criterion
\[
\mathrm{AIC}=2K-2\,\ell(\hat\theta)
\]

\(K\): the number of estimated parameters.
More parameters: more freedom to adapt to its own sample; when a model contains another as a special case, its maximum cannot be lower.
Lowest AIC: preferred; only differences between models fitted to the same observations in the same units are meaningful.
It estimates: the distance to the data generating process when predicting new data.
AICc: adds \(2K(K+1)/(n-K-1)\) for small samples; an approximation.


Owls: Poisson, \(K=1\), \(\ell=-634.16\); Negative Binomial, \(K=2\), \(\ell=-299.44\). Difference in AIC about 667; AICc adds only 0.03 and 0.10.

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
text:
Using AIC

It ranks the candidates that we give it.
It does not show that the best one describes the data well.
“Reject unless AIC drops by two units”: null hypothesis testing in disguise.
One criterion among others: for evidence and prediction.


Negative Binomial far better than Poisson for the owls, and still an approximation (visits to the same nest).

An Exponential model (\(K=1\)) and a Gamma model (\(K=2\)) are fitted to the same waiting times between visits of pollinators to a flower. The maximum log-likelihoods are \(-231.0\) and \(-230.4\).

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis

A recipe for a fit

Write the model: random variable, distribution, assumptions.
Write the NLL: getAll(), log = TRUE, transformations.

Minimise it: optim(), method = "BFGS", check convergence.
Transform back: compare the fitted model with the data.

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
section: Where we are: the modelling cycle
text:
Where we are: the modelling cycle


Red numbers: chapters of the course. This lecture: groups (7) and the marginal likelihood (7).

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
text:
Observations in groups

Group: observations on the same individual, site, nest or tank, which share its conditions.


Observational unit: the entity of one observation; several in each group.
Shared conditions: observations of a group resemble each other more.
Process variation: it would remain with perfect measurements.
Treated as independent: standard errors too small, intervals too narrow.


Tadpoles sharing a tank (Chapter 4); tanks as \(n\) in AICc and BIC (Chapter 6).


A grouped model describes the dependence explicitly.

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
section: Response curves measured on the same groups
text:
Response curves measured on the same groups





One curve per group: every group measured at the same values of the predictor.
The curve: \(\mu(x)=a\left(1-e^{-b(x-c)}\right)\); asymptote \(a\), rate \(b\), zero at \(x=c\).
The parameter that varies: the one in which the groups differ most.


12 plants: 2 origins × 2 treatments × 3 plants, 7 concentrations, 84 measurements. The asymptote varies among plants.



Blue: CO₂ uptake (µmol/m²/s) of each plant against the concentration of CO₂ (µL/L). Rows: treatment. Columns: origin.

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
text:
Conditional distributions

Conditional distribution: the probabilities of the values of \(X_1\) among the outcomes in which \(X_2=x_2\).

\[
P(X_1=x_1\mid X_2=x_2)=\frac{P(X_1=x_1,X_2=x_2)}{P(X_2=x_2)}
\]

The bar: “for a given value of”, here of another random variable.
Joint over marginal: the given value must have a probability above zero.
Independence: conditional = marginal, for every given value.


Two seeds (Chapter 2): \(P(X_1=0\mid X_2=0)=0.28/0.70=0.4=P(X_1=0)\): independent.

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
text:
Marginal distributions
\[
P(X_1=x_1,X_2=x_2)=P(X_1=x_1\mid X_2=x_2)\,P(X_2=x_2)
\]
\[
f_X(x)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)\,f_Y(y)\,dy
\]

Joint: conditional × marginal.
Marginal: sum the joint probabilities over the other variable; integrate densities.
In plain words: the conditional distributions averaged, weighted by the given value.
A grouped model: the value of a group first, then the observations for that value.


Beta-Binomial (Chapter 6): Binomial for a given probability, Beta among tanks; closed form. A random effect: Normal on a transformed scale; usually no closed form.

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
section: A model with a random asymptote
text:
A model with a random asymptote
\[
u_j\sim\operatorname{Normal}\left(0,\sigma^2_{\mathrm{group}}\right),
\qquad
Y_{ij}\mid u_j\sim\operatorname{Normal}\left(\mu_j(x_{ij}),\sigma^2_{\mathrm{obs}}\right)
\]
\[
\mu_j(x)=a\,e^{u_j}\left(1-e^{-b(x-c)}\right)
\]

\(Y_{ij}\): observation \(i\) of group \(j\); \(u_j\): its deviation (log asymptote).
\(a_j=a\,e^{u_j}\): always positive; deviations multiply (\(u_j=0.1\): about 10% higher).
For a given \(u_j\): the observations of a group are independent.
Marginally: dependent, because they share \(u_j\); different groups are independent.


12 plants (\(j\)), 7 concentrations (\(i\)), \(\sigma^2_{\mathrm{plant}}\); \(b\) and \(c\) shared by all plants.


Independent for a given group effect, dependent marginally.

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
text:
Fixed effects and random effects

Fixed effects: parameters shared by all groups, including the effects of group-level predictors.


Random effects: the deviations of the groups, described by a distribution.


Mixed-effects model: both kinds; also called a hierarchical or multilevel model, because it describes the data in levels.
“Random”: described by a distribution; not allocated at random, and not without cause.


\(a\), \(b\) and \(c\) are fixed effects; \(u_1,\ldots,u_{12}\) are random effects.

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
section: Practice 1: two seedlings in one quadrat
text:
Practice 1: two seedlings in one quadrat

3 minutes: on paper.
A quadrat is favourable or unfavourable for seedlings, each with probability 0.5. A seedling survives with probability 0.8 in a favourable quadrat and 0.2 in an unfavourable one, independently of the other seedlings. Two seedlings are planted in a quadrat whose quality was not recorded; \(X_1\) and \(X_2\) are 1 if a seedling survives.

Calculate the joint distribution of \(X_1\) and \(X_2\), and \(P(X_1=1)\).
Calculate \(P(X_1=1\mid X_2=1)\).
Are the two seedlings independent? Are they independent for a given quality?

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
text:
Three ways to share information

Complete pooling: one value; assumes that the groups do not differ, so their variation goes into the observation variance.
No pooling: an ordinary parameter per group; the measured groups only.
Partial pooling: values from a distribution with an estimated variance; the measured groups and groups in general.
Its costs: an assumed distribution (Normal here) and an integral in the likelihood.


Measurements around one curve: standard deviation 8.2 µmol/m²/s; around each plant’s curve: 1.9. No pooling: asymptotes 14.2 to 45.0 µmol/m²/s.


Each group informs the distribution, and the distribution informs each group.

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
section: Discussion: which pooling answers which question?
text:
Discussion: which pooling answers which question?
Newts are counted five times in each of 20 ponds of a region.

Which of these 20 ponds has the most newts?
How much does the density of newts vary among the ponds of the region?
How many newts should we expect in a pond that was not surveyed?
Does the density increase with the area of a pond, and how precisely do we know it?


Complete pooling · No pooling · Partial pooling


3 minutes: match each question with a neighbour.

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
text:
The marginal likelihood
\[
L_j(\boldsymbol\theta)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
f(\mathbf y_j\mid u,\boldsymbol\theta)\,f(u\mid\sigma_{\mathrm{group}})\,du,
\qquad
L(\boldsymbol\theta)=\prod_{j}L_j(\boldsymbol\theta)
\]

Random effects are not observed: the likelihood is the probability of the observations with the effects integrated out.
One group: the likelihood of its observations, averaged over the values of its effect, weighted by their density.
Independent groups: a product over groups, a sum of log-likelihoods.
Why not estimate each \(u_j\)? That is no pooling. One variance replaces them, so the number of parameters stays fixed as groups are added.


\(\boldsymbol\theta\): \(a\), \(b\), \(c\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{plant}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{obs}}\); 12 integrals, one for each plant.

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
text:
The Laplace approximation




Solid: the integrand of plant Mc2 at the estimates. Dashed: its Laplace approximation.



Near the peak: the log integrand is close to a parabola.
Area: height of the peak × width from the curvature.
Accurate: many, nearly Normal observations per group.
Less accurate: few observations, counts near zero, binary data.


Mc2: area 0.3% too small; log-likelihood off by 0.003.



RTMB does it for every group, at every evaluation of the NLL.

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
text:
Random effects in RTMB



Joint NLL: random effects and observations for given effects.
Parameters: a vector of random effects, starting at zero.
Order: their density before they are used (to simulate).
random = "u": integrates them out; fn and gr are the marginal NLL and its gradient, par the other parameters.



mixed_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  # The density of the deviations comes first.
  nll = -sum(dnorm(x = u, mean = 0,
                   sd = exp(log_sd_plant), log = TRUE))
  a = exp(log_asym + u)
  mu = a[plant] *
    (1 - exp(-exp(log_rate) * (conc - c0)))
  nll - sum(dnorm(x = uptake, mean = mu,
                  sd = exp(log_sd_obs), log = TRUE))
}
mixed_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(mixed_nll, co2_data),
  list(log_asym = log(30), log_rate = log(0.01),
       c0 = 50, log_sd_plant = log(0.1),
       log_sd_obs = log(2), u = rep(0, 12)),
  random = "u", silent = TRUE)

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
text:
Variance components and predicted effects

Variance components: \(\sigma^2_{\mathrm{group}}\) among groups, \(\sigma^2_{\mathrm{obs}}\) around each group’s curve.




"fixed": estimates and standard errors of \(\boldsymbol\theta\).
"random": predicted group effects (conditional modes): predictions, not estimates.
Log scale: a small standard deviation ≈ a coefficient of variation; \(u_j=0\) gives the median, not the mean.



mixed_sd = sdreport(mixed_obj)
summary(mixed_sd, select = "fixed")
# sd_plant 0.34 (log scale),
# sd_obs 2.0 µmol/m²/s, a 30.9 µmol/m²/s

summary(mixed_sd, select = "random")
# Quebec positive; Mc1, Mc2, Mc3:
# -0.370, -0.755, -0.422

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
text:
Group-level predictors

Group-level predictor: measured on the group, shared by its observations (origin, treatment, habitat).


A fixed effect on the parameter that varies among groups, on its log scale.
On the log scale the effects add; on the original scale they multiply.
Interaction: the effect of one predictor depends on the level of the other.


\(\log(a_j)=\log(a)+\beta_{\mathrm{miss}}M_j+\beta_{\mathrm{chill}}C_j+\beta_{\mathrm{int}}M_jC_j+u_j\); \(\hat\sigma_{\mathrm{plant}}\) 0.34 → 0.079. Chilling: × 0.90 (Quebec), × 0.59 (Mississippi).


Predictors explain variation among groups; the variance describes what remains.

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
text:
Two ways to encode groups


One parameter per group
Each combination of predictors has its own typical value.

Baseline plus effects
One group is the baseline; the others are differences from it, with an interaction.


The same model: parameters, maximum likelihood and fitted curves.
Baseline plus effects: differences with standard errors and intervals; leave a term out for a simpler model.


Four typical log asymptotes, or \(\log(a)\) and three \(\beta\): NLL 192.086 in both forms.


Choose the form whose parameters answer the question.

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
text:
Shrinkage




Open: no pooling. Filled: predicted. Dashed: median (top) or typical asymptote (bottom).



Shrinkage: predicted effects pulled towards the typical value of groups with the same predictors.


Stronger with few or noisy observations and a small variance among groups.
Regularisation: each group less sensitive to noise.
Part of the model: it follows from the distribution of group effects.


Mc2: 14.2 → 14.5 µmol/m²/s without predictors; → 15.6 with them (typical 18.5).

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
section: Practice 2: wing length of chicks in nests

Practice 2: wing length of chicks in nests

Wing length of chicks of the same age, with a random effect for each nest: \(\sigma^2_{\mathrm{nest}}=4\) mm² and \(\sigma^2_{\mathrm{obs}}=4\) mm². In nest A two chicks were measured, in nest B eight; in both, the mean is 3 mm above the common mean. section: Live demo: from pooling to partial pooling
text:
Live demo: from pooling to partial pooling

Complete pooling: one curve, and the spread of the observations around it.
No pooling: one asymptote for each group.

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
section: Uncertainty of variance components and REML
text:
Uncertainty of variance components and REML

A variance among groups is informed by the groups, not the observations; use the likelihood profile of its log standard deviation.
Maximum likelihood underestimates variances when fixed effects are estimated from the same data (the \(n-1\) of Chapter 3).
REML: the fixed effects are integrated out as well; add them to random.
Cautions: approximate for non-linear or non-Normal models; compare models with their maximum likelihood fits.


\(\hat\sigma_{\mathrm{plant}}=0.079\), profile interval 0.045 to 0.139 (variance 0.0020 to 0.019): 84 measurements, but 12 plants. REML: 0.105.


To estimate a variance among groups more precisely, observe more groups.

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
section: Curves for observed and new groups
text:
Curves for observed and new groups





Observed group: its predicted effect, shrunk towards the typical curve.
Typical curve: \(u_j=0\); the median group, not the mean.
New group: a new draw of \(u\); 95% within \(a_{\mathrm{typ}}e^{\pm1.96\,\sigma_{\mathrm{group}}}\).
At the estimates: the range leaves out their uncertainty.


Chilled Mississippi plants: typical 18.5, new plants 15.8 to 21.5 µmol/m²/s.



Measured groups: their own curves. Groups in general: typical curve and range.

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
section: Practice 3: sapling growth in forest stands
text:
Practice 3: sapling growth in forest stands

3 minutes: R as a calculator.
The typical growth rate of the saplings of stand \(j\) is \(r\,e^{u_j}\), with \(u_j\sim\operatorname{Normal}(0,\sigma^2_{\mathrm{stand}})\), \(r=20\) cm/year and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{stand}}=0.4\).

Between which values lie the typical growth rates of 95% of new stands?
A surveyed stand has a predicted effect of 0.5. What is its typical growth rate? Which answer would you use to plan a planting in a stand that was not surveyed?

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
text:
Checking a grouped model





Unconditional simulation: obj$simulate() draws new group effects, then new observations.
Observation residuals: share their group’s effect; a pattern may come from a few groups.
Group residuals: DHARMa::recalculateResiduals() with group.


Dispersion 0.80. Mc2: group residual 0.010, not unusual among 12 plants.



Each level can hide a problem at the other: check both.

title: Ecological Models and Data Analysis
text:
AIC for grouped models
\[
\mathrm{AIC}=2K-2\,\ell(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta})
\]

\(\ell(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta})\): the maximum marginal log-likelihood.
\(K\): the fixed effects and the variance parameters, not the random effects; the length of par.
Boundary: a model without random effects has \(\sigma_{\mathrm{group}}=0\), at the edge of the range, so AIC is then an approximate guide.
No AICc or BIC: the number of independent observations lies somewhere between the number of groups and the number of observations.


Random asymptote: \(K=5\), not 17; the 12 deviations cost one parameter, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{plant}}\). And \(n\): 84 measurements or 12 plants?

Leave-one-group-out cross-validation

Leave-one-group-out: hold out one whole group, refit every parameter to the other groups, and score the held-out group by its marginal log-likelihood.


Whole groups: a held-out observation of a fitted group is easier to predict than a new group.
Marginal log-likelihood: all observations of the group together, its effect integrated out.
map in MakeADFun(): fixes the parameters at the estimates; fn then returns the marginal NLL of the held-out group.
Fixed starting values; count the fits that did not converge.
