Its means are the parameters of the model, and its covariance matrix contains the variance of the estimator of each parameter on the diagonal and the covariance between the estimators of each pair of parameters outside the diagonal. The Wald interval of one parameter uses only its variance, through the standard error, which is the square root of the variance. What maximum likelihood adds to Chapter 3 is a way to estimate this covariance matrix from the log-likelihood of the sample, for any model, also when there is no formula for the variance of the estimator.

6.1.1 Curvature and standard errors
The Normal approximation of the sampling distribution has a counterpart in the shape of the log-likelihood: in a large sample the log-likelihood near its maximum is close to a parabola,
\[
\ell(\theta)-\ell(\hat\theta)\approx
-\frac{(\theta-\hat\theta)^2}{2\,\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\hat\theta)^2},
\]
that is, a polynomial of degree two in the parameter, with its maximum at the estimate and a width set by the standard error. With several parameters it is a polynomial of degree two in all of them, with a squared term for each parameter and a product term for each pair. The two approximations go together, and the Wald interval relies on both: it amounts to replacing the log-likelihood by this parabola, which is why it is also called a quadratic interval.
The curvature of the log-likelihood at its maximum measures how fast the log-likelihood falls as we move away from the estimate, and it determines the standard error. A log-likelihood that falls slowly has a small curvature: many parameter values are almost equally well supported by the data, which corresponds to a large standard error. A log-likelihood that falls quickly has a large curvature: the data discriminate well among parameter values, and the standard error is small. For one parameter the relation follows from the parabola above, whose curvature is \(1/\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\hat\theta)^2\)10. That is, the standard error is one over the square root of the curvature, so a log-likelihood that is four times as sharply curved gives half the standard error. A larger sample contains more information about the parameter, which gives a more sharply curved log-likelihood and a smaller standard error.
With several parameters, the curvatures of the log-likelihood along each parameter and for each pair of parameters give the whole covariance matrix of the estimates. The tilted contours of the surface in the parameterisation with \(k\) and \(p\) (Figure 4) are an example: they describe estimates that are correlated. The boxes below give the mathematics of these statements.
The approximation is good when the log-likelihood is close to a parabola on the scale of the parameter. When it is not, for example when the log-likelihood is asymmetric like the curve of the ten quadrats (Figure 1), the standard error describes only the curvature at the maximum and the Wald interval is less accurate.






NoteAsymptotic normality of maximum likelihood estimators



For a large sample of i.i.d. observations from the model, the sampling distribution of maximum likelihood estimators is approximately (multivariate) Normal and centred on the parameters. Its covariance matrix is estimated from the curvature of the log-likelihood at its maximum: the more sharply curved the log-likelihood, the smaller the standard errors.








CautionStatistical detail: Fisher information





The curvature of the log-likelihood at the estimate is the observed information, which is the negative of its second derivative there. Its inverse estimates the variance of the estimator:
\[
\hat{\mathcal I}=-\ell''(\hat\theta),
\qquad
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\theta)=\frac{1}{\hat{\mathcal I}},
\qquad
\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\hat\theta)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\hat{\mathcal I}}}.
\]
The asymptotic result is usually stated with the Fisher information \(\mathcal I(\theta)\), also called the expected information: the expectation of \(-\ell''(\theta)\) across hypothetical samples, which measures how much information a sample of this size contains about \(\theta\). Then
\[
\hat\theta \overset{\mathrm{approx}}{\sim}
\operatorname{Normal}\left(\theta,\frac{1}{\mathcal I(\theta)}\right)
\quad\text{for sufficiently large }n.
\]
The observed information is calculated from the log-likelihood of the sample that we have, and the two agree in large samples.11 In plain English, the more information the sample contains, the narrower the bell of the sampling distribution.
For the Poisson model the calculation can be done by hand. The second derivative of its log-likelihood is \(\ell''(\lambda)=-\sum x_i/\lambda^2\) (see the box of Section 4). At \(\hat\lambda=\overline x\) the sum of the counts is \(n\hat\lambda\), so for the ten quadrats
\[
\hat{\mathcal I}=\frac{n\hat\lambda}{\hat\lambda^2}=\frac{n}{\hat\lambda}=\frac{10}{2.2}\approx 4.55,
\qquad
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\lambda)=\frac{\hat\lambda}{n}=0.22,
\qquad
\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\hat\lambda)=\sqrt{0.22}\approx 0.47.
\]
The result, \(\sqrt{\hat\lambda/n}\), is the plug-in standard error that we obtained in Chapter 3 from the variance of a mean. For all 50 quadrats it gives the 0.21 seedlings per quadrat of that chapter.









CautionStatistical detail: the Hessian matrix





With several parameters the observed information is a matrix. The matrix of second derivatives of a function is called its Hessian, and the Hessian of the NLL at the estimates is the observed information matrix. For two parameters \(\theta_1\) and \(\theta_2\),
\[
\mathbf H=
\begin{pmatrix}
\dfrac{\partial^2(-\ell)}{\partial\theta_1^2} &
\dfrac{\partial^2(-\ell)}{\partial\theta_1\,\partial\theta_2}\\[2ex]
\dfrac{\partial^2(-\ell)}{\partial\theta_2\,\partial\theta_1} &
\dfrac{\partial^2(-\ell)}{\partial\theta_2^2}
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\hat{\boldsymbol\Sigma}=\mathbf H^{-1},
\]
where the derivatives are evaluated at the estimates (see the calculus supplement for partial derivatives) and \(\hat{\boldsymbol\Sigma}\) is the estimate of the covariance matrix of the estimates. In plain English, the inverse of the Hessian has the variances of the estimates on its diagonal and their covariances outside it. The elements outside the diagonal of the Hessian measure how the slope of the NLL along one parameter changes with the other parameter, which is what makes the contours of a likelihood surface tilted.
The Hessian refers to the parameters that the optimiser searched over. For the ten quadrats, written in terms of \(\log(\lambda)\), the NLL is \(\sum_i\left(e^{\log(\lambda)}-x_i\log(\lambda)\right)\) plus a constant, so its second derivative with respect to \(\log(\lambda)\) is \(n\lambda\). At the estimate this is \(10\times 2.2=22\), and the standard error of the estimate of \(\log(\lambda)\) is \(1/\sqrt{22}\approx 0.213\).
In R, optim() returns a numerical Hessian of the function that it minimised when it is called with hessian = TRUE, and solve() inverts a matrix. sdreport() does both steps for us, so we use it instead (the practical takes the Hessian from optim() once, for comparison).





6.1.2 Standard errors with TMB
The function sdreport() of RTMB calculates the standard errors of any model processed with MakeADFun(). It takes the object after the fit (it reads the estimates from the object), calculates the curvature of the NLL at the estimates and converts it into the covariance matrix of the estimates. summary() of its result is a table with one row per parameter, on the scale that was optimised, and two columns:

Estimate, the estimate of the parameter;
Std. Error, its standard error.

For the ten quadrats, the parameter that was optimised is \(\log(\lambda)\):

# sdreport() calculates the standard errors from the curvature at the estimates.
summary(sdreport(fir_ten_obj))

            Estimate Std. Error
log_lambda 0.7884573  0.2132007


The object returned by sdreport() also keeps the covariance matrix of the estimates in its element cov.fixed. A covariance divided by the two standard errors is the correlation between the estimates, which Chapter 2 introduced as a parameter of the bivariate Normal distribution, and cov2cor() does this conversion for a whole matrix. For the owl model we calculate the correlation in both parameterisations of Figure 4:

# Standard errors of log(mu) and log(k), and the correlation between their estimates.
owl_sd = sdreport(owl_obj)
summary(owl_sd)

        Estimate Std. Error
log_mu  1.559007  0.1635722
log_k  -1.116410  0.1654527

cov2cor(owl_sd$cov.fixed)

             log_mu        log_k
log_mu 1.000000e+00 6.196508e-08
log_k  6.196508e-08 1.000000e+00

# The correlation in the parameterisation with k and p.
cov2cor(sdreport(owl_prob_obj)$cov.fixed)

            log_k   logit_p
log_k   1.0000000 0.7111355
logit_p 0.7111355 1.0000000


For the estimates of \(\log(\mu)\) and \(\log(k)\) the correlation is zero to four decimals, because the contours of Figure 3 are not tilted. For those of \(\log(k)\) and \(\operatorname{logit}(p)\) it is 0.71: hypothetical samples that overestimate \(k\) would also tend to overestimate \(p\). This is the tilt of the contours in Figure 4 expressed as a number.


6.1.3 Standard errors on the original scale
The standard errors of sdreport() refer to the scale that was optimised. For the ten quadrats this is the standard error of the estimate of \(\log(\lambda)\), 0.213, and not of \(\hat\lambda\). The estimate can be transformed back with exp(), because by invariance the result is the MLE of \(\lambda\). The standard error cannot: exp(0.213) is 1.24, which is not a standard error of \(\hat\lambda\). It could not have been one, because the exponential of a positive number is always larger than one, so it would stay above 1 seedling per quadrat however many quadrats we sampled, whereas a standard error becomes smaller as the sample grows.
The reason is that a non-linear function does not pass through an average. For a non-linear function \(g\) and a random variable \(X\) that varies, in general
\[
E[g(X)]\neq g(E[X]).
\]
In plain English, the mean of a transformed variable is not the transformation of the mean. A variance is an average, the expectation of the squared distance from the mean (see Chapter 2), and a standard error is its square root, so neither of them can be carried to a new scale by applying the transformation to it. An estimate and the endpoints of an interval are values of the parameter and not averages, which is why they can be transformed back.
The standard error on the new scale is calculated instead with the delta method, which treats the transformation as a straight line near the estimate and multiplies the standard error by the slope of that line. It is an approximation, because the transformation is not a straight line, but it is good when the standard error is small and it is widely used. The box on the delta method below gives its formula, and Chapter 6 applies it to a fitted curve, a quantity that depends on several parameters. In TMB we ask for it with the function ADREPORT(). Placed inside the NLL, ADREPORT(x) tells sdreport() to report the quantity x, calculated from the parameters, with its standard error: TMB applies the delta method and adds a row for x to the table.






CautionStatistical detail: Jensen’s inequality





Jensen’s inequality gives the direction of the difference between \(E[g(X)]\) and \(g(E[X])\): \(E[g(X)]\ge g(E[X])\) if \(g\) is convex (its curve bends upwards, as the exponential does) and \(E[g(X)]\le g(E[X])\) if \(g\) is concave (its curve bends downwards, as the logarithm does). So the curvature of the function decides the sign of the difference, but the difference exists for any non-linear function. For example, if \(X\) takes the values 0 and 2 with equal probabilities, the exponential of its mean is \(\exp(1)\approx 2.72\), whereas the mean of its exponential is \((\exp(0)+\exp(2))/2\approx 4.19\).









CautionStatistical detail: the delta method





The delta method uses the first derivative of the transformation \(g\) at the estimate (see the rules of differentiation of the calculus supplement), which tells us how much the function stretches small differences around the estimate:
\[
\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(g(\hat\theta))\approx
\left|g'(\hat\theta)\right|\,\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\hat\theta).
\]
In plain English, the standard error on the new scale is approximately the standard error on the old scale multiplied by the slope of the transformation at the estimate. Each transformation therefore has its own correction:

For a log-transformed parameter, the transformation back is the exponential, whose derivative is the exponential itself. The delta method multiplies the standard error on the log scale by the estimate: for the ten quadrats, \(\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\hat\lambda)\approx\hat\lambda\,\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\log(\hat\lambda))=2.2\times 0.213\approx 0.47\), the standard error of the box on Fisher information.12
For a probability fitted on the logit scale, the transformation back is the inverse logit, \(p=1/(1+e^{-\operatorname{logit}(p)})\), whose derivative is \(p(1-p)\). The delta method multiplies the standard error on the logit scale by \(\hat p(1-\hat p)\).

For a quantity that depends on several parameters the slope becomes a vector of partial derivatives, which is combined with the covariance matrix of the estimates (Chapter 6).



For the ten quadrats we add one line to the Poisson NLL, ADREPORT(lambda), which asks for the standard error of \(\lambda\) itself. sdreport() reads the estimates from the processed object, so we process the new NLL and fit it again (the estimate does not change) before we call it:

# The Poisson NLL with one more line.
poisson_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  lambda = exp(log_lambda)
  # Ask for the standard error of lambda itself.
  ADREPORT(lambda)
  -sum(dpois(x = counts, lambda = lambda, log = TRUE))
}

# Process the new NLL for the ten quadrats, fit it again and calculate the standard errors.
fir_ten_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(poisson_nll, list(counts = ten_counts)),
  list(log_lambda = log(1)),
  silent = TRUE
)
fir_ten_fit = optim(
  par = fir_ten_obj$par,
  fn = fir_ten_obj$fn,
  gr = fir_ten_obj$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)
fir_ten_summary = summary(sdreport(fir_ten_obj))
fir_ten_summary

            Estimate Std. Error
log_lambda 0.7884573  0.2132007
lambda     2.1999999  0.4690415


The last row is the quantity that we asked for with ADREPORT(). Its standard error, 0.47 seedlings per quadrat, is the estimate multiplied by the standard error of \(\log(\hat\lambda)\), \(2.2\times 0.213\), as the delta method for the exponential says. For the owl model we add ADREPORT(k) in the same way:

# The Negative Binomial NLL with one more line.
nb_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  mu = exp(log_mu)
  k = exp(log_k)
  # Ask for the standard error of k itself.
  ADREPORT(k)
  -sum(dnbinom2(x = calls, mu = mu, size = k, log = TRUE))
}

# Process the new NLL, fit it again and calculate the standard errors.
owl_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(nb_nll, list(calls = call_counts)),
  list(log_mu = log(mu_mom), log_k = log(k_mom)),
  silent = TRUE
)
owl_fit = optim(par = owl_obj$par, fn = owl_obj$fn, gr = owl_obj$gr, method = "BFGS")
owl_sd = sdreport(owl_obj)
owl_summary = summary(owl_sd)
owl_summary

         Estimate Std. Error
log_mu  1.5590071 0.16357220
log_k  -1.1164100 0.16545266
k       0.3274532 0.05417801


The standard error of \(\hat k\) in the last row, 0.054, is again the estimate multiplied by the standard error of \(\log(\hat k)\), \(0.327\times 0.165\).


6.1.4 Wald intervals on the original and log scales
With a standard error on each scale we can calculate a Wald interval for \(\lambda\) in two ways: on the original scale, from the row lambda, or on the log scale, from the row log_lambda, with its endpoints transformed back with exp(). Unlike a standard error, the endpoints of an interval can be transformed directly:13

# Wald intervals for the Poisson mean of the ten quadrats, in seedlings per quadrat.
critical_value = qnorm(p = 0.975)

# On the original scale, from the row of ADREPORT().
wald_original = fir_ten_summary["lambda", "Estimate"] +
  c(-1, 1) * critical_value * fir_ten_summary["lambda", "Std. Error"]

# On the log scale, with the endpoints transformed back.
wald_log = exp(
  fir_ten_summary["log_lambda", "Estimate"] +
    c(-1, 1) * critical_value * fir_ten_summary["log_lambda", "Std. Error"]
)

rbind(wald_original, wald_log)

                  [,1]     [,2]
wald_original 1.280695 3.119304
wald_log      1.448591 3.341177


The interval from the log scale (1.45 to 3.34 seedlings per quadrat) differs from the interval on the original scale (1.28 to 3.12), although both are 95% Wald intervals for the same parameter and the same data. This is not due to the back-transformation of the endpoints but because Wald intervals rely on the sampling distribution being Normal, and how well this holds depends on the scale of the parameter. The sampling distribution of a parameter that was transformed to make it unconstrained approaches the Normal distribution faster (in terms of sample size) than on the original scale, because constraints on parameter values make sampling distributions skewed when the standard error is relatively large. In terms of the log-likelihood, the curve is closer to a parabola when the parameter is on the log scale. So the transformation of parameters is not only useful for the optimisation algorithm, it also makes Wald intervals more reliable, and we calculate them on the scale that was optimised. We do the same for the owl model, where we also calculate the interval for \(k\) on the original scale, from the row of ADREPORT():

# Lower and upper endpoints of a Wald interval for every row of the table.
owl_lower = owl_summary[, "Estimate"] - critical_value * owl_summary[, "Std. Error"]
owl_upper = owl_summary[, "Estimate"] + critical_value * owl_summary[, "Std. Error"]

# Rows log_mu and log_k: intervals on the log scales, with the endpoints transformed back.
owl_wald_mu = exp(c(owl_lower[["log_mu"]], owl_upper[["log_mu"]]))
owl_wald_k = exp(c(owl_lower[["log_k"]], owl_upper[["log_k"]]))

# Row k, from ADREPORT(): interval for k on the original scale.
owl_wald_k_original = c(owl_lower[["k"]], owl_upper[["k"]])

We compare these intervals with the likelihood profile intervals in Section 6.2.






Practice 3: an interval from the log scale



In Practice 2, about ticks on lizards, the fit on the log scale returned par = 0.92. For that parameter, sdreport() reports a standard error of 0.141. Calculate a 95% Wald interval for the mean number of ticks per lizard. Why is it not symmetric around the estimate?






TipSolution





The standard error is that of the estimate of the logarithm of the mean, so we calculate the interval on the log scale and transform its endpoints:

# Wald interval on the log scale, back-transformed to ticks per lizard.
exp(0.92 + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(p = 0.975) * 0.141)

[1] 1.903406 3.308037


The interval goes from approximately 1.9 to 3.3 ticks per lizard, around an estimate of 2.5. It is symmetric on the log scale, and exp() stretches the part above the estimate more than the part below it.

title: Maximum likelihood estimation
text:
6.2 Likelihood profile intervals
The Wald interval uses the curvature of the log-likelihood at one point, its maximum. The likelihood profile interval uses the whole curve: it contains all the values of the parameter whose relative profile log-likelihood is above a cutoff, that is, the values that the data support almost as well as the estimate. The cutoff is chosen so that, in a large sample, the interval contains the parameter in approximately 95% of hypothetical samples. It is half the 0.95 quantile of a chi-squared distribution with one degree of freedom, a result known as Wilks’ theorem (stated in the box below). In R, the quantiles of a chi-squared distribution are calculated with qchisq():

# Cutoff for the relative profile log-likelihood: half the 95% quantile of a
# chi-squared distribution with one degree of freedom.
cutoff = qchisq(p = 0.95, df = 1) / 2
cutoff

[1] 1.920729








NoteLikelihood profile interval



An approximate 95% confidence interval for a parameter contains all the values whose profile log-likelihood is within 1.92 units of the maximum log-likelihood (half the 0.95 quantile of a chi-squared distribution with one degree of freedom). The other parameters of the model are re-estimated for each value.








CautionStatistical detail: Wilks’ theorem





The cutoff of the likelihood profile interval comes from Wilks’ theorem,14 which describes how far below its maximum the log-likelihood is at the parameter value that generated the data. Let \(\theta_0\) be that value for the parameter of interest. Then
\[
2\left[\ell(\hat\theta)-\ell_{\mathrm{prof}}(\theta_0)\right]
\overset{\mathrm{approx}}{\sim}\chi^2_1
\quad\text{for sufficiently large }n,
\]
where \(\ell(\hat\theta)\) is the maximum of the log-likelihood, \(\ell_{\mathrm{prof}}(\theta_0)\) is the profile log-likelihood at \(\theta_0\) (with a single parameter it is the log-likelihood itself) and \(\chi^2_1\) is the chi-squared distribution with one degree of freedom, which is the distribution of the square of a standard Normal variable. In plain English, across hypothetical samples the parameter value that generated the data is rarely far down the slope of the profile: twice its distance to the top behaves like the square of a standard Normal variable.15 So in about 95% of hypothetical samples the profile log-likelihood at \(\theta_0\) is within \(3.84/2=1.92\) units of the maximum. The likelihood profile interval contains \(\theta_0\) in exactly those samples, which gives it a coverage of approximately 95%.



The calculation of a likelihood profile interval follows the same two steps for every model and parameter. First, the profile: the parameter of interest is moved away from its estimate in small steps, the other parameters are re-estimated at each step by an optimisation of their own (an inner fit), and the NLL is recorded. With a single parameter there is nothing to re-estimate, and the profile is the log-likelihood itself. Second, the endpoints: the two values of the parameter, one below and one above the estimate, at which the relative profile log-likelihood crosses the cutoff. We do not program these steps ourselves, because two functions do them:

TMB::tmbprofile() calculates the profile of one parameter of a model that was processed with MakeADFun(). Its main arguments are the object and name, the name of the parameter to profile as it is written in the list of parameters; trace = FALSE stops the printing of progress. It returns a data frame with the values of the parameter and the NLL at each of them. The function belongs to the package TMB, on which RTMB is built and which is installed with it, so we write TMB::tmbprofile().
confint() takes the result of tmbprofile() and finds the two crossings of the cutoff, that is, the endpoints of the 95% likelihood profile interval.

The profile is calculated on the scale that was optimised, so we transform the endpoints back.

6.2.1 One parameter
The Poisson model has one parameter, so the endpoints of the interval are the two values of \(\lambda\) at which the relative log-likelihood of the ten quadrats equals \(-1.92\). We profile log_lambda in the object of the ten quadrats and collect the interval with the two Wald intervals:

# Profile of log(lambda) for the ten quadrats and its 95% interval, transformed back.
fir_ten_profile = TMB::tmbprofile(fir_ten_obj, name = "log_lambda", trace = FALSE)
likelihood_interval = exp(confint(fir_ten_profile))

# The three intervals for lambda (seedlings per quadrat) from the ten quadrats.
intervals_ten = rbind(wald_original, wald_log, likelihood_interval)
dimnames(intervals_ten) = list(
  c("Wald, original scale", "Wald, log scale", "Likelihood"),
  c("lower", "upper")
)
intervals_ten

                        lower    upper
Wald, original scale 1.280695 3.119304
Wald, log scale      1.448591 3.341177
Likelihood           1.404039 3.251559


The likelihood interval is not symmetric: it extends 0.80 below the estimate and 1.05 above it, following the asymmetry of the curve (Figure 5). It also does not depend on the scale, because a value of \(\lambda\) and its logarithm have the same likelihood: tmbprofile() searched over \(\log(\lambda)\), and the transformed endpoints are exactly the values of \(\lambda\) at which the curve of Figure 5 crosses the cutoff. The Wald interval on the original scale is the interval of the parabola: because \(z_{0.975}^2/2=1.92\), the parabola crosses the cutoff exactly at its endpoints. Where the curve is not a parabola, as on the left of the estimate, the two intervals disagree. The Wald interval from the log scale is closer to the likelihood interval, as expected from the previous section.








Figure 5: Relative log-likelihood of the counts of fir seedlings in the first ten quadrats (solid line) and its quadratic approximation on the original scale (dashed line). The horizontal line is the cutoff of the 95% interval, at -1.92. The likelihood interval contains the values where the curve is above the cutoff (dotted lines), and the Wald interval on the original scale those where the parabola is above it.





With all 50 quadrats the three intervals nearly coincide: 1.73 to 2.55 seedlings per quadrat for the Wald interval on the original scale (the interval of Chapter 3), 1.77 to 2.59 from the log scale and 1.76 to 2.57 for the likelihood interval. The log-likelihood of a larger sample is closer to a parabola around its maximum, so the quadratic approximation behind the Wald interval is better, and it hardly matters which interval we report.


6.2.2 Two parameters
The owl model has two parameters, so the interval of each of them is calculated from its profile (Section 5). At each value of \(\log(k)\) that it visits, tmbprofile() makes an inner fit that re-estimates \(\log(\mu)\), and the other way round when we profile \(\log(\mu)\). We do this for both parameters and collect the results with the Wald intervals:

# Profiles of log(mu) and log(k), and their 95% intervals transformed back.
owl_profile_mu = TMB::tmbprofile(owl_obj, name = "log_mu", trace = FALSE)
owl_profile_k = TMB::tmbprofile(owl_obj, name = "log_k", trace = FALSE)
owl_interval_mu = exp(confint(owl_profile_mu))
owl_interval_k = exp(confint(owl_profile_k))

# Profile intervals next to the Wald intervals.
owl_intervals = rbind(
  owl_interval_mu, owl_wald_mu, owl_interval_k, owl_wald_k, owl_wald_k_original
)
dimnames(owl_intervals) = list(
  c("mu, profile", "mu, Wald from the log scale",
    "k, profile", "k, Wald from the log scale", "k, Wald on the original scale"),
  c("lower", "upper")
)
owl_intervals

                                  lower     upper
mu, profile                   3.4877013 6.6831687
mu, Wald from the log scale   3.4501283 6.5509016
k, profile                    0.2354070 0.4506711
k, Wald from the log scale    0.2367640 0.4528797
k, Wald on the original scale 0.2212663 0.4336402


For both parameters the Wald interval from the log scale is close to the likelihood profile interval (0.237 to 0.453 against 0.235 to 0.451 for \(k\)). The Wald interval for \(k\) on the original scale (0.221 to 0.434) is not: it is symmetric around the estimate, whereas the likelihood profile interval extends further above the estimate than below it, so both of its endpoints are too low. This is why we calculate Wald intervals on the scale that was optimised and transform their endpoints, and why the likelihood profile interval is the reference with which we compare them.

title: Maximum likelihood estimation
text:
6.3 Joint confidence regions
A joint confidence region is the counterpart of a confidence interval for two parameters at once. It is defined in the same way as the likelihood profile interval, with a cutoff of 3.00 units of log-likelihood instead of 1.92 (half the 0.95 quantile of a chi-squared distribution with two degrees of freedom, qchisq(p = 0.95, df = 2) / 2). The combinations of \(\mu\) and \(k\) whose relative log-likelihood is above \(-3.00\) form an approximate 95% joint confidence region, which is the area inside one contour of the likelihood surface (Figure 6). The region extends beyond the likelihood profile interval of each parameter, because it answers a question about both parameters at once: in about 95% of hypothetical samples it contains the pair of values that generated the data, which is more demanding than containing one of them. We use an interval when a question is about one parameter and a region when it is about a combination of parameters.








Figure 6: Approximate joint 95% confidence region for the mean and the shape of the Negative Binomial model fitted to the owl data (contour in vermillion). The segments along the axes are the 95% likelihood profile intervals of each parameter.











CautionStatistical detail: the cutoff for a joint region





Wilks’ theorem also applies to several parameters at once. If we fix two parameters at the same time, twice the drop in log-likelihood from the maximum follows approximately a chi-squared distribution with two degrees of freedom (the distribution of the sum of the squares of two independent standard Normal variables). The cutoff for the joint region is half its 0.95 quantile (5.99), qchisq(p = 0.95, df = 2) / 2.
A likelihood profile interval is a statement about one parameter, whatever the value of the other: it is the range that the contour at \(-1.92\) covers along one axis. Capturing two parameters simultaneously is more demanding than capturing one, so the cutoff of the joint region is further from the maximum. Note that the joint region is not the rectangle formed by the two separate intervals: the shape of the likelihood contours matters.

title: Maximum likelihood estimation
text:
6.4 Coverage checked by simulation
As in Chapter 3, we check the coverage of the intervals with a simulation in which we know the parameters. To simulate from a model that is written as an NLL, we mark the data inside it with OBS(). The object returned by MakeADFun() then has a function simulate(), which draws one hypothetical sample of the size of the data for the parameter values that we give it, on the scale that was optimised:

# The complete NLL of the Negative Binomial model.
nb_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  # Mark the data as observations, so that they can be simulated.
  calls = OBS(calls)
  mu = exp(log_mu)
  k = exp(log_k)
  ADREPORT(k)
  -sum(dnbinom2(x = calls, mu = mu, size = k, log = TRUE))
}

We process and fit it as before (the estimates do not change) and give simulate() the estimates on the log scale, which are in the element par of the fit. It returns a list in which the simulated data have the name that they have in the NLL (calls). For example, these are the first 20 counts of one hypothetical sample of 122 visits:

# Process and fit as before.
owl_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(nb_nll, list(calls = call_counts)),
  list(log_mu = log(mu_mom), log_k = log(k_mom)),
  silent = TRUE
)
owl_fit = optim(par = owl_obj$par, fn = owl_obj$fn, gr = owl_obj$gr, method = "BFGS")

# One hypothetical sample of 122 visits at the estimates: its first 20 counts.
set.seed(seed = 700)
owl_obj$simulate(owl_fit$par)$calls[1:20]

 [1]  2  6  0  4  7  9  0  0  2  3  7  1 10  4  0 18  0  0 32  7


For each hypothetical sample we calculate both types of interval and record whether each of them contains the parameter used to simulate (the code is not shown). We consider two cases with small samples, where the coverage of the intervals is not guaranteed (Figure 7). The first uses a Poisson model with a mean of 0.5 seedlings per quadrat and 5,000 hypothetical samples of ten quadrats, and compares the Wald interval on the original scale with the likelihood interval. The coverage of the Wald interval is 0.878, far from the intended 0.95, and that of the likelihood interval is 0.924.16 The second uses the Negative Binomial model with the owl estimates as parameters and 2,000 hypothetical samples of 20 visits, and compares, for the shape \(k\), the Wald interval calculated on the log scale with the likelihood profile interval. The coverages are 0.945 and 0.942, so here the two intervals perform equally well.








Figure 7: Simulated coverage of nominal 95% Wald and likelihood intervals. Poisson case: 5,000 hypothetical samples, interval for the mean on the original scale. Negative Binomial case: 2,000 hypothetical samples, interval for the shape k, with the Wald interval calculated on the log scale. The dashed line is the nominal level.





So the Wald interval fails on the original scale when the counts are few, where the log-likelihood is far from a parabola, and the likelihood interval is clearly better there. A Wald interval calculated on a suitable scale, such as the logarithm of a positive parameter, can be just as good as the likelihood profile interval, and it needs one fit instead of many. In the practical you will run a simulation of this kind for another model.






NoteWald and likelihood profile intervals



In this course we prefer likelihood profile intervals, because in small samples their coverage tends to be closer to the intended 95% than that of Wald intervals: they follow the shape of the log-likelihood instead of approximating it by a parabola at its maximum. The price is computation. A Wald interval needs only the fit and its Hessian, whereas a likelihood profile interval needs one optimisation of the other parameters for every value of the parameter on the profile, which takes longer and gives more fits that can fail. When this cost matters, a Wald interval calculated on a scale where the log-likelihood is close to a parabola (the logarithm of a positive parameter) is a reasonable approximation.

title: Maximum likelihood estimation
text:
7.1 Consistency and asymptotic normality
Maximum likelihood estimators are consistent when the observations are i.i.d. from the model: the chance that the estimate misses the parameter by more than any given margin becomes small as the sample grows. In the simulation we can calculate the fraction of the estimates that miss \(k\) by 0.1 or more (colMeans() takes the mean of each column, one per sample size, and the mean of TRUE and FALSE values is the fraction of TRUE values):

# Fraction of the estimates that differ by 0.1 or more from the shape used to simulate,
# for 20, 122 and 500 visits.
colMeans(abs(sim_k_ml - k_mle) >= 0.1)

[1] 0.447 0.066 0.000


The fraction is 45% with 20 visits, 7% with 122 visits and zero with 500 visits.






CautionStatistical detail: why maximum likelihood estimators are consistent





Why should the maximum of the likelihood be close to the parameter in a large sample (in the sense of the box on consistency in Chapter 3)?17 If we divide the log-likelihood by \(n\), which does not move its maximum, we obtain
\[
\frac{1}{n}\ell(\theta)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log\left(P(X_i=x_i\mid\theta)\right),
\]
the mean of \(\log(P(X=x\mid\theta))\) over the sample. This is an expectation under the empirical distribution of the sample (Chapter 3). As the sample grows, the empirical distribution converges to the distribution that generated the data (the Glivenko–Cantelli theorem), so the function that we maximise converges to the expectation of \(\log(P(X=x\mid\theta))\) under that distribution. It can be shown that this expectation is highest when \(\theta\) is the parameter that generated the data (the box on the Kullback–Leibler divergence in Section 7.4 says why).



How large the sample needs to be for the Normal approximation of Section 6 depends on the model and on the parameter (Figure 8). With 20 visits the estimates of \(k\) are strongly skewed: half of them are below 0.36, but a long tail to the right reaches values above 1, and their mean is 0.40, against the 0.327 used to simulate. With 500 visits their mean is 0.329, their distribution is nearly symmetric and the Normal curve is close to it.








Figure 8: Maximum likelihood estimates of the shape k from 2,000 hypothetical samples of 20 and of 500 visits, simulated from a Negative Binomial model with the estimates for the owls as parameters. The vertical line is the shape used in the simulation and the curves are Normal distributions with the mean and standard deviation of the estimates.





The simulation also checks the standard error of the owl fit. The hypothetical samples of 122 visits have the size of the owl data and were simulated with its estimates, so the standard deviation of their estimates of \(\log(k)\) is what the standard error of \(\log(\hat k)\) from sdreport() (0.165) approximates:

# Standard deviation of the estimates of log(k) across the hypothetical samples
# of 122 visits (second column of sim_k_ml).
sd(log(sim_k_ml[, 2]))

[1] 0.1617958


The two agree closely (0.162 against 0.165), so with a sample of this size the standard error from one fit describes the variation across hypothetical samples well.

title: Maximum likelihood estimation
text:
7.2 Efficiency
An estimator is more efficient than another estimator of the same parameter when its estimates vary less across hypothetical samples. This is the property that separates maximum likelihood from the method of moments. Both estimators of \(k\) are consistent, but they use different information from the sample: the method of moments reproduces the mean and the variance of the sample, whereas maximum likelihood makes every observed count as probable as possible. To compare them, we calculate the method-of-moments estimate of \(k\) from each of the hypothetical samples that we kept:

# Method-of-moments estimates of k from the same hypothetical samples. k exists only
# when the variance is larger than the mean; otherwise the estimate stays NA.
sim_k_mom = matrix(NA, nrow = n_samples, ncol = length(visit_sizes))
for (s in seq_along(visit_sizes)) {
  for (i in seq_len(n_samples)) {
    sim_mu = mean(sim_samples[[s]][i, ])
    sim_var = mean((sim_samples[[s]][i, ] - sim_mu)^2)
    if (sim_var > sim_mu) {
      sim_k_mom[i, s] = sim_mu^2 / (sim_var - sim_mu)
    }
  }
}

We then compare the standard deviations and the mean squared errors (MSE, Chapter 3) of the two sets of estimates; in the column names ml stands for maximum likelihood and mom for the method of moments:

# Standard deviation and mean squared error of both estimators of k for each number of
# visits. na.rm = TRUE skips any sample without a method-of-moments estimate.
efficiency_table = data.frame(
  visits = visit_sizes,
  sd_ml = apply(sim_k_ml, 2, sd),
  sd_mom = apply(sim_k_mom, 2, sd, na.rm = TRUE),
  mse_ml = colMeans((sim_k_ml - k_mle)^2),
  mse_mom = colMeans((sim_k_mom - k_mle)^2, na.rm = TRUE)
)
signif(efficiency_table, digits = 3)

  visits  sd_ml sd_mom   mse_ml mse_mom
1     20 0.1980 0.2800 0.043900 0.11700
2    122 0.0547 0.0862 0.003060 0.00849
3    500 0.0242 0.0421 0.000587 0.00186


With 122 visits the standard deviation of the estimates is 0.055 for maximum likelihood against 0.086 for the method of moments, and the gap remains with 500 visits (0.024 against 0.042). Standard errors decrease with the square root of the sample size, so the method of moments would need about \((0.086/0.055)^2\approx 2.5\) times as many visits to estimate \(k\) with the precision that maximum likelihood achieves with 122.
What the simulation shows for this model is a general property. An MLE is asymptotically efficient: in large samples no other regular estimator of the same parameter is more precise, because the variance that an MLE approaches, the one given by the curvature of the log-likelihood (the inverse of the Fisher information, see the box in Section 6.1.1), is the smallest that such an estimator can have. For your own analysis, this is the reason to fit a model by maximum likelihood whenever you can write its likelihood.






CautionStatistical detail: the Cramér–Rao bound





How small can the variance of an estimator be? The Cramér–Rao bound states that no unbiased estimator has a variance smaller than the inverse of the Fisher information:18
\[
\operatorname{Var}(\tilde\theta)\ge\frac{1}{\mathcal I(\theta)}
\quad\text{for any unbiased estimator }\tilde\theta.
\]
In plain English, the information in a sample sets a limit to the precision with which a parameter can be estimated from it, whatever the method. The variance of an MLE approaches this limit as the sample grows, which is what asymptotic efficiency means.

title: Maximum likelihood estimation
text:
7.3 Bias in finite samples
As for the estimators of Chapter 3, the large-sample results say little about small samples, where MLEs are in general biased. The relative bias of \(\hat k\) in the simulation is:

# Relative bias of the maximum likelihood estimator of k for each number of visits.
data.frame(visits = visit_sizes, relative_bias = colMeans(sim_k_ml) / k_mle - 1)

  visits relative_bias
1     20   0.213488485
2    122   0.026271812
3    500   0.005605524


With 20 visits, \(\hat k\) is on average 21% larger than the \(k\) used to simulate, with 122 visits 2.6% and with 500 visits 0.6%. The bias decreases faster than the standard error as the sample grows, so in a large sample it is negligible compared with the variation of the estimates across hypothetical samples.19 For a small sample, the properties of this section are approximations, and simulation is the way to check them.

title: Maximum likelihood estimation
text:
7.4 Misspecified models
This section can be skipped at a first reading: the rest of the chapter does not depend on it. All the properties above assume that the observations are a random sample from the model. Chapter 1 described the model as an approximation of the data generating process, so this assumption is never exactly right. A model is misspecified when it does not contain the distribution of the data generating process, whatever the values of its parameters. What does the MLE estimate in that case?
The answer is that, as the sample grows, the MLE converges to the parameter values for which the model distribution is closest to the distribution of the data generating process. That is, the fitted model is the best approximation that the model can offer, and the estimates are the parameters of that approximation (the box below says how closeness is measured). The standard errors and confidence intervals of Section 6 are calculated as if the model had generated the data, so with a misspecified model they are approximations too.






CautionStatistical detail: the Kullback–Leibler divergence





The closeness between the model and the data generating process is measured by the Kullback–Leibler divergence,20 which for a discrete variable is
\[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\theta)
= E_g\left[\log\left(\frac{g(X)}{P(X\mid\theta)}\right)\right]
= \sum_x g(x)\log\left(\frac{g(x)}{P(X=x\mid\theta)}\right),
\]
where \(g(x)\) is the probability with which the data generating process produces the value \(x\), \(P(X=x\mid\theta)\) is the probability that the model assigns to it, and \(E_g\) is an expectation (Chapter 2) calculated with the probabilities \(g\). In plain English, the divergence is the average, over the values that the data generating process produces, of the logarithm of the ratio between the probability of a value and the probability that the model gives to it. It is zero when the model assigns the right probability to every value, and positive otherwise.
This completes the intuition given in the box on consistency. The expectation of \(\log(P(X\mid\theta))\), which the log-likelihood divided by \(n\) approaches in a large sample, is the only part of the divergence that depends on \(\theta\), and it enters with a minus sign. Maximising the likelihood therefore amounts to minimising the divergence between the model and the data generating process. When the model contains the distribution that generated the data, the minimum is zero and it is reached at the parameter that generated them, which is consistency. When it does not, the MLE settles on the best approximation that the model can offer.

title: Maximum likelihood estimation
text:
Footnotes


The vertical bar reads “for a given value of”: \(P(X=x\mid\theta)\) is the probability of \(x\) for a given value of \(\theta\), and \(L(\theta\mid x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) is the likelihood of \(\theta\) for a given sample. The same symbol is used for conditional distributions, which are introduced in Chapter 7.↩︎
Fisher introduced the maximum likelihood method in 1912, in a paper that he wrote as an undergraduate student and in which he called it an “absolute criterion”. He introduced the word likelihood in 1921, to keep this quantity apart from a probability, and the name “maximum likelihood” in 1922, in the paper that set out the theory of the method. Choosing the parameter value under which the observations are most probable had been anticipated in the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries by Lambert, Daniel Bernoulli and Gauss, although without a reasoned defence of the method. If you want to read more about this history, see Aldrich (1997), “R. A. Fisher and the making of maximum likelihood 1912–1922”, Statistical Science 12: 162–176, and Stigler (2007), “The epic story of maximum likelihood”, Statistical Science 22: 598–620.↩︎
The likelihood is also at the core of Bayesian inference. There it is multiplied by a prior distribution, which describes what is known about the parameter before seeing the data, and the product is rescaled to give a probability distribution for the parameter (the posterior distribution). Chapter 1 explains why this book stays with the Frequentist interpretation.↩︎
The Normal model is another of them. The MLE of \(\mu\) is the mean of the sample and the MLE of \(\sigma^2\) is the variance with divisor \(n\), that is, the method-of-moments estimators of Chapter 3. The MLE of the variance is therefore biased.↩︎
The derivative of the log-likelihood with respect to a parameter is called the score. The MLE is the value of the parameter(s) at which the score is zero.↩︎
See Zehna (1966), “Invariance of maximum likelihood estimators”, Annals of Mathematical Statistics 37: 744, for the general statement.↩︎
The interval is named after Abraham Wald, who developed in 1943 the large-sample test on which it is based.↩︎
Fisher used the large-sample standard error of maximum likelihood estimators in 1922 and developed the concept of information in 1925, with arguments that were not rigorous. The result was made rigorous by Wald (1943) and by Cramér (1946), whose treatment states the conditions explicitly.↩︎
These results require some conditions on the model, known as regularity conditions. In words: the parameter is not on the boundary of its range (e.g., a variance of exactly zero), the support of the distribution does not depend on the parameter, the log-likelihood is a smooth function of the parameters, and the number of parameters does not grow with the sample size.↩︎
Mathematically the curvature is given by the negative of the second derivative↩︎
Efron and Hinkley (1978) compared them and argued for the observed information.↩︎
The two numbers agree exactly because both come from the curvature of the same log-likelihood at its maximum. Both are still large-sample approximations of the standard deviation of \(\hat\lambda\) across hypothetical samples.↩︎
That is because the logarithm is an increasing function: \(\log(\lambda)\) lies between the two endpoints on the log scale exactly when \(\lambda\) lies between their exponentials. So the interval contains the parameter in the same hypothetical samples on both scales, and its coverage is kept.↩︎
Wilks (1938). The theorem is about the ratio between two maximised likelihoods (a difference between two log-likelihoods is the logarithm of a likelihood ratio), and it holds under the regularity conditions that asymptotic normality requires. The likelihood profile interval follows from it.↩︎
The same result is the basis of the likelihood ratio test, which compares two nested models by calculating a p-value from the chi-squared distribution. As with p-values in general, we do not use it in this course.↩︎
A sample in which all the quadrats are empty gives an estimate of zero. The Wald interval on the original scale then collapses to \([0,0]\). The simulation counts such a sample as a miss for both intervals; it happens in less than 1% of these samples.↩︎
The consistency of maximum likelihood estimators was proved rigorously, under regularity conditions, by Abraham Wald (1949).↩︎
The bound was derived independently in the 1940s by Fréchet, Darmois, Rao and Cramér, and it carries the names of the last two. Fisher had already obtained a version for large samples in 1925.↩︎
Corrections of the bias exist for particular models. Dividing by \(n-1\) in the estimator of a variance is one of them (Chapter 3). Restricted maximum likelihood (REML) is the general approach to reduce the bias of the estimates of variance parameters, and it is used with the models for grouped observations of Chapter 7.↩︎
Kullback and Leibler (1951) introduced this measure of “information for discrimination” between two distributions, which is now called the Kullback–Leibler divergence. Maximum likelihood estimation under a misspecified model is studied by White (1982), “Maximum likelihood estimation of misspecified models”, Econometrica; Huber (1967) is an earlier treatment.↩︎
Akaike (1973, 1974) derived the criterion as an estimate of a loss based on the Kullback–Leibler divergence. Reading the term \(2K\) as a correction for using the same data twice is the usual interpretation of the criterion.↩︎
The correction was derived by Sugiura (1978) for linear regression with Normal errors and extended by Hurvich and Tsai (1989), “Regression and time series model selection in small samples”, Biometrika. Burnham and Anderson (2002), Model selection and multimodel inference, recommend AICc whenever \(n/K\) is smaller than about 40.↩︎

title: Chapter 4: Maximum likelihood estimation — solutions
text:
The fully worked first exercise is on the student practical page. These solutions use the same data, tasks and seeds as Exercises 2–5 on that page. Exercises 1 to 4 are the core of the practical and Exercise 5 is extra practice.
As on that page, we load RTMB first and RTMBdist second, and define the helper cmb() that connects a likelihood to a data set:
# Load RTMB first and RTMBdist second.
library(RTMB)
library(RTMBdist)

# Connect a likelihood to a data set.
cmb = function(f, d) function(p) f(p, d)

title: Chapter 4: Maximum likelihood estimation — solutions
text:
1.1 Solution

1.1.1 Question 1
The observational unit is one quadrat. As in the Chapter 3 practical, the method of moments equates the mean and the variance of the model with those of the sample, which gives \(\hat\mu=\overline x\) and \(\hat k_{\mathrm{MM}}=\hat\mu^2/(\hat\sigma^2-\hat\mu)\), where \(\hat\sigma^2\) is the variance of the sample with divisor \(n\):

# Method-of-moments estimates, as in the practical of Chapter 3: the mean, the variance
# with divisor n, and the shape k from variance = mu + mu^2 / k.
mu_mom_lily = mean(lily_counts)
var_mom_lily = mean((lily_counts - mu_mom_lily)^2)
k_mom_lily = mu_mom_lily^2 / (var_mom_lily - mu_mom_lily)

c(
  n_quadrats = n_lily,
  mean = mu_mom_lily,
  var = var_mom_lily,
  k_mom = k_mom_lily,
  fraction_empty = mean(lily_counts == 0),
  maximum = max(lily_counts)
)

    n_quadrats           mean            var          k_mom fraction_empty 
   256.0000000      3.9570312     54.3458099      0.3107457      0.4960938 
       maximum 
    72.0000000 


There are 256 quadrats, with a mean of 3.96 seedlings per quadrat and a variance of 54.3, almost 14 times the mean. The method-of-moments estimate of the shape is therefore small, \(\hat k_{\mathrm{MM}}\approx 0.31\). Half of the quadrats have no seedlings (127 of 256, a fraction of 0.496), while the largest count is 72 seedlings.


1.1.2 Question 2
The NLL is the one of the theory, with dnbinom2() and with \(\log\mu\) and \(\log k\) as parameters, so that both stay positive. Here the data are called counts, so that is the name that the list of data must use when we connect the NLL to the seedling counts. We start the search at the method-of-moments estimates. The function fn of the object returns the NLL for any vector of parameters on the log scale, so we also use it to calculate the log-likelihood at the method-of-moments estimates:

# Negative log-likelihood of the Negative Binomial model with mean mu and shape k.
nb_nll = function(parms, data) {
  # Make the elements of both lists available by name.
  getAll(parms, data)
  # Transform the parameters to the original scale.
  mu = exp(log_mu)
  k = exp(log_k)
  -sum(dnbinom2(x = counts, mu = mu, size = k, log = TRUE))
}

# Process the NLL of the seedling counts, starting from the method-of-moments estimates
# on the log scale.
lily_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(nb_nll, list(counts = lily_counts)),
  list(log_mu = log(mu_mom_lily), log_k = log(k_mom_lily)),
  silent = TRUE
)

# Log-likelihood at the method-of-moments estimates, on the log scale.
loglik_mom_lily = -lily_obj$fn(c(log(mu_mom_lily), log(k_mom_lily)))

# Fit with BFGS and check the convergence code.
lily_fit = optim(par = lily_obj$par, fn = lily_obj$fn, gr = lily_obj$gr, method = "BFGS")
lily_fit$convergence

[1] 0

# Estimates on the original scale.
mu_mle_lily = unname(exp(lily_fit$par["log_mu"]))
k_mle_lily = unname(exp(lily_fit$par["log_k"]))
c(mu_mle = mu_mle_lily, k_mle = k_mle_lily)

   mu_mle     k_mle 
3.9570312 0.2615053 

# Log-likelihood at the maximum likelihood estimates and at the method-of-moments estimates.
loglik_mle_lily = -lily_fit$value
c(mle = loglik_mle_lily, mom = loglik_mom_lily)

      mle       mom 
-564.2299 -565.3384 


The convergence code is 0. The maximum likelihood estimates are \(\hat\mu\approx 3.96\) seedlings per quadrat, which is the mean of the sample (as for any Negative Binomial model), and \(\hat k\approx 0.26\), somewhat smaller than the method-of-moments estimate of 0.31. The log-likelihood is \(-564.2\) at the maximum likelihood estimates and \(-565.3\) at the method-of-moments estimates. The difference of 1.1 units means that the observed counts are about three times more probable (\(e^{1.1}\)) under the former.


1.1.3 Question 3
The grids of the question contain both pairs of estimates with some margin. We fill a matrix that has one row per value of \(\mu\) and one column per value of \(k\). Inside the loops we call lily_obj$fn() with the logarithms of the candidate values and change the sign of the NLL that it returns. The cutoff for a joint region of two parameters is half the 0.95 quantile of a chi-squared distribution with two degrees of freedom (see Uncertainty from the likelihood):

# Grids of candidate values for the mean (seedlings per quadrat) and the shape.
mu_grid_lily = seq(from = 2.5, to = 6, length.out = 71)
k_grid_lily = seq(from = 0.17, to = 0.42, length.out = 71)

# Fill a matrix with two nested loops: row i is the i-th mean and column j the j-th shape.
# fn() takes log(mu) and log(k) and returns the NLL.
loglik_surface_lily = matrix(NA, nrow = length(mu_grid_lily), ncol = length(k_grid_lily))
for (i in seq_along(mu_grid_lily)) {
  for (j in seq_along(k_grid_lily)) {
    loglik_surface_lily[i, j] = -lily_obj$fn(c(log(mu_grid_lily[i]), log(k_grid_lily[j])))
  }
}

# Relative log-likelihood: the difference from the maximum found by optim().
relative_surface_lily = loglik_surface_lily - loglik_mle_lily

# Cutoff of the relative log-likelihood for a joint 95% region of two parameters:
# half the 95% quantile of a chi-squared distribution with two degrees of freedom.
joint_cutoff = qchisq(p = 0.95, df = 2) / 2
joint_cutoff

[1] 2.995732


The function contour() draws the matrix, as in the Chapter 1 practical. A second call with add = TRUE draws the contour of the joint region on top of the first plot, and points() adds the two pairs of estimates:

# Contours of the relative log-likelihood with base R, then the joint region on top.
contour(
  x = mu_grid_lily,
  y = k_grid_lily,
  z = relative_surface_lily,
  levels = c(-12, -9, -6, -4, -2, -1),
  xlab = "Mean (seedlings per quadrat)",
  ylab = "Shape (k)"
)
contour(
  x = mu_grid_lily,
  y = k_grid_lily,
  z = relative_surface_lily,
  levels = -joint_cutoff,
  lwd = 2,
  col = "#D55E00",
  add = TRUE,
  drawlabels = FALSE
)

# Maximum likelihood estimate (circle) and method-of-moments estimate (triangle).
points(x = mu_mle_lily, y = k_mle_lily, pch = 16, col = "#D55E00")
points(x = mu_mom_lily, y = k_mom_lily, pch = 17)







Figure 1: Contours of the relative log-likelihood of the glacier lily seedling counts as a function of the mean and the shape of the Negative Binomial model. The circle is the maximum likelihood estimate, the triangle is the method-of-moments estimate and the thick contour is the approximate joint 95% confidence region.





The cutoff is 3.00. The thick contour in Figure 1 joins the combinations of \(\mu\) and \(k\) whose log-likelihood is 3.00 units below the maximum, and the area inside it is the approximate joint 95% confidence region. As for the owls in the theory, the contours are not tilted: with the mean as a parameter, the estimates of \(\mu\) and \(k\) hardly depend on each other. The method-of-moments estimate lies inside the region, near its upper edge in \(k\) (its relative log-likelihood is \(-1.1\), as we saw in question 2). So for these data the method-of-moments estimates are among the combinations of parameter values that the likelihood supports.


1.1.4 Question 4
For the Wald interval, sdreport() gives the standard errors of the estimates of \(\log\mu\) and \(\log k\). We calculate the interval for \(\log k\) and transform its endpoints with exp():

# 0.975 quantile of the standard Normal distribution.
critical_value = qnorm(p = 0.975)

# Standard errors of the estimates of log(mu) and log(k).
lily_sd = sdreport(lily_obj)
lily_summary = summary(lily_sd)
lily_summary

        Estimate Std. Error
log_mu  1.375494  0.1261932
log_k  -1.341301  0.1170098

# Wald interval for k: calculate on the log scale and back-transform the endpoints.
wald_k_lily = exp(
  lily_summary["log_k", "Estimate"] +
    c(-1, 1) * critical_value * lily_summary["log_k", "Std. Error"]
)
wald_k_lily

[1] 0.2079130 0.3289118


The standard errors are 0.126 for the estimate of \(\log\mu\) and 0.117 for the estimate of \(\log k\), and the Wald interval for \(k\) goes from 0.208 to 0.329.
For the likelihood profile interval we follow the theory. TMB::tmbprofile() moves \(\log k\) away from its estimate and re-estimates \(\log\mu\) at each step, and confint() locates the two values at which the relative profile log-likelihood crosses the cutoff. The profile is calculated for \(\log k\), so we transform the endpoints with exp():

# Profile of log(k) and the endpoints of its 95% interval, transformed back.
lily_profile_k = TMB::tmbprofile(lily_obj, name = "log_k", trace = FALSE)
exp(confint(lily_profile_k))

          lower     upper
log_k 0.2072426 0.3279545


The likelihood profile interval for \(k\) goes from 0.207 to 0.328. The Wald interval goes from 0.208 to 0.329, so the two intervals agree to two decimals. With 256 quadrats the profile log-likelihood is close to a parabola on the log scale of \(k\), and the fast approximation gives the same answer as the reference method.


1.1.5 Question 5
We calculate the relative frequency of every count, from zero to the largest one in the sample, and its probability under both models. For the Poisson model the MLE of \(\lambda\) is the mean of the sample, so no optimisation is needed. The AIC is \(2K-2\ell(\hat\theta)\), with \(K=1\) for the Poisson model and \(K=2\) for the Negative Binomial model:

# Relative frequency of every count from zero to the largest one: the fraction of
# quadrats with that number of seedlings.
count_values_lily = 0:max(lily_counts)
observed_lily = rep(NA, times = length(count_values_lily))
for (i in seq_along(count_values_lily)) {
  observed_lily[i] = mean(lily_counts == count_values_lily[i])
}

# Fitted probabilities of every count under the Negative Binomial and Poisson models. The
# MLE of the Poisson mean is the sample mean.
lambda_mle_lily = mean(lily_counts)
nb_probability = dnbinom2(x = count_values_lily, mu = mu_mle_lily, size = k_mle_lily)
poisson_probability = dpois(x = count_values_lily, lambda = lambda_mle_lily)

# Fraction of empty quadrats: observed and under each model.
c(
  observed = mean(lily_counts == 0),
  negative_binomial = dnbinom2(x = 0, mu = mu_mle_lily, size = k_mle_lily),
  poisson = dpois(x = 0, lambda = lambda_mle_lily)
)

         observed negative_binomial           poisson 
       0.49609375        0.48326452        0.01911979 

# Log-likelihood of the Poisson model at its maximum, and AIC = 2K - 2 * log-likelihood
# of both models, with K the number of estimated parameters.
loglik_poisson_lily = sum(dpois(x = lily_counts, lambda = lambda_mle_lily, log = TRUE))
n_parms_lily = c(poisson = 1, negative_binomial = 2)
loglik_lily = c(poisson = loglik_poisson_lily, negative_binomial = loglik_mle_lily)
aic_lily = 2 * n_parms_lily - 2 * loglik_lily
aic_lily

          poisson negative_binomial 
         2731.833          1132.460 

# AICc adds 2K(K + 1) / (n - K - 1) to the AIC, with n the number of quadrats.
aicc_lily = aic_lily + 2 * n_parms_lily * (n_parms_lily + 1) / (n_lily - n_parms_lily - 1)
aicc_lily

          poisson negative_binomial 
         2731.849          1132.507 



# Relative frequencies of the sample as vertical lines, up to 40 seedlings.
plot(
  x = count_values_lily,
  y = observed_lily,
  type = "h",
  lwd = 3,
  col = "grey60",
  xlim = c(0, 40),
  xlab = "Number of seedlings per quadrat",
  ylab = "Relative frequency or probability"
)

# Probabilities under the two fitted models, as points joined by lines.
lines(x = count_values_lily, y = nb_probability, type = "o", pch = 16, col = "#D55E00")
lines(x = count_values_lily, y = poisson_probability, type = "o", pch = 1, lty = 2)
legend(
  "topright",
  legend = c("Sample", "Negative Binomial", "Poisson"),
  col = c("grey60", "#D55E00", "black"),
  lty = c(1, 1, 2),
  lwd = c(3, 1, 1),
  pch = c(NA, 16, 1),
  bty = "n"
)







Figure 2: Relative frequencies of the number of seedlings per quadrat (grey vertical lines) and probabilities under the fitted Negative Binomial and Poisson models, up to 40 seedlings.





The observed fraction of empty quadrats is 0.496. The fitted Negative Binomial model gives a probability of 0.483 to an empty quadrat and the Poisson model only 0.019. Figure 2 shows the same for the other counts (the horizontal axis ends at 40 seedlings, which leaves out the quadrat with 72). The Poisson distribution concentrates its probability around its mean of 4 seedlings, whereas the Negative Binomial distribution follows both the many empty quadrats and the long tail of large counts.
The AIC is 2731.8 for the Poisson model and 1132.5 for the Negative Binomial model. The difference of 1,599 units is very large compared with the two units that the additional parameter costs, so the Negative Binomial model is strongly preferred. AIC ranks the candidates that we give it. Whether there is a better description of the empty quadrats than the Negative Binomial model is the question of Exercise 3.
The AICc is also 2731.8 and 1132.5 (to one decimal), so the comparison is the same. The correction is negligible because 256 quadrats are many more than one or two parameters.

title: Chapter 4: Maximum likelihood estimation — solutions
text:
2.1 Solution

2.1.1 Question 1
The function follows the two cases of the mass function. It first calculates the Poisson probability of every count multiplied by \(1-p_0\), and then adds \(p_0\) where the count is zero. ifelse() applies its test to every element of x and returns the second argument where the test is TRUE and the third where it is FALSE, so the function accepts a vector of counts, like the d* functions of R. With log = TRUE it returns the logarithm of the result:

# Mass function of a zero-inflated Poisson distribution: with probability pzero a quadrat
# cannot have seedlings, otherwise the count follows a Poisson distribution.
my_dzipois = function(x, lambda, pzero, log = FALSE) {
  # Poisson probability scaled by the probability of belonging to the Poisson part.
  result = (1 - pzero) * dpois(x = x, lambda = lambda)
  # An empty quadrat can come from either part, so pzero is added to the probability of zero.
  result = ifelse(x == 0, pzero + result, result)
  if (log) {
    log(result)
  } else {
    result
  }
}

# The probabilities add up to one over a wide range of counts.
sum(my_dzipois(x = 0:200, lambda = 7.9, pzero = 0.5))

[1] 1

sum(my_dzipois(x = 0:200, lambda = 2, pzero = 0.1))

[1] 1

# The same probabilities from dzipois() of RTMBdist, for the counts 0 to 3, and the
# largest difference between the two functions over all the counts.
my_dzipois(x = 0:3, lambda = 2, pzero = 0.1)

[1] 0.2218018 0.2436035 0.2436035 0.1624023

dzipois(x = 0:3, lambda = 2, zeroprob = 0.1)

[1] 0.2218018 0.2436035 0.2436035 0.1624023

max(abs(
  my_dzipois(x = 0:200, lambda = 7.9, pzero = 0.5) -
    dzipois(x = 0:200, lambda = 7.9, zeroprob = 0.5)
))

[1] 1.387779e-17


Both sums are 1, as they should be for a probability mass function. We used two different pairs of parameter values, the first of which is close to the estimates of question 2. Our function and dzipois() return the same probabilities (the largest difference is of the order of \(10^{-17}\), the precision of the computer), so from here on we use dzipois().


2.1.2 Question 2
Both parameters are constrained. The mean \(\lambda\) is positive, so we search over \(\log\lambda\), and \(p_0\) is a probability, so we search over \(\operatorname{logit}p_0\) and transform it with plogis(). For the starting values, suppose that every empty quadrat is one that cannot have seedlings. Then \(p_0\) is the fraction of empty quadrats and \(\lambda\) is the mean of the quadrats that have seedlings:

# Negative log-likelihood of the zero-inflated Poisson model.
zip_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  # Transform the parameters to the original scale.
  lambda = exp(log_lambda)
  pzero = plogis(logit_pzero)
  -sum(dzipois(x = counts, lambda = lambda, zeroprob = pzero, log = TRUE))
}

# Starting values from the data: the mean of the non-empty quadrats for lambda and the
# fraction of empty quadrats for pzero.
lambda_start = mean(lily_counts[lily_counts > 0])
pzero_start = mean(lily_counts == 0)
c(lambda_start = lambda_start, pzero_start = pzero_start)

lambda_start  pzero_start 
   7.8527132    0.4960938 

# Process the NLL with the starting values on the optimised scale, and fit it.
zip_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(zip_nll, list(counts = lily_counts)),
  list(log_lambda = log(lambda_start), logit_pzero = qlogis(p = pzero_start)),
  silent = TRUE
)
zip_fit = optim(par = zip_obj$par, fn = zip_obj$fn, gr = zip_obj$gr, method = "BFGS")
zip_fit$convergence

[1] 0

# Estimates on the original scale and the maximum log-likelihood.
lambda_zip = unname(exp(zip_fit$par["log_lambda"]))
pzero_zip = unname(plogis(zip_fit$par["logit_pzero"]))
loglik_zip = -zip_fit$value
c(lambda = lambda_zip, pzero = pzero_zip, loglik = loglik_zip)

      lambda        pzero       loglik 
   7.8496514    0.4958972 -848.0293019 

# Probability of a count of zero under a Poisson distribution with the estimated lambda.
dpois(x = 0, lambda = lambda_zip)

[1] 0.0003898879


The convergence code is 0. The estimates are \(\hat\lambda\approx 7.85\) seedlings per quadrat and \(\hat p_0\approx 0.496\), and the maximum log-likelihood is \(-848.0\). According to this model, about half of the quadrats cannot have seedlings and the other half have 7.85 seedlings on average. The estimates are almost identical to the starting values (7.85 and 0.496). The reason is that a Poisson distribution with a mean of 7.85 gives a probability of only 0.0004 to a count of zero, so the model attributes practically all the empty quadrats to the zero inflation.


2.1.3 Question 3
The zero-inflated Poisson model has two parameters, like the Negative Binomial model:

# AIC of the zero-inflated Poisson model (K = 2) next to the Negative Binomial model of
# Exercise 2 (K = 2): with the same K, the comparison is a comparison of log-likelihoods.
aic_zip = 2 * 2 - 2 * loglik_zip
c(zero_inflated_poisson = aic_zip, negative_binomial = aic_lily[["negative_binomial"]])

zero_inflated_poisson     negative_binomial 
             1700.059              1132.460 

# AICc of both models: the correction 2K(K + 1) / (n - K - 1) is the same for both.
aicc_zip = aic_zip + 2 * 2 * (2 + 1) / (n_lily - 2 - 1)
c(zero_inflated_poisson = aicc_zip, negative_binomial = aicc_lily[["negative_binomial"]])

zero_inflated_poisson     negative_binomial 
             1700.106              1132.507 


The AIC is 1700.1 for the zero-inflated Poisson model and 1132.5 for the Negative Binomial model. Both models have \(K=2\), so the term \(2K\) cancels in the difference and the comparison comes down to the maximum log-likelihoods: the difference of 567.6 units of AIC is twice the difference of 283.8 units of log-likelihood (\(-564.2\) against \(-848.0\)). The Negative Binomial model is strongly preferred. The Poisson model without zero inflation had an AIC of 2731.8 in Exercise 2, so allowing for quadrats that cannot have seedlings improves the Poisson model a great deal, but not enough. The AICc is 1700.1 and 1132.5. The correction of 0.047 units is the same for both models, because they have the same \(K\) and the same \(n\), so the difference does not change either.


2.1.4 Question 4
We calculate the two probabilities under each model, together with the corresponding fractions of the sample. The probability of 20 or more seedlings is one minus the probability of 19 or fewer, which the cumulative distribution functions pzipois() and pnbinom2() of RTMBdist give. One minus the sum of the probabilities of 0 to 19 seedlings, for example 1 - sum(dzipois(x = 0:19, lambda = lambda_zip, zeroprob = pzero_zip)), gives the same result:

# Probabilities of every count under the zero-inflated Poisson model, for the figure.
zip_probability = dzipois(x = count_values_lily, lambda = lambda_zip, zeroprob = pzero_zip)

# Probability of zero and of 20 or more seedlings: observed, zero-inflated Poisson and
# Negative Binomial.
c(
  zero_observed = mean(lily_counts == 0),
  zero_zip = dzipois(x = 0, lambda = lambda_zip, zeroprob = pzero_zip),
  zero_nb = dnbinom2(x = 0, mu = mu_mle_lily, size = k_mle_lily)
)

zero_observed      zero_zip       zero_nb 
    0.4960938     0.4960937     0.4832645 

c(
  twenty_or_more_observed = mean(lily_counts >= 20),
  twenty_or_more_zip = 1 - pzipois(q = 19, lambda = lambda_zip, zeroprob = pzero_zip),
  twenty_or_more_nb = 1 - pnbinom2(q = 19, mu = mu_mle_lily, size = k_mle_lily)
)

twenty_or_more_observed      twenty_or_more_zip       twenty_or_more_nb 
           0.0390625000            0.0001003246            0.0494588951 



# Relative frequencies of the sample as vertical lines, up to 40 seedlings.
plot(
  x = count_values_lily,
  y = observed_lily,
  type = "h",
  lwd = 3,
  col = "grey60",
  xlim = c(0, 40),
  xlab = "Number of seedlings per quadrat",
  ylab = "Relative frequency or probability"
)

# Probabilities under the two fitted models, as points joined by lines.
lines(x = count_values_lily, y = nb_probability, type = "o", pch = 16, col = "#D55E00")
lines(x = count_values_lily, y = zip_probability, type = "o", pch = 1, lty = 2)
legend(
  "topright",
  legend = c("Sample", "Negative Binomial", "Zero-inflated Poisson"),
  col = c("grey60", "#D55E00", "black"),
  lty = c(1, 1, 2),
  lwd = c(3, 1, 1),
  pch = c(NA, 16, 1),
  bty = "n"
)







Figure 3: Relative frequencies of the number of seedlings per quadrat (grey vertical lines) and probabilities under the fitted zero-inflated Poisson and Negative Binomial models, up to 40 seedlings.





The zero-inflated Poisson model reproduces the fraction of empty quadrats exactly (0.496) and the Negative Binomial model almost (0.483). The models differ at the other end of the distribution (Figure 3). Ten of the 256 quadrats (3.9%) have 20 or more seedlings. The Negative Binomial model gives a probability of 0.049 to such counts and the zero-inflated Poisson model 0.0001. In the latter, the quadrats that are not empty follow a Poisson distribution, whose variance equals its mean of 7.85, and that makes counts of 20 or more almost impossible. Each of those ten quadrats then contributes a very low probability to the likelihood, which is where the zero-inflated Poisson model loses most of its log-likelihood.
The two models describe the origin of the counts differently. In the zero-inflated Poisson model there are two kinds of quadrats: those that cannot have seedlings, and those in which seedlings occur with one common mean and little variation around it. In the Negative Binomial model there is one kind of quadrat, and the counts vary strongly around a common mean, which produces both the many empty quadrats and the few crowded ones. AIC tells us that the second description fits these counts much better. It does not tell us why the seedlings are distributed in this way. As Chapter 2 explains, a distribution does not identify the source of the overdispersion, and different processes (for example, the dispersal of seeds around the parent plants, or differences in how suitable the quadrats are for germination) can produce the same distribution of counts. The two mechanisms could also act together, as in the zero-inflated Negative Binomial distribution of the supplement, which we do not fit here. To learn about the cause we would need other measurements on the quadrats in addition to the counts.

title: Chapter 4: Maximum likelihood estimation — solutions
text:
3.1 Solution

3.1.1 Question 1
The observational unit is one tree, and the data are the 31 volumes in cubic feet. dgamma() returns a density, so the NLL is minus the sum of the log densities. Both parameters are positive and we search over their logarithms. The line with OBS() marks the data as observations, which does not change the fit and allows us to simulate from the model in Exercise 5. For the starting values we solve \(E[X]=k/r\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=k/r^2\) for the parameters, which gives \(k=E[X]^2/\operatorname{Var}(X)\) and \(r=E[X]/\operatorname{Var}(X)\), and we insert the mean and the variance of the sample (with divisor \(n\)):

# Load the black cherry data from the datasets package and keep the timber volume (cubic feet).
data(trees, package = "datasets")
tree_volume = trees$Volume
n_trees = length(tree_volume)

# Negative log-likelihood of the Gamma model with shape k and rate r.
# dgamma() returns a density, so these are log densities.
gamma_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  # Mark the data as observations, so that they can be simulated in Exercise 5.
  x = OBS(x)
  # Transform the parameters to the original scale.
  shape = exp(log_shape)
  rate = exp(log_rate)
  -sum(dgamma(x = x, shape = shape, rate = rate, log = TRUE))
}

# Method-of-moments starting values from E[X] = k / r and Var(X) = k / r^2,
# which give k = mean^2 / variance and r = mean / variance.
volume_mean = mean(tree_volume)
volume_variance = mean((tree_volume - volume_mean)^2)
shape_mom_volume = volume_mean^2 / volume_variance
rate_mom_volume = volume_mean / volume_variance

# Process the NLL of the tree volumes and fit it.
volume_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(gamma_nll, list(x = tree_volume)),
  list(log_shape = log(shape_mom_volume), log_rate = log(rate_mom_volume)),
  silent = TRUE
)
volume_fit = optim(
  par = volume_obj$par,
  fn = volume_obj$fn,
  gr = volume_obj$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)
volume_fit$convergence

[1] 0

# Estimates on the original scale and the mean of the fitted model, by invariance.
shape_volume = unname(exp(volume_fit$par["log_shape"]))
rate_volume = unname(exp(volume_fit$par["log_rate"]))
c(
  shape = shape_volume,
  rate_per_ft3 = rate_volume,
  mean_ft3 = shape_volume / rate_volume,
  sample_mean_ft3 = volume_mean,
  nll = volume_fit$value
)

          shape    rate_per_ft3        mean_ft3 sample_mean_ft3             nll 
      3.8860256       0.1288004      30.1709132      30.1709677     125.7260431 


The convergence code is 0. The estimates are \(\hat k\approx 3.89\), which has no units, and \(\hat r\approx 0.129\)/ft³. The rate has the units of one over the measurement, so that \(k/r\) is a volume. By invariance, the MLE of the mean volume is \(\hat k/\hat r\approx 30.2\) ft³. It equals the mean of the sample: as for the Negative Binomial model, the MLE of the mean of a Gamma model is the sample mean. The minimum of the NLL is 125.7, that is, a maximum log-likelihood of \(-125.7\).


3.1.2 Question 2
sdreport() keeps the inverse of the Hessian in its element cov.fixed, and cov2cor() converts it into correlations. For the surface we use the same nested loops as in Exercise 2, now with volume_obj$fn():

# Correlation between the estimates of log(k) and log(r), from the covariance matrix
# kept by sdreport().
volume_sd = sdreport(volume_obj)
cov2cor(volume_sd$cov.fixed)

          log_shape  log_rate
log_shape 1.0000000 0.9367653
log_rate  0.9367653 1.0000000

# Grids of candidate values for the shape and the rate (1/ft³).
shape_grid = seq(from = 1.5, to = 8, length.out = 71)
rate_grid = seq(from = 0.04, to = 0.3, length.out = 71)

# Fill the matrix of log-likelihoods with two nested loops; fn() takes log(k) and log(r)
# and returns the NLL.
loglik_surface_volume = matrix(NA, nrow = length(shape_grid), ncol = length(rate_grid))
for (i in seq_along(shape_grid)) {
  for (j in seq_along(rate_grid)) {
    loglik_surface_volume[i, j] = -volume_obj$fn(c(log(shape_grid[i]), log(rate_grid[j])))
  }
}
relative_surface_volume = loglik_surface_volume + volume_fit$value


# Contours of the relative log-likelihood and the maximum likelihood estimate.
contour(
  x = shape_grid,
  y = rate_grid,
  z = relative_surface_volume,
  levels = c(-12, -9, -6, -4, -2, -1),
  xlab = "Shape (k)",
  ylab = "Rate (r, 1/ft³)"
)
points(x = shape_volume, y = rate_volume, pch = 16, col = "#D55E00")







Figure 4: Contours of the relative log-likelihood of the tree volumes as a function of the shape and the rate of the Gamma model. The circle is the maximum likelihood estimate.





The correlation between the estimates of \(\log k\) and \(\log r\) is 0.94, and the contours of Figure 4 are strongly tilted: a larger shape goes with a larger rate (the outer contours are cut by the edges of the grid). The reason is the same as for the parameters size and prob of the Negative Binomial distribution in the theory. The data determine the mean volume \(k/r\) well, so a higher value of \(k\) can be compensated by a higher value of \(r\) that keeps the mean close to 30 ft³, with little loss of likelihood. The tilt means that the estimates of the two parameters depend on each other: a hypothetical sample that overestimates the shape would tend to overestimate the rate too.


3.1.3 Question 3
The slice fixes the rate at its estimate and varies the shape, so we evaluate volume_obj$fn() on a grid of 261 values of the shape.
