The profile re-estimates the rate for every value of the shape, which is what tmbprofile() does. From the columns log_shape and value of its result we calculate the shape and the relative log-likelihood, and with ytol = 6 the profile continues until a drop of six units, so that the plot covers the same range as the slice:

# Cutoff for a 95% interval of one parameter: half the 95% quantile of a chi-squared
# distribution with one degree of freedom.
cutoff = qchisq(p = 0.95, df = 1) / 2

# Slice: the rate is fixed at its estimate and the shape varies over a grid.
shape_fine = seq(from = 1.5, to = 8, length.out = 261)
slice_relative_volume = rep(NA, times = length(shape_fine))
for (i in seq_along(shape_fine)) {
  # Both values are NLLs, so the order of the difference is reversed.
  slice_relative_volume[i] =
    volume_fit$value - volume_obj$fn(c(log(shape_fine[i]), log(rate_volume)))
}

# Profile: for each shape the rate is re-estimated. ytol is the drop in log-likelihood
# at which the profile stops.
volume_profile_shape = TMB::tmbprofile(
  volume_obj,
  name = "log_shape",
  ytol = 6,
  trace = FALSE
)
profile_shape_volume = exp(volume_profile_shape$log_shape)
profile_relative_volume = volume_fit$value - volume_profile_shape$value

# Range of shapes within the cutoff of the maximum: from the grid for the slice and
# from confint() for the profile.
range(shape_fine[slice_relative_volume >= -cutoff])

[1] 3.275 4.550

exp(confint(volume_profile_shape))

             lower    upper
log_shape 2.321927 6.062832



# Relative log-likelihood along the profile, with the slice and the cutoff added.
plot(
  x = profile_shape_volume,
  y = profile_relative_volume,
  type = "l",
  xlim = c(1.5, 8),
  ylim = c(-6, 0),
  xlab = "Shape (k)",
  ylab = "Relative log-likelihood"
)
lines(x = shape_fine, y = slice_relative_volume, lty = 2)
abline(h = -cutoff, col = "grey40")
legend("topright", legend = c("Profile", "Slice"), lty = c(1, 2), bty = "n")







Figure 5: Slice (dashed line) and profile (solid line) of the relative log-likelihood for the shape of the Gamma model fitted to the tree volumes. The horizontal line is at minus half the 95% quantile of the chi-squared distribution with one degree of freedom.





The slice is within 1.92 units of the maximum for shapes between 3.28 and 4.55 (the grid has a step of 0.025, so these endpoints are accurate to about that amount), and the profile for shapes between 2.32 and 6.06. The range of the profile is the approximate 95% confidence interval for the shape. The slice is about a third as wide (Figure 5). It describes what the data would say about the shape if we knew that the rate is exactly 0.129/ft³. The rate is estimated from the same 31 trees, and because the two estimates are strongly correlated, fixing one of them removes most of the uncertainty about the other. The profile follows the ridge of the surface in Figure 4 and takes that uncertainty into account.

title: Chapter 4: Maximum likelihood estimation — solutions
text:
4.1 Solution

4.1.1 Question 1
The three lines inside the loop fit the model to the sample x as we fitted it to the tree volumes in Exercise 4: cmb() connects gamma_nll() to x, MakeADFun() processes it with the starting values of the question, optim() minimises it, and exp() turns the estimate of \(\log k\) into the shape. In the call we use the estimates of Exercise 4, shape_volume and rate_volume:

# Simulate n_samples hypothetical samples of n_obs observations from a Gamma model with
# the given shape and rate, and estimate the shape in each of them.
simulate_gamma_samples = function(n_obs, shape, rate, n_samples) {
  # One row per sample; the loop replaces the zeros by the results.
  results = data.frame(
    shape_ml = rep(0, times = n_samples),
    shape_mom = rep(0, times = n_samples),
    se_log_shape = rep(0, times = n_samples),
    converged = rep(FALSE, times = n_samples)
  )
  # An object with placeholder data of the right length, from which the samples are
  # simulated: the values of the data are not used.
  placeholder_obj = MakeADFun(
    cmb(gamma_nll, list(x = rep(0, times = n_obs))),
    list(log_shape = 0, log_rate = 0),
    silent = TRUE
  )
  for (i in seq_len(n_samples)) {
    # One hypothetical sample (simulate() takes the parameters on the log scale).
    x = placeholder_obj$simulate(log(c(shape, rate)))$x

    # Method-of-moments estimate of the shape, from the mean and the variance (divisor n).
    x_mean = mean(x)
    x_variance = mean((x - x_mean)^2)
    shape_mom = x_mean^2 / x_variance

    # Maximum likelihood fit, started at a shape of 1 and at the rate that gives the mean
    # of the sample, and the estimate of the shape on the original scale.
    sim_obj = MakeADFun(
      cmb(gamma_nll, list(x = x)),
      list(log_shape = log(1), log_rate = log(1 / x_mean)),
      silent = TRUE
    )
    fit = optim(par = sim_obj$par, fn = sim_obj$fn, gr = sim_obj$gr, method = "BFGS")
    shape_ml = exp(fit$par[["log_shape"]])

    # Store the results of this sample.
    results$shape_ml[i] = shape_ml
    results$shape_mom[i] = shape_mom
    results$se_log_shape[i] = summary(sdreport(sim_obj))["log_shape", "Std. Error"]
    results$converged[i] = fit$convergence == 0
  }
  results
}

# 2,000 hypothetical samples of 31 trees from the Gamma model fitted to the volumes.
set.seed(seed = 801)
trees_31 = simulate_gamma_samples(
  n_obs = 31,
  shape = shape_volume,
  rate = rate_volume,
  n_samples = 2000
)

# Number of samples in which the fit did not converge.
sum(!trees_31$converged)

[1] 0


The bias of an estimator is the difference between the mean of its estimates and the shape that we used to simulate, and the mean squared error (MSE) is the mean of the squared differences between the estimates and that shape:

# Mean, standard deviation and mean squared error of both estimators of the shape.
data.frame(
  estimator = c("maximum likelihood", "method of moments"),
  mean = c(mean(trees_31$shape_ml), mean(trees_31$shape_mom)),
  sd = c(sd(trees_31$shape_ml), sd(trees_31$shape_mom)),
  mse = c(
    mean((trees_31$shape_ml - shape_volume)^2),
    mean((trees_31$shape_mom - shape_volume)^2)
  )
)

           estimator     mean       sd      mse
1 maximum likelihood 4.331801 1.195417 1.627022
2  method of moments 4.434555 1.298154 1.985246

# Relative bias of both estimators: the mean estimate divided by the shape, minus one.
c(ml = mean(trees_31$shape_ml), mom = mean(trees_31$shape_mom)) / shape_volume - 1

       ml       mom 
0.1147123 0.1411542 


The shape used to simulate is 3.89. Across the 2,000 hypothetical samples, the maximum likelihood estimates have a mean of 4.33, a standard deviation of 1.20 and an MSE of 1.63. The method-of-moments estimates have a mean of 4.43, a standard deviation of 1.30 and an MSE of 1.99. No fit failed. So with 31 trees both estimators are biased upwards, by 11% and 14%, and the MLE is the better of the two: it has the smaller bias, the smaller standard deviation and the smaller MSE. These summaries are themselves estimates from 2,000 samples and they change somewhat with the seed.


4.1.2 Question 2
The endpoints are the logarithm of each estimate plus or minus critical_value standard errors, transformed back with exp(). The interval contains the shape when the lower endpoint is at most the shape and the upper endpoint at least the shape, which & combines into one logical value per sample:

# 95% Wald intervals for the shape in every sample: calculated on the log scale, with the
# endpoints transformed back.
lower = exp(log(trees_31$shape_ml) - critical_value * trees_31$se_log_shape)
upper = exp(log(trees_31$shape_ml) + critical_value * trees_31$se_log_shape)
# TRUE for the samples whose interval contains the shape used to simulate.
covered = lower <= shape_volume & shape_volume <= upper

# Coverage: the fraction of samples whose interval contains the shape.
mean(covered)

[1] 0.9305


The coverage is 0.931. A coverage simulated with 2,000 samples has a standard error of about 0.006 (\(\sqrt{0.93\times 0.07/2000}\)), so it is below the nominal 0.95 by about three standard errors. With 31 trees the Wald interval is an approximation, and it contains the shape slightly less often than its confidence level states.


4.1.3 Question 3
We call the same function with a sample size of 150 and the same shape and rate, and repeat the summaries of question 1 and the lines of question 2 with trees_150:

# 2,000 hypothetical samples of 150 trees from the Gamma model fitted to the volumes.
set.seed(seed = 802)
trees_150 = simulate_gamma_samples(
  n_obs = 150,
  shape = shape_volume,
  rate = rate_volume,
  n_samples = 2000
)
sum(!trees_150$converged)

[1] 0

# Mean, standard deviation and mean squared error of both estimators, and the relative
# bias of the maximum likelihood estimator.
data.frame(
  estimator = c("maximum likelihood", "method of moments"),
  mean = c(mean(trees_150$shape_ml), mean(trees_150$shape_mom)),
  sd = c(sd(trees_150$shape_ml), sd(trees_150$shape_mom)),
  mse = c(
    mean((trees_150$shape_ml - shape_volume)^2),
    mean((trees_150$shape_mom - shape_volume)^2)
  )
)

           estimator     mean        sd       mse
1 maximum likelihood 3.956943 0.4407889 0.1992269
2  method of moments 3.984846 0.5064105 0.2660889

mean(trees_150$shape_ml) / shape_volume - 1

[1] 0.01824931

# Wald intervals and their coverage, as in question 2.
lower = exp(log(trees_150$shape_ml) - critical_value * trees_150$se_log_shape)
upper = exp(log(trees_150$shape_ml) + critical_value * trees_150$se_log_shape)
covered = lower <= shape_volume & shape_volume <= upper
mean(covered)

[1] 0.95


No fit failed. With 150 trees the maximum likelihood estimates have a mean of 3.96, against the shape of 3.89 used to simulate, so the relative bias is 1.8% (11.5% with 31 trees). Their standard deviation falls from 1.20 to 0.44, and the coverage of the Wald interval is 0.950, equal to its confidence level within the simulation error of about 0.005. The model is the same in both simulations, so the change comes from the sample size alone. As the sample grows, the sampling distribution of the maximum likelihood estimator gets closer to a Normal distribution centred at the parameter, which is the large-sample result behind the Wald interval (see Properties of maximum likelihood estimators). With 31 trees that result is only an approximation.


4.1.4 Question 4
The simulations describe the estimators and the interval for a model whose parameters we chose: a Gamma model with the estimates of Exercise 4 as parameters. The parameters of the data generating process of the real trees are unknown, and the estimates differ from them. The difference can be considerable, since the confidence interval for the shape goes from 2.3 to 6.1 and question 1 shows that the estimate tends to be too large. The bias and the coverage would be somewhat different for another shape.
The simulated observations are also exactly i.i.d. from a Gamma distribution, whereas for the real measurements the Gamma model is an approximation, and the trees need not be independent of each other. With a misspecified model the properties of the estimators and of the intervals change (see Misspecified models), which these simulations do not explore. So the results approximate the behaviour of the estimators for the real data, and the approximation is better the closer the fitted model is to the data generating process.

title: Chapter 5: Deterministic functions in ecology
text:
Exercise 1 analyses one function from end to end, with data on the amount of virus in the blood of infected rabbits. Exercises 2 to 5 are drills without data, one for each skill of the chapter: limits, derivatives, special points and parameters. Exercises 6 and 7 are cases with real data: the rate of an enzymatic reaction (the data set Puromycin, which comes with R), the fecundity of fir trees and the recruitment of a reef fish. The data of Exercises 1 and 7 are in the package emdbook, which you need to install once with install.packages("emdbook"). As in the theory, the curves are placed over the data by eye and nothing is fitted, which is the topic of Chapter 6.
Before you start, read the entries of the function supplement that the exercises name. If derivatives are no longer familiar, work through the calculus refresher first. Questions that start with “On paper” and the drills of Exercises 2 to 5 are meant to be done with pen and paper before you open R (a calculator is fine for logarithms and exponentials). Work through the first exercise before trying the remaining ones. The ideas and notation are introduced in the Chapter 5 theory.

title: Chapter 5: Deterministic functions in ecology
text:
1.1 Solution

1.1.1 Question 1
The units follow from the two rules of the theory. The argument of an exponential has no units, so in \(e^{-bx}\) the parameter \(b\) must have the inverse units of \(x\): 1/day. The factor \(e^{-bx}\) then has no units either, so the product \(ax\) must have the units of \(f(x)\). As \(x\) is in days, \(a\) is in units of titre/day.
At \(x=0\) the function is \(f(0)=a\times0\times e^{0}=0\). As \(x\to\infty\) the factor \(x\) grows without bound while \(e^{-bx}\) goes to zero, so we have to find out which of the two wins. An exponential dominates any power of \(x\) (see Limits and asymptotes), so
\[
\lim_{x\to\infty}a\,x\,e^{-bx}=\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{a\,x}{e^{bx}}=0.
\]
The same result follows from L’Hôpital’s rule: the derivative of the numerator is \(a\) and that of the denominator is \(b\,e^{bx}\), and \(a/(b\,e^{bx})\to0\). So the function starts at zero and returns to zero, which is what a hump-shaped function has to do.


1.1.2 Question 2
The function is the product of \(g(x)=ax\) and \(h(x)=e^{-bx}\), with \(g'(x)=a\) and, by the rule for the exponential, \(h'(x)=-b\,e^{-bx}\). The product rule gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
f'(x) &= g'(x)\,h(x)+g(x)\,h'(x)\\
&= a\,e^{-bx}-ab\,x\,e^{-bx}\\
&= a\,(1-bx)\,e^{-bx}.
\end{aligned}
\]
At \(x=0\) the slope is \(f'(0)=a\). So \(a\) is the initial slope of the function, which agrees with its units (titre/day). As \(x\to\infty\) the slope goes to zero, by the same argument as in question 1, because the exponential dominates the factor \(1-bx\).
At the peak the slope is zero. Since \(a\) and \(e^{-bx}\) are positive, \(f'(x)=0\) only where \(1-bx=0\):
\[
x_{\max}=\frac{1}{b}, \qquad
f(x_{\max})=a\,\frac{1}{b}\,e^{-1}=\frac{a}{b\,e}.
\]
The slope is positive for \(x<1/b\) and negative for \(x>1/b\), so this critical point is a maximum. The location of the peak, \(1/b\), is in days, and its height is in units of titre, as it should be.


1.1.3 Question 3
We differentiate \(f'(x)=a(1-bx)e^{-bx}\), again with the product rule. The derivative of \(a(1-bx)\) is \(-ab\) and that of \(e^{-bx}\) is \(-b\,e^{-bx}\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
f''(x) &= -ab\,e^{-bx}-ab\,(1-bx)\,e^{-bx}\\
&= -ab\,(2-bx)\,e^{-bx}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The second derivative is zero where \(2-bx=0\), that is, at \(x=2/b\), which is twice the location of the peak. For \(x<2/b\) it is negative, so the function is concave (it bends downwards), and for \(x>2/b\) it is positive, so the function is convex (it bends upwards). The sign changes at \(x=2/b\), which makes it an inflection point. The value of the function and its slope at that point are
\[
f\!\left(\frac{2}{b}\right)=\frac{2a}{b\,e^{2}}, \qquad
f'\!\left(\frac{2}{b}\right)=a\,(1-2)\,e^{-2}=-\frac{a}{e^{2}}.
\]
This is the steepest decline of the function. Note that the value at the inflection point is \(2/e\approx0.74\) times the height of the peak.


1.1.4 Question 4
We plot the 27 observations (Figure 1):

# Titre against the day of the observation.
plot(titer ~ day, data = grade_1,
     xlab = "Time since infection (days)", ylab = "Virus titre (log10 infectious doses)")







Figure 1: Titre of the myxoma virus of grade 1 in the blood of rabbits against the time since infection.





The titre increases from about 5.5 on day 2 and levels off between 7 and 8 from day 6 onwards. The observations do not show a clear decline, so the location of the peak can only be read roughly. We take a peak on day 6 with a titre of 7.6. With the two results of question 2 we can go from the peak to the parameters. From \(x_{\max}=1/b\),
\[
b=\frac{1}{x_{\max}}=\frac{1}{6}\approx0.167 \text{/day},
\]
and from \(f(x_{\max})=a/(be)\),
\[
a=f(x_{\max})\,b\,e=\frac{7.6\times2.718}{6}\approx3.44 \text{ units of titre/day}.
\]
That is, a curve with this peak starts with a slope of 3.44 units of titre/day. Its inflection point is at \(2/b=12\) days, where the titre is \(2\times7.6/e\approx5.59\) and the slope is \(-3.44/e^2\approx-0.47\) units of titre/day. The observations end on day 9, so the inflection point lies outside the data.


1.1.5 Question 5
We write the function with the input first and the parameters after it, and draw it with the values of question 4 (Figure 2). The dashed lines mark the peak and the triangle marks the inflection point:

# Ricker function: initial slope a and rate b.
ricker = function(x, a = 1, b = 1) {
  a * x * exp(-b * x)
}

# Parameters calculated from a peak on day 6 with a titre of 7.6.
b_titre = 1 / 6
a_titre = 7.6 * exp(1) / 6

# The observations, with axes that start at zero and include the inflection point.
plot(titer ~ day, data = grade_1, xlim = c(0, 14), ylim = c(0, 10),
     xlab = "Time since infection (days)", ylab = "Virus titre (log10 infectious doses)")

# The curve, and dashed lines at the location and at the height of the peak.
curve(ricker(x, a = a_titre, b = b_titre), add = TRUE, col = "#D55E00")
abline(v = 1 / b_titre, h = 7.6, lty = 2)

# The inflection point: twice the location of the peak.
points(x = 2 / b_titre, y = ricker(2 / b_titre, a = a_titre, b = b_titre),
       pch = 17, col = "#D55E00")







Figure 2: The same observations with a Ricker function whose parameters were calculated from a peak read by eye (a = 3.44, b = 1/6). Dashed lines mark the peak and the triangle marks the inflection point.





We can verify our math with R:

# Peak of the function on a fine grid of days: location and height.
day_grid = seq(0, 14, by = 0.001)
titre_values = ricker(day_grid, a = a_titre, b = b_titre)
day_grid[which.max(titre_values)]

[1] 6

max(titre_values)

[1] 7.6

# Derivative with D() and with the formula of question 2, on day 2.
ricker_derivative = D(expression(a * x * exp(-b * x)), "x")
ricker_derivative

a * exp(-b * x) - a * x * (exp(-b * x) * b)

eval(ricker_derivative, list(a = a_titre, b = b_titre, x = 2))

[1] 1.644753

a_titre * (1 - b_titre * 2) * exp(-b_titre * 2)

[1] 1.644753

# Value of the function on days 2, 9 and 12 (the inflection point).
ricker(c(2, 9, 12), a = a_titre, b = b_titre)

[1] 4.934260 6.914450 5.591768


The highest value on the grid is 7.6 on day 6, as intended. D() does not simplify its result, but it returns the same slope as our formula: on day 2 the titre increases by 1.64 units of titre/day, about half of the initial slope. The value on day 12 is 5.59, as calculated on paper.
The curve passes through the middle of the observations between days 3 and 7. It gives a titre of 4.9 on day 2, a little below most of the observations of that day, and of 6.9 on day 9, where the observed titre is 7.7. The reason is the one that we met in the theory for the size of the tadpoles: in the Ricker function the parameter \(b\) sets both the location of the peak and the rate of the decline after it, so with a peak on day 6 the curve has to decline at a given rate, whether the observations do or not. A function with a third parameter, such as the generalised Ricker function, could separate the two. Whether the extra parameter is supported by the data needs fitted curves: the Chapter 6 practical fits the Ricker function to these data and gives the tools for the comparison.

title: Fitting ecological response curves
text:
In this chapter, we learn how to fit an ecological response curve to data: a deterministic function of a predictor describes one parameter of the distribution of each observation (usually its mean), and the parameters of the function are estimated by maximum likelihood. Once the curve is fitted, we estimate the uncertainty of its parameters and of the curve itself, check whether the fitted model describes the data, revise the model where it does not, and compare it with alternative models.
The chapter brings together the two pillars of the book, probability distributions and likelihood (Chapter 2 to Chapter 4) and deterministic functions (Chapter 5). What is new is the likelihood of a response curve, in which every observation has a distribution of its own; how RTMB calculates the gradient of the negative log-likelihood that the optimiser uses; the uncertainty of a fitted curve; residuals calculated by simulation from the fitted model; and two further tools for comparing models, the Bayesian information criterion and cross-validation. One example runs through the chapter, the functional response of dragonfly larvae that prey on reed frog tadpoles (Vonesh and Bolker 2005).1 These are the data that Chapter 5 used as a backdrop and for which it read starting values by eye. The observations are numbers of tadpoles killed out of a known number, so the distributions of the chapter are the Binomial and the Beta-Binomial, and the residuals are calculated with the package DHARMa. Every tank is treated as an independent observation; Chapter 7 extends the models to observations that come in groups.

title: Fitting ecological response curves
text:
4.1 The gradient and automatic differentiation
Since Chapter 4 we have given every NLL to MakeADFun() before fitting it. There we said that this step processes the NLL so that the tools of the course can work with it, and that RTMB supplies the slope that BFGS uses. We can now say what that slope is. The gradient of the NLL is the vector of its partial derivatives with respect to the parameters (Chapter 5), that is, its slope in the direction of each parameter. RTMB calculates it by automatic differentiation: from the code of the NLL, exactly up to rounding error, and without a formula from us. The element gr of the object returns the gradient at the parameter values that we give it, on the scale that is optimised, with one column per parameter in the order of the list of parameters:

# The gradient of the NLL at the starting values and at the estimates.
binomial_obj$gr(binomial_obj$par)

          [,1]     [,2]
[1,] -4.299806 3.199816

binomial_obj$gr(binomial_fit$par)

            [,1]         [,2]
[1,] 0.002183858 -0.004839986


At the starting values the gradient is not zero, and its signs tell BFGS in which direction to move each parameter to lower the NLL. At the estimates both elements are close to zero, as they should be at a minimum.
An exact gradient matters for response curves for three reasons. First, BFGS uses the gradient at every step to decide in which direction to move. Without gr, optim() approximates it by evaluating the NLL at nearby values of every parameter (Chapter 8 explains how), which costs time and accuracy. Second, the parameters of a curve are often correlated, as we will see in Section 5, so that the NLL forms a narrow and tilted valley like the one of the owl model in Chapter 4. In such a valley the direction of the next step depends on small differences between the partial derivatives, and an inexact gradient can stop the search before it reaches the minimum. Third, the same derivatives are behind the other tools of the course: sdreport() calculates the curvature of the NLL from them, ADREPORT() uses them for the standard errors of quantities calculated from the parameters (Section 5.3), and in Chapter 7 they are needed to integrate random effects out of the likelihood.
For RTMB to calculate these derivatives, the NLL must be written with operations and functions that RTMB knows. This is the reason why the probability mass and density functions of the course come from RTMB and RTMBdist.






CautionTechnical detail: how automatic differentiation works





RTMB is an R interface to the package Template Model Builder (TMB). MakeADFun() runs the NLL once, at the starting values, and records every elementary operation that the function carries out on the parameters (each sum, product, division, exponential and logarithm), in the order in which they happen. This record is called a tape. The derivative of each of these operations is known (they are the rules of differentiation), and the chain rule combines them along the tape into the derivative of the NLL with respect to every parameter. In plain English, RTMB differentiates the code of the NLL step by step, as we would differentiate a formula by hand. The result is exact up to rounding error: it is neither an algebraic formula nor a numerical approximation. The elements fn, gr and he (the Hessian) of the object all work from the tape. Because the tape runs through TMB’s compiled code, it cannot be stepped through like ordinary R code.









WarningWhen automatic differentiation needs care



RTMB works out the derivatives from the calculations that the NLL carried out when MakeADFun() ran it at the starting values, so every calculation that involves a parameter must have a derivative. A branch that depends on a parameter (an if that compares a parameter with a value) does not: if it were recorded, only the side taken at the starting values would be used afterwards. RTMB therefore refuses such a comparison, and MakeADFun() stops with the error “Comparison is generally unsafe for AD types”. In the same way, a curve with a sharp change at an unknown threshold has no derivative at the change. Such calculations need special care, and a smooth curve that approximates the sharp change is the usual solution. Check the NLL on sensible parameter values in R first (a function written with getAll() can be called directly with two lists), and inspect binomial_obj$fn(binomial_obj$par) and binomial_obj$gr(binomial_obj$par) before fitting.

title: Fitting ecological response curves
section: 5.1 Standard errors and correlation of the parameters
text:
5.1 Standard errors and correlation of the parameters
sdreport() calculates the standard errors and the covariance matrix of the estimates from the curvature of the NLL, as in Chapter 4. Two features are typical of the parameters of a curve. Their estimates are often strongly correlated, because different combinations of the parameters give similar curves over the range of the data. And how precisely each parameter is estimated depends on where along \(x\) the observations lie. Chapter 5 showed with partial derivatives that a curve responds to each parameter in a different part of its range; the observations that inform a parameter are those made where the curve responds to it. So data that cover only the rise of a saturating curve determine its initial slope better than its asymptote. The correlation also depends on the parameterisation, whereas the fit does not (see “Parameterisation, slices and profiles” in Chapter 4).
For the tanks, summary() gives the estimates and standard errors on the optimised scales, and cov2cor() turns the covariance matrix in the element cov.fixed into correlations:

# Standard errors on the optimised scales, and the correlation between the estimates.
binomial_sd = sdreport(binomial_obj)
summary(binomial_sd)

              Estimate Std. Error
logit_alpha  0.1035076  0.2850642
log_H       -4.0984242  0.2941594

cov2cor(binomial_sd$cov.fixed)

            logit_alpha     log_H
logit_alpha   1.0000000 0.8239933
log_H         0.8239933 1.0000000


The correlation between the estimates of \(\operatorname{logit}(\alpha)\) and \(\log(H)\) is 0.82. It is positive because a steeper initial rise of the curve (a larger \(\alpha\)) must be compensated by a stronger levelling off (a larger \(H\)) for the curve to pass through the tanks at high density, so hypothetical samples that overestimate one parameter tend to overestimate the other. In the Michaelis–Menten form, with \(\log(a)\) and \(\log(b)\), the same model has the same maximum and a correlation of 0.98: the estimates of the asymptote and of the half-maximum are almost interchangeable, because the data determine mainly their ratio, the initial slope \(a/b=\alpha\). This is what Chapter 5 found when it read starting values from these data (“Starting values by eye”). The densities of the experiment stop at 100 tadpoles per tank, below the estimated half-maximum of 115, so the tanks cover less than half of the rise of the curve. They determine \(\alpha\), which describes the start of the curve, much better than \(H\), which describes its end, as the intervals of the next section show.

title: Fitting ecological response curves
section: 5.2 Likelihood profile intervals of the parameters
text:
5.2 Likelihood profile intervals of the parameters
Likelihood profile intervals are calculated with TMB::tmbprofile() and confint(), as in Chapter 4, and they remain the reference method. With a response curve, the profile of a poorly determined parameter is often asymmetric, because the data rule out values on one side of the estimate much more strongly than on the other. The endpoints of the interval can be transformed with any monotonic function to give an interval for a quantity calculated from the parameter: an increasing function keeps their order and a decreasing function swaps them. We profile both parameters, transform the endpoints back, and calculate the interval of the largest number of tadpoles killed, \(1/H\), from that of \(H\):

# Profiles of logit(alpha) and log(H). Each profile contains the estimate twice, so
# confint() warns that it collapses repeated values; the warning can be ignored.
binomial_profile_alpha = TMB::tmbprofile(binomial_obj, name = "logit_alpha", trace = FALSE)
binomial_profile_H = TMB::tmbprofile(binomial_obj, name = "log_H", trace = FALSE)

# 95% intervals transformed back to the original scale.
alpha_interval = plogis(confint(binomial_profile_alpha))
H_interval = exp(confint(binomial_profile_H))

# 1 / H decreases with H, so the endpoints swap.
profile_intervals = rbind(alpha_interval, H_interval, rev(1 / H_interval))
dimnames(profile_intervals) = list(c("alpha", "H", "1/H"), c("lower", "upper"))
profile_intervals

             lower        upper
alpha  0.402430935   0.68246512
H      0.006988006   0.02638401
1/H   37.901737130 143.10233922


The interval for the attack rate, 0.40 to 0.68 per experiment, is narrow compared with the interval for the handling time, which spans almost a factor of four. Accordingly, the interval for the largest number of tadpoles that the larvae could kill in one experiment runs from 38 to 143 around an estimate of 60: it extends 22 tadpoles below the estimate and 83 above it, and its upper end lies beyond the largest density of the experiment. The data rule out a low asymptote, because the larvae killed up to 35 tadpoles, but not a high one. The profile is asymmetric even on the log scale, so the Wald interval from the log scale (34 to 107 tadpoles) misses most of the upper part of the profile interval.

title: Fitting ecological response curves
text:
5.3 Uncertainty of the fitted curve
A point of the curve, such as the expected number killed at a given density, is a quantity calculated from the parameters. Its standard error is requested with ADREPORT(), as in Chapter 4, where TMB applies the delta method (the box below gives the formula for several parameters). ADREPORT() of a vector reports every element with its own standard error, so if we pass a grid of predictor values in the list of data and calculate the curve on that grid inside the NLL, sdreport() returns the curve and its standard error at every point of the grid. From them we calculate a Wald interval at each point, on a scale on which the quantity is unbounded, and transform the endpoints back, for the same reasons as for the parameters in Chapter 4. For a probability that scale is the logit. Together the intervals form a confidence band.
The band is pointwise: at each value of \(x\), the interval contains the value of the curve under the data generating process at that \(x\) in approximately 95% of hypothetical samples. This is not the same as a band that contains the whole curve in 95% of hypothetical samples, which would be wider. The band also says nothing about where the observations of new tanks would fall: that is described by the distribution of the observations around the curve (Figure 1), which is much wider.
For the reed frogs we add a grid of densities from 0 to 100 tadpoles per tank to the list of data, as initial_grid:

# A grid of densities (tadpoles per tank), added to the list of data.
initial_grid = seq(from = 0, to = 100, by = 1)
frog_data$initial_grid = initial_grid

The NLL gains three lines, which calculate the probability that a tadpole is killed at every density of the grid, its logit with qlogis(), and ask for the standard error of every element with ADREPORT(). We process the new NLL, fit it again (the estimates do not change) and call sdreport():

# The Binomial NLL with three more lines.
binomial_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  alpha = plogis(logit_alpha)
  H = exp(log_H)
  p = alpha / (1 + alpha * H * initial)
  # The logit of the probability of being killed at every density of the grid.
  p_grid = alpha / (1 + alpha * H * initial_grid)
  logit_p_grid = qlogis(p_grid)
  ADREPORT(logit_p_grid)
  -sum(dbinom(x = killed, size = initial, prob = p, log = TRUE))
}

# Process the new NLL, fit it again and calculate the standard errors.
binomial_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(binomial_nll, frog_data),
  list(logit_alpha = qlogis(0.5), log_H = log(1 / 60)),
  silent = TRUE
)
binomial_fit = optim(
  par = binomial_obj$par,
  fn = binomial_obj$fn,
  gr = binomial_obj$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)
binomial_sd = sdreport(binomial_obj)

With the argument select = "report", summary() returns only the rows of the quantities requested with ADREPORT(), here one row per density of the grid. We calculate the Wald interval of each row on the logit scale, transform the endpoints back with plogis() and multiply them by the density to obtain the band for the expected number killed:

# Rows of logit_p_grid: one per density of the grid.
band_summary = summary(binomial_sd, select = "report")

# Wald intervals on the logit scale.
critical_value = qnorm(p = 0.975)
logit_lower = band_summary[, "Estimate"] - critical_value * band_summary[, "Std. Error"]
logit_upper = band_summary[, "Estimate"] + critical_value * band_summary[, "Std. Error"]

# The curve and its band for the expected number killed.
curve_band = data.frame(
  initial = initial_grid,
  killed = initial_grid * plogis(band_summary[, "Estimate"]),
  lower = initial_grid * plogis(logit_lower),
  upper = initial_grid * plogis(logit_upper)
)

Figure 3 shows the band with the data, the formula of the model and the estimates. On the logit scale the band is narrowest near 50 tadpoles per tank and wider towards both ends. The tanks at low density hold few tadpoles each, so most of the information about the curve comes from the denser tanks, and the band widens away from the middle of that information. For the expected number killed the band also widens with density because the probability is multiplied by the number of tadpoles; at the highest density it runs from about 24 to 33 tadpoles killed. So within the range of the data the curve is well determined, although its asymptote is not. Beyond 100 tadpoles per tank the band would widen quickly, because there the curve depends more and more on the asymptote.






CautionStatistical detail: the delta method for several parameters





Let \(g(\boldsymbol\theta)\) be a quantity calculated from the vector of parameters \(\boldsymbol\theta\) (on the scale that was optimised), such as the logit of the curve at one density. Close to the estimates, the function \(g\) is replaced by its tangent plane, the extension of the tangent line of the one-parameter case to several parameters. The variance of a linear function of the estimates follows from their covariance matrix, which gives
\[
\operatorname{Var}\left(g(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta})\right)\approx
\nabla g(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta})^{\top}\,\hat{\boldsymbol\Sigma}\,
\nabla g(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}),
\]
where \(\nabla g\) is the gradient of \(g\), the vector of its partial derivatives with respect to each parameter (Chapter 5), evaluated at the estimates; \(\hat{\boldsymbol\Sigma}\) is the covariance matrix of the estimates, the element cov.fixed of sdreport(); and \(^{\top}\) turns the column of partial derivatives into a row. For two parameters the product is
\[
\left(\frac{\partial g}{\partial\theta_1}\right)^2\hat\sigma_1^2+
\left(\frac{\partial g}{\partial\theta_2}\right)^2\hat\sigma_2^2+
2\,\frac{\partial g}{\partial\theta_1}\,\frac{\partial g}{\partial\theta_2}\,\hat\sigma_{12},
\]
where \(\hat\sigma_1^2\) and \(\hat\sigma_2^2\) are the variances of the two estimates and \(\hat\sigma_{12}\) their covariance. In plain English, each parameter contributes its variance multiplied by the square of the slope of \(g\) in its direction, and each pair of parameters contributes its covariance multiplied by the two slopes. With one parameter only the first term remains, and its square root is the formula of the box on the delta method in Chapter 4. For the curve of the reed frogs a larger \(\alpha\) raises the curve and a larger \(H\) lowers it, so the two slopes have opposite signs. Their estimates are positively correlated, so the last term is negative: the two errors partly cancel on the curve, which is estimated more precisely than the separate standard errors suggest.
RTMB calculates \(\nabla g\) by automatic differentiation (Section 4.1), which is why ADREPORT() is called inside the NLL: the quantity has to be calculated there for RTMB to differentiate it. The approximation is good when \(g\) is close to a plane over the range of parameter values that the uncertainty of the estimates covers. It is poor when \(g\) bends noticeably over that range, which happens when the standard errors are large (in small samples) and when the quantity is close to a bound of its range on the scale on which it is calculated; this is why the band is calculated on the logit scale.











Figure 3: Number of tadpoles killed in each of the 16 tanks (points), with the expected number killed under the Binomial model with the Holling type II curve fitted by maximum likelihood (line) and its pointwise 95% confidence band (shaded), calculated from Wald intervals on the logit scale. The inset gives the model, the estimates and their 95% likelihood profile intervals; α is per experiment, H in experiments per tadpole killed and 1/H in tadpoles killed per experiment.





Whether these intervals have a coverage close to 95% with 16 tanks can be checked by simulation, in the same way as in “Coverage checked by simulation” in Chapter 4; the extra exercise of the practical does this for a quantity of a fitted curve.






Practice 2: handling time of a ladybird



A Holling type II curve is fitted to the number of aphids eaten by ladybird larvae in one hour, with the handling time \(H\) (hours per aphid) optimised on the log scale. The fit gives \(\log(\hat H)=-3.2\), and sdreport() gives a standard error of 0.20 for it. Calculate a 95% Wald interval for \(H\), and from it an interval for the largest number of aphids that a larva can eat per hour, \(1/H\). Why are the endpoints swapped in the second interval?






TipSolution





We calculate the interval on the log scale, transform its endpoints with exp(), and then take the inverse of both endpoints:

# Wald interval for H (hours per aphid), from the log scale.
H_wald = exp(-3.2 + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(p = 0.975) * 0.20)
H_wald

[1] 0.02754339 0.06032509

# Interval for 1 / H (aphids/hour): the inverse of the two endpoints, in reverse order.
rev(1 / H_wald)

[1] 16.57685 36.30636


The interval for \(H\) goes from approximately 0.028 to 0.060 hours per aphid, and the interval for the largest feeding rate from approximately 17 to 36 aphids/hour, around an estimate of \(1/e^{-3.2}\approx24.5\). The function \(1/H\) decreases as \(H\) increases, so the lower endpoint of \(H\) gives the upper endpoint of \(1/H\), and the other way round. Because the function is monotonic, the second interval contains \(1/H\) in exactly the hypothetical samples in which the first contains \(H\), so it has the same coverage.

title: Fitting ecological response curves
text:
6.1 Simulating from the fitted model
With its parameters at the estimates, a fitted model is a data generating process from which we can simulate. As in “Coverage checked by simulation” in Chapter 4, we mark the response with OBS() inside the NLL, and the function simulate() of the processed object then draws one hypothetical sample for the parameter values that we give it. A hypothetical sample has the same design as the data: the same observations, with the same values of the predictor. Each simulated value is drawn from the distribution of its observation, so the simulation contains the variation of the observations around the curve, which is what the check needs.
For the reed frogs, the NLL gains one line, killed = OBS(killed). We process it and fit it again (the estimates do not change):

# The Binomial NLL with one more line.
binomial_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  # Mark the response as observations, so that they can be simulated.
  killed = OBS(killed)
  alpha = plogis(logit_alpha)
  H = exp(log_H)
  p = alpha / (1 + alpha * H * initial)
  p_grid = alpha / (1 + alpha * H * initial_grid)
  logit_p_grid = qlogis(p_grid)
  ADREPORT(logit_p_grid)
  -sum(dbinom(x = killed, size = initial, prob = p, log = TRUE))
}

# Process the new NLL and fit it again.
binomial_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(binomial_nll, frog_data),
  list(logit_alpha = qlogis(0.5), log_H = log(1 / 60)),
  silent = TRUE
)
binomial_fit = optim(
  par = binomial_obj$par,
  fn = binomial_obj$fn,
  gr = binomial_obj$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)
binomial_fit$convergence

[1] 0


Each call to simulate() returns the numbers killed in 16 simulated tanks with the initial numbers of the experiment. We store 1,000 hypothetical samples in a matrix with one row per tank and one column per hypothetical sample:

# 1,000 hypothetical samples of the 16 tanks at the estimates: one row per tank and one
# column per hypothetical sample.
n_sim = 1000
binomial_simulations = matrix(NA, nrow = length(frog_data$killed), ncol = n_sim)
set.seed(seed = 601)
for (j in seq_len(n_sim)) {
  binomial_simulations[, j] = binomial_obj$simulate(binomial_fit$par)$killed
}

# The first five hypothetical samples of the first four tanks (5, 5, 10 and 10 tadpoles).
binomial_simulations[1:4, 1:5]

     [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] [,5]
[1,]    2    3    3    2    3
[2,]    2    4    2    3    3
[3,]    8    6    6    6    3
[4,]    5    3    5    7    6

title: Fitting ecological response curves
text:
6.2 Scaled quantile residuals
The scaled quantile residual of an observation is the fraction of its simulated values that are smaller than the observed value. An observation in the middle of its simulated values has a residual close to 0.5, one below all of them a residual of 0 and one above all of them a residual of 1. For a discrete response, the observed value is often equal to some of the simulated values, and the residual is then drawn at random between the fraction of simulated values that are smaller and the fraction that are smaller or equal. If the model describes the data generating process, each observation behaves like one more draw from its own distribution, so it is equally likely to fall anywhere among its simulated values. The residuals are then approximately uniform between 0 and 1, whatever the distribution of the observations and whatever the values of the predictor. This is what makes them useful for response curves: they put observations with different distributions on one common scale.2
Three kinds of pattern show that the model disagrees with the data:

a distribution of the residuals that is not uniform: too many residuals near 0 and 1 mean that the observations vary more around the curve than the model allows, and too many near 0.5 that they vary less;
a trend of the residuals against the predictor or against the fitted values, which means that the curve misses a systematic change of the response;
residuals of exactly 0 or 1, from observations outside the range of all their simulated values, which DHARMa marks as outliers.

The function DHARMa::createDHARMa() calculates the residuals from simulations that we supply. Its arguments are:

simulatedResponse, the matrix of simulated values, with one row per observation;
observedResponse, the observed values;
fittedPredictedResponse, the expected value of each observation under the fitted model, which DHARMa uses in its plots and in the dispersion statistic below;
integerResponse = TRUE for a discrete response, so that ties are drawn at random as described above.

plot() of the result draws two panels: on the left a quantile–quantile plot of the residuals against a uniform distribution, and on the right the residuals against the fitted values, on the scale of their ranks, with the quartiles 0.25, 0.5 and 0.75 as dashed lines. DHARMa::plotResiduals() with the argument form draws the residuals against any predictor. For the reed frogs the expected number killed increases with the initial number of tadpoles, so the right panel already shows the residuals in the order of the densities. We calculate the expected number killed in each tank and the residuals:

# Expected number killed in each tank under the fitted model.
binomial_expected = frog_data$initial * alpha_mle /
  (1 + alpha_mle * H_mle * frog_data$initial)

# Scaled quantile residuals from the simulations, and the two standard panels.
binomial_residuals = DHARMa::createDHARMa(
  simulatedResponse = binomial_simulations,
  observedResponse = frog_data$killed,
  fittedPredictedResponse = binomial_expected,
  integerResponse = TRUE
)
plot(binomial_residuals)







Figure 4: Scaled quantile residuals of the Binomial model with the Holling type II curve fitted to the 16 tanks, from 1,000 hypothetical samples, as drawn by DHARMa. Left: quantile–quantile plot against a uniform distribution. Right: residuals against the rank of the expected number killed, with the quartiles of a uniform distribution (dashed lines) and lines fitted to the quartiles of the residuals. The star marks a tank whose observed number lies outside the range of its simulated values.





The residuals do not follow a uniform distribution: in the quantile–quantile plot the upper half of the residuals lies above the line, so more tanks than expected have residuals close to 1, and one tank, with 50 tadpoles of which 5 were killed, lies below all its simulated values (the star). In the right panel the lines fitted to the quartiles of the residuals lie on or outside the dashed lines, the upper one well above 0.75: the tanks spread further from the middle of their simulated values than the model allows. There is no clear trend against density, so the curve itself does not miss a systematic change.
DHARMa summarises the spread with a dispersion statistic: the variance of the observed values around their expected values, divided by the average of the same variance in the simulated samples. It is close to one when the model allows the right amount of variation. The function DHARMa::testDispersion() calculates it; we keep only its element statistic:

# Observed spread around the curve relative to the simulated spread.
DHARMa::testDispersion(binomial_residuals, plot = FALSE)$statistic

dispersion 
  2.925697 


The numbers killed vary around the curve almost three times as much (as a variance) as the Binomial model allows. This is overdispersion relative to the Binomial distribution, which Chapter 2 introduced for counts relative to the Poisson distribution (“Overdispersion”). The two tanks with 50 tadpoles, with 5 and 21 killed, show it in the data: under the Binomial model they share the same distribution, in which 5 killed is very unlikely. The model assumes that every tadpole of a tank has the same probability of being killed, independently of the other tadpoles, and these tanks differ more than that assumption allows.
DHARMa also prints tests with p-values, on its plots and in functions such as testDispersion(). We read the plots and the dispersion statistic as exploratory evidence and do not rest decisions on the p-values, for the reasons given in Chapter 1 and at the end of Chapter 4: with 16 tanks a large p-value mainly says that there are few data, and a small one does not say how much the disagreement matters.






WarningWhat a residual check can and cannot show



A residual check shows where a fitted model disagrees with the data. It does not say which assumption is wrong: overdispersion can come from the distribution, from a predictor that is missing from the curve, or from observations that are not independent. Nor does a plot without a pattern show that the model is right or that the observations are independent; with few observations only large disagreements are visible.

title: Fitting ecological response curves
text:
8.1 Information criteria
Chapter 4 introduced AIC and its corrected version AICc,
\[
\mathrm{AIC}=2K-2\,\ell(\hat\theta),
\qquad
\mathrm{AICc}=\mathrm{AIC}+\frac{2K(K+1)}{n-K-1},
\]
where \(K\) is the number of estimated parameters, \(n\) the number of observations and \(\ell(\hat\theta)\) the maximum log-likelihood. With 16 observations and up to three parameters the correction of AICc is not negligible. The Bayesian information criterion (BIC)3 has a penalty that grows with the number of observations:
\[
\mathrm{BIC}=K\log(n)-2\,\ell(\hat\theta),
\]
with the same symbols. Each parameter costs \(\log(n)\) units instead of two, which is more than two when \(n\) is larger than \(e^2\approx7.4\), so for most data sets BIC penalises additional parameters more strongly than AIC. The two criteria also have different aims. AIC estimates how well the fitted model would predict new data from the same process. BIC tends, as the sample grows, to select the model with the fewest parameters among the candidates that contain the data generating process. So in large samples BIC tends to prefer simpler models than AIC does. Like AIC, BIC is used as a difference between models fitted to the same observations, the lowest value is preferred, and it ranks the candidates without showing that the best of them describes the data well.
In AICc and BIC, \(n\) is the number of independent observations, which is the number of tanks, 16, and not the 610 tadpoles that they contained: under the Beta-Binomial model the tadpoles of a tank share the probability of that tank, so they are not independent observations. The same \(n\) must be used for every model that is compared. We add the three criteria to the table:

# AIC, AICc and BIC, with the number of tanks as the number of observations.
n_tanks = length(frog_data$killed)
comparison$aic = 2 * comparison$K - 2 * comparison$loglik
comparison$aicc = comparison$aic +
  2 * comparison$K * (comparison$K + 1) / (n_tanks - comparison$K - 1)
comparison$bic = comparison$K * log(n_tanks) - 2 * comparison$loglik

title: Fitting ecological response curves
text:
8.2 Cross-validation
Cross-validation estimates how well a model predicts observations that were not used to fit it. The observations are split into parts, the model is fitted to all but one part and scored on the part that was held out, and this is repeated until every part has been held out once. In leave-one-out cross-validation each part is a single observation: every parameter of the model is estimated again from the other \(n-1\) observations, and the held-out observation is scored by its log score, the log probability (or log density) that the refitted model assigns to it. The score of the model is the sum of the log scores of the \(n\) observations, and a larger (less negative) score is better.
The log score uses the whole distribution of the observation, and not only its distance from the curve, so it can be calculated for any observation model, and it rewards a model that describes the spread of the observations as well as their mean. A model that adapts too closely to the data used to fit it predicts the held-out observations badly, so cross-validation needs no penalty for the number of parameters. Leave-one-out cross-validation and AIC agree in large samples: AIC is approximately \(-2\) times the leave-one-out log score.4 When fitting the model \(n\) times takes too long, the observations are split into a few groups that are held out in turn, often 5 or 10, which is called 5-fold or 10-fold cross-validation. When the observations are ordered in time or space, so that neighbouring observations are similar, each held-out part should be a block of neighbouring observations; otherwise its neighbours in the fit make it look easier to predict than a new observation would be.
For the reed frogs we leave out one tank at a time. A function keeps some of the tanks in the list of data (the grid of densities stays):

# Keep only the given tanks in the list of data.
subset_tanks = function(data, tanks) {
  data$initial = data$initial[tanks]
  data$killed = data$killed[tanks]
  data
}

For each model and each tank, we fit the model to the other 15 tanks, from the same starting values as before. The NLL of the held-out tank at these estimates is minus the log probability of that tank, so we calculate it by calling the NLL directly with two lists: the estimates (as.list() turns the vector par into a list) and the data of the held-out tank. A negative index removes the tank from the data, and we count the fits that did not converge:

# Leave-one-out log score of each model: fit to 15 tanks, score the tank held out.
comparison$loo = NA
n_failed = 0
for (m in seq_along(models)) {
  score = 0
  for (i in seq_len(n_tanks)) {
    fit = fit_model(models[[m]]$nll, models[[m]]$start, subset_tanks(frog_data, -i))
    n_failed = n_failed + (fit$convergence != 0)
    # Minus the NLL of the held-out tank is its log probability.
    score = score - models[[m]]$nll(as.list(fit$par), subset_tanks(frog_data, i))
  }
  comparison$loo[m] = score
}
n_failed

[1] 0


All 64 fits converged.

title: Fitting ecological response curves
text:
8.3 Comparing the four models
Only differences between models matter for each criterion, so we calculate the difference of each model from the best one: the lowest AIC, AICc and BIC, and the highest leave-one-out score (whose differences are therefore zero or negative):

# Differences from the best model for each criterion.
data.frame(
  model = comparison$model,
  K = comparison$K,
  loglik = round(comparison$loglik, 2),
  delta_aic = round(comparison$aic - min(comparison$aic), 2),
  delta_aicc = round(comparison$aicc - min(comparison$aicc), 2),
  delta_bic = round(comparison$bic - min(comparison$bic), 2),
  delta_loo = round(comparison$loo - max(comparison$loo), 2)
)

                  model K loglik delta_aic delta_aicc delta_bic delta_loo
1     constant_binomial 1 -52.22     15.70      13.99     14.16     -8.17
2      holling_binomial 2 -46.72      6.71       5.63      5.94     -4.21
3 constant_betabinomial 2 -44.73      2.72       1.64      1.95      0.00
4  holling_betabinomial 3 -42.37      0.00       0.00      0.00     -0.94


Recall that a difference of one unit in the log score corresponds to about two units of AIC. For the variation among tanks the criteria agree: with either curve, every criterion prefers the Beta-Binomial model to the Binomial model, by 6.7 (Holling type II) and 13.0 (constant probability) units of AIC, and by 3.3 and 8.2 units of log score. This agrees with the residuals of Section 6.
For the density dependence of the risk the answer depends on the distribution. Under the Binomial models, the Holling type II curve is clearly better than a constant probability (9.0 units of AIC, 4.0 of log score). Under the Beta-Binomial models the difference is small, and the criteria do not agree on its sign: AIC, AICc and BIC prefer the Holling type II curve by 2.7, 1.6 and 2.0 units, whereas the leave-one-out score prefers the constant probability by 0.9 units. The Binomial models overstated the evidence for density dependence for the same reason that they understated the standard errors: they treated the tadpoles as independent trials. With 16 tanks that vary among themselves, the data say clearly that a tadpole is killed with a probability of about one half at low density, and that the tanks vary more than a Binomial model allows, but they hardly distinguish a probability that decreases with density from a constant one over densities of 5 to 100 tadpoles per tank.
For the ecological answer we use the Beta-Binomial model with the Holling type II curve, which three of the four criteria prefer and which contains the constant probability as the case \(H=0\), and we calculate likelihood profile intervals for its parameters as in Section 5:

# Profiles of logit(alpha) and log(H) of the Beta-Binomial model (confint() warns
# about repeated values, as before).
betabinomial_profile_alpha = TMB::tmbprofile(
  betabinomial_obj, name = "logit_alpha", trace = FALSE
)
betabinomial_profile_H = TMB::tmbprofile(betabinomial_obj, name = "log_H", trace = FALSE)

# 95% intervals on the original scale; 1 / H decreases with H, so the endpoints swap.
H_interval_bb = exp(confint(betabinomial_profile_H))
betabinomial_intervals = rbind(
  plogis(confint(betabinomial_profile_alpha)),
  H_interval_bb,
  rev(1 / H_interval_bb)
)
dimnames(betabinomial_intervals) = list(c("alpha", "H", "1/H"), c("lower", "upper"))
betabinomial_intervals

             lower        upper
alpha  0.378117272   0.75898209
H      0.001874648   0.03757276
1/H   26.615029908 533.43348014


The attack rate is estimated at 0.54 per experiment, with an interval from 0.38 to 0.76: at low density, between about two fifths and three quarters of the tadpoles are killed on average in the 14 days. The handling time is estimated at 0.018 experiments per tadpole killed, but its interval runs from 0.0019 to 0.038, so the largest number of tadpoles that three larvae could kill in one experiment, about 56, has an interval from 27 to more than 500. The lower end of the interval of \(H\) is close to zero, which is the constant probability, and this agrees with the comparison. The tanks rule out a low maximum but say little about how high it is, as we found in Section 5, and allowing for the variation among tanks widens the interval further. To estimate the handling time, an experiment would need tanks with densities well above the half-maximum, where the curve levels off.

title: Fitting ecological response curves
text:
Footnotes


Vonesh, J. R. and Bolker, B. M. (2005), “Compensatory larval responses shift trade-offs associated with predator-induced hatching plasticity”, Ecology 86: 1580–1591. The data are in the package emdbook.↩︎
Dunn and Smyth (1996) defined these residuals from the cumulative probability function of the model and transformed them to the scale of a standard Normal distribution: Dunn, P. K. and Smyth, G. K. (1996), “Randomized quantile residuals”, Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics 5: 236–244. The package DHARMa calculates them from simulations and keeps them between 0 and 1: Hartig, F. (2026), DHARMa: Residual diagnostics for hierarchical (multi-level / mixed) regression models, R package version 0.5.0.↩︎
Schwarz, G. (1978), “Estimating the dimension of a model”, Annals of Statistics 6: 461–464. The name comes from its derivation, as a large-sample approximation in Bayesian inference, but it is used in the same way as AIC.↩︎
Stone, M. (1977), “An asymptotic equivalence of choice of model by cross-validation and Akaike’s criterion”, Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B 39: 44–47.↩︎

title: Chapter 6: Fitting ecological response curves — solutions
text:
These solutions use the same data, tasks and seeds as the student practical page. Exercise 1 is worked in full on both pages, because Exercise 4 continues with its objects. Exercises 1 to 3 are the core of the practical and Exercise 4 is extra practice. The exercises run in one R session: later exercises reuse the helper cmb() and the objects critical_value and n_sim of Exercise 1.
As on that page, we load RTMB first and RTMBdist second:
# Load RTMB first and RTMBdist second.
library(RTMB)
library(RTMBdist)

title: Chapter 6: Fitting ecological response curves — solutions
text:
1.1 Solution

1.1.1 Question 1
Let \(Y_i\) be the titre of observation \(i\) and \(x_i\) the day after infection on which it was measured. The curve describes the mean titre on each day, and the titres vary around it according to a Normal distribution:
\[
Y_i \sim \operatorname{Normal}\left(f(x_i),\,\sigma^2\right),
\qquad
f(x)=a\,x\,e^{-bx},
\qquad i=1,\ldots,27,
\]
where \(f(x_i)\) is the mean titre on day \(x_i\) and \(\sigma\) is the standard deviation of the titres around the curve, the same on every day (\(\sigma^2\) is the variance of the model). The mean of a Normal distribution can take any real value, so the curve needs no outer function to give it the right range (see From a response curve to a model for observations). The units of \(a\) and \(b\) are those of Chapter 5: \(b\) is in 1/day, because \(bx\) is the argument of an exponential and has no units, and \(a\) is in units of titre/day, because \(ax\) must have the units of the titre. The standard deviation \(\sigma\) measures the spread of the observations, so it has the units of the titre (log10 infectious doses).
A Normal model gives a positive probability to negative titres, which do not occur in these data. This does not matter when that probability is negligible. The titres lie between 4.2 and 8.5 and vary by about one unit among the observations of the same day, so if the curve passes near the observations its value lies many standard deviations above zero. We check this after the fit.


1.1.2 Question 2
The NLL has the form of the theory: a list of parameters, with the logarithms of the three positive parameters, and a list of data, with the predictor (day) and the response (titre). Because day is a vector, the line of the curve returns the mean titre of every observation, and dnorm() uses the mean of each observation:

# Negative log-likelihood of the Ricker curve with a Normal observation model.
normal_nll = function(parms, data) {
  # Make the elements of both lists available by name.
  getAll(parms, data)
  # Transform the parameters to the original scale.
  a = exp(log_a)
  b = exp(log_b)
  sigma = exp(log_sigma)
  # Mean titre on the day of each observation.
  mu = a * day * exp(-b * day)
  -sum(dnorm(x = titre, mean = mu, sd = sigma, log = TRUE))
}

We start from the values read by eye in Chapter 5. For \(\sigma\) we take 1 unit of titre, roughly the spread of the observations of one day. We give the starting values to MakeADFun() on the log scale and fit the model:

# Connect a likelihood to a data set.
cmb = function(f, d) function(p) f(p, d)

# Starting values: the values read by eye in the Chapter 5 practical, and sigma = 1.
titre_start = list(log_a = log(3.44), log_b = log(1 / 6), log_sigma = log(1))

# Process the NLL, minimise it with BFGS and check the convergence code.
normal_obj = MakeADFun(cmb(normal_nll, titre_data), titre_start, silent = TRUE)
normal_fit = optim(
  par = normal_obj$par,
  fn = normal_obj$fn,
  gr = normal_obj$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)
normal_fit$convergence

[1] 0

# Estimates on the original scale.
a_mle = exp(normal_fit$par[["log_a"]])
b_mle = exp(normal_fit$par[["log_b"]])
sigma_mle = exp(normal_fit$par[["log_sigma"]])
c(a = a_mle, b = b_mle, sigma = sigma_mle)

        a         b     sigma 
3.4181655 0.1652275 0.6700115 


The convergence code is 0. The estimates are \(\hat a\approx3.42\) units of titre/day, \(\hat b\approx0.165\)/day and \(\hat\sigma\approx0.67\) units of titre. The first two are close to the values read by eye (3.44 and 0.167). We can now check the argument of question 1. The lowest mean titre in the data is the one of day 2, and the probability that the fitted model gives to a negative titre on that day is the cumulative probability of zero:

# Ricker function: initial slope a and rate b.
ricker = function(x, a = 1, b = 1) {
  a * x * exp(-b * x)
}

# Mean titre on day 2 under the fitted model, and the probability of a negative titre.
ricker(2, a = a_mle, b = b_mle)

[1] 4.912565

pnorm(q = 0, mean = ricker(2, a = a_mle, b = b_mle), sd = sigma_mle)

[1] 1.133199e-13


The mean titre on day 2 is 4.9, more than seven standard deviations above zero, and the probability of a negative titre is of the order of \(10^{-13}\). The Normal model can be used here because the titres are far from zero compared with their spread.
We draw the fitted curve over the data, together with the curve by eye of Chapter 5 (Figure 1):

# Observations, with axes that start at zero.
plot(titre ~ day, data = titre_data, xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(0, 10),
     xlab = "Time since infection (days)", ylab = "Virus titre (log10 infectious doses)")

# Fitted curve and curve by eye.
curve(ricker(x, a = a_mle, b = b_mle), add = TRUE, col = "#D55E00")
curve(ricker(x, a = 3.44, b = 1 / 6), add = TRUE, lty = 2)
legend("bottomright", legend = c("Maximum likelihood", "By eye (Chapter 5)"),
       lty = c(1, 2), col = c("#D55E00", "black"), bty = "n")







Figure 1: Titre of the myxoma virus of grade 1 against the time since infection, with the Ricker curve fitted by maximum likelihood under a Normal model (solid line) and the curve read by eye in Chapter 5 (dashed line).





The two curves are almost the same. The peak that we read by eye happened to be close to the peak of the fitted curve, and in the Ricker function the peak determines both parameters.


1.1.3 Question 3
The time and the height of the peak are quantities calculated from the parameters, so we ask for their standard errors with ADREPORT() inside the NLL, as in Uncertainty of the fitted curve. We also mark the titres with OBS(), which question 4 needs in order to simulate. We process the new NLL and fit it again (the estimates do not change):

# The NLL with the time and the height of the peak in ADREPORT(), and the titres marked
# as observations for the simulations of question 4.
normal_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  titre = OBS(titre)
  a = exp(log_a)
  b = exp(log_b)
  sigma = exp(log_sigma)
  # Time (days) and height (units of titre) of the peak of the curve.
  peak_time = 1 / b
  peak_titre = a / (b * exp(1))
  ADREPORT(peak_time)
  ADREPORT(peak_titre)
  mu = a * day * exp(-b * day)
  -sum(dnorm(x = titre, mean = mu, sd = sigma, log = TRUE))
}

# Process the new NLL and fit it again.
normal_obj = MakeADFun(cmb(normal_nll, titre_data), titre_start, silent = TRUE)
normal_fit = optim(
  par = normal_obj$par,
  fn = normal_obj$fn,
  gr = normal_obj$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)
normal_fit$convergence

[1] 0


summary() of the result of sdreport() has one row for each parameter, on the scale that was optimised, and one row for each quantity in ADREPORT(), on the scale on which it was calculated. cov2cor() gives the correlations between the estimates of the parameters:

# Standard errors of the parameters (log scale) and of the two quantities of the peak.
normal_sd = sdreport(normal_obj)
summary(normal_sd)

             Estimate Std. Error
log_a       1.2291040 0.05942752
log_b      -1.8004320 0.06327389
log_sigma  -0.4004604 0.13607803
peak_time   6.0522616 0.38295013
peak_titre  7.6105545 0.15035055

cov2cor(normal_sd$cov.fixed)

                 log_a         log_b     log_sigma
log_a     1.000000e+00  9.500711e-01  3.801877e-05
log_b     9.500711e-01  1.000000e+00 -1.961625e-05
log_sigma 3.801877e-05 -1.961625e-05  1.000000e+00


The standard errors on the log scale are about 0.06 for \(\log(\hat a)\) and \(\log(\hat b)\), so both parameters are estimated to within a few percent, and 0.14 for \(\log(\hat\sigma)\). The estimates of \(\log(a)\) and \(\log(b)\) are strongly correlated (0.95): a curve with a steeper initial rise (a larger \(a\)) must also decline sooner (a larger \(b\)) to keep its peak at the height of the observations.
We asked for the time and the height of the peak on their original scale, in days and in units of titre, so their Wald intervals are calculated on that scale. The theory calculates Wald intervals on a scale on which the quantity is unbounded (Uncertainty of the fitted curve), because an interval on the original scale can cross the bound when the estimate is close to it. Both quantities are positive, but their estimates lie about 16 and 50 standard errors above zero, so here an interval on the original scale cannot reach the bound:

# 95% Wald intervals of the time and the height of the peak, on the original scale.
critical_value = qnorm(p = 0.975)
peak_summary = summary(normal_sd, select = "report")
cbind(
  estimate = peak_summary[, "Estimate"],
  lower = peak_summary[, "Estimate"] - critical_value * peak_summary[, "Std. Error"],
  upper = peak_summary[, "Estimate"] + critical_value * peak_summary[, "Std. Error"]
)

           estimate    lower    upper
peak_time  6.052262 5.301693 6.802830
peak_titre 7.610554 7.315873 7.905236


The peak is estimated on day 6.05 (95% Wald interval from 5.30 to 6.80 days) at a titre of 7.61 (from 7.32 to 7.91). The height is well determined because many observations lie near the peak.
For the likelihood profile interval we profile \(\log(b)\), transform the endpoints back with exp(), and obtain the interval for the time of the peak from that of \(b\). The function \(1/b\) decreases as \(b\) increases, so the endpoints swap:

# Profile of log(b). The profile contains the estimate twice, so confint() warns that it
# collapses repeated values; the warning can be ignored.
normal_profile_b = TMB::tmbprofile(normal_obj, name = "log_b", trace = FALSE)

# 95% interval for b (1/day), and for the time of the peak (days).
b_interval = exp(confint(normal_profile_b))
b_interval

          lower     upper
log_b 0.1439547 0.1864634

rev(1 / b_interval)

[1] 5.362984 6.946631


The likelihood profile interval of \(b\) goes from 0.144/day to 0.186/day, almost symmetrically around the estimate of 0.165. The corresponding interval for the time of the peak goes from 5.36 to 6.95 days: it extends 0.69 days below the estimate and 0.89 days above it, because \(1/b\) is a curve that stretches the values of \(b\) below the estimate more than those above it. The Wald interval for the time of the peak (5.30 to 6.80 days) is symmetric by construction, because the delta method treats \(1/b\) as a straight line near the estimate. So, compared with the profile interval, it is shifted towards earlier days. The two intervals differ by less than a fifth of a day at each end, which is small compared with their width; the extra Exercise 4 shows what it means for the coverage of the Wald interval.


1.1.4 Question 4
The titres are marked with OBS(), so the function simulate() of the object draws one hypothetical sample of 27 titres, on the same days as the data, for the parameter values that we give it. We store 1,000 hypothetical samples in a matrix with one row per observation:

# 1,000 hypothetical samples of the 27 titres at the estimates: one row per observation
# and one column per hypothetical sample.
n_sim = 1000
normal_simulations = matrix(NA, nrow = length(titre_data$titre), ncol = n_sim)
set.seed(seed = 611)
for (j in seq_len(n_sim)) {
  normal_simulations[, j] = normal_obj$simulate(normal_fit$par)$titre
}

DHARMa::createDHARMa() calculates the residuals from the simulations, with the arguments of the theory. The expected value of each observation is the mean titre of its day, and the titres are continuous, so integerResponse = FALSE: two titres are almost never equal, and no ties need to be drawn at random. plot() draws the two standard panels (Figure 2), and DHARMa::plotResiduals() with the argument form draws the residuals against the day (Figure 3):

# Expected titre of each observation under the fitted model.
normal_expected = ricker(titre_data$day, a = a_mle, b = b_mle)

# Scaled quantile residuals from the simulations, and the two standard panels.
normal_residuals = DHARMa::createDHARMa(
  simulatedResponse = normal_simulations,
  observedResponse = titre_data$titre,
  fittedPredictedResponse = normal_expected,
  integerResponse = FALSE
)
plot(normal_residuals)







Figure 2: Scaled quantile residuals of the Normal model with the Ricker curve, from 1,000 hypothetical samples. Left: quantile–quantile plot against a uniform distribution. Right: residuals against the rank of the expected titre.






# Residuals against the day of the observation.
DHARMa::plotResiduals(normal_residuals, form = titre_data$day)







Figure 3: Scaled quantile residuals of the Normal model with the Ricker curve against the day of the observation.





In the quantile–quantile plot the residuals follow the line, so their distribution is close to uniform, and none lies outside the range of its simulations. The right panel of Figure 2 orders the observations by their expected titre, which first increases and then decreases with the day, so the pattern in time is clearer in Figure 3. There the residuals tend to lie above 0.5 on the first days and on the last days, and below 0.5 around the peak: the observations lie slightly above the curve at both ends and slightly below it in the middle. This agrees with what we saw by eye in Chapter 5: the titre levels off after day 6, while the Ricker curve must decline after its peak. In Figure 3 DHARMa draws the line of the upper quartile in red, because its test gives a small p-value. As in the theory, we read the plot as exploratory evidence and not as a decision: with 27 observations and one to six per day the pattern rests on few observations, but it suggests that the Ricker curve describes the titre after the peak only approximately. A curve with a third parameter, such as the generalised Ricker function, could be fitted and compared with it.
DHARMa also calculates a dispersion statistic, but for a Normal model it is not informative: \(\sigma\) is estimated from the spread of the observations around the curve, so the simulated spread matches the observed spread almost by construction.


1.1.5 Question 5
A Gamma distribution with shape \(k\) and scale \(\mu/k\) has mean \(\mu\) and variance \(k(\mu/k)^2=\mu^2/k\), so its standard deviation is \(\mu/\sqrt{k}\): the spread of the titres is proportional to the mean, with a coefficient of variation \(1/\sqrt{k}\) that is the same on every day. In the Normal model the spread is the same on every day, whatever the mean. The Gamma model also gives a probability of zero to negative titres. The NLL takes the logarithm of the shape as its third parameter; we start from the values by eye and a shape of 10:

# Negative log-likelihood of the Ricker curve with a Gamma observation model.
gamma_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  a = exp(log_a)
  b = exp(log_b)
  shape = exp(log_shape)
  mu = a * day * exp(-b * day)
  # A scale of mu / shape gives each observation the mean mu.
  -sum(dgamma(x = titre, shape = shape, scale = mu / shape, log = TRUE))
}

# Process the NLL and fit it.
gamma_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(gamma_nll, titre_data),
  list(log_a = log(3.44), log_b = log(1 / 6), log_shape = log(10)),
  silent = TRUE
)
gamma_fit = optim(
  par = gamma_obj$par,
  fn = gamma_obj$fn,
  gr = gamma_obj$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)
gamma_fit$convergence

[1] 0

# Estimates on the original scale.
c(a = exp(gamma_fit$par[["log_a"]]), b = exp(gamma_fit$par[["log_b"]]),
  shape = exp(gamma_fit$par[["log_shape"]]))

         a          b      shape 
 3.5612471  0.1713291 90.5119351 


The fit converged, with \(\hat a\approx3.56\) units of titre/day, \(\hat b\approx0.171\)/day and a shape of about 90, which gives a coefficient of variation of about 0.11 (a standard deviation of about 0.8 units of titre at the peak and 0.5 on day 2). Both models have three parameters and are fitted to the same 27 titres in the same units, so we can compare them with the criteria of the theory, with \(n=27\):

# AIC, AICc and BIC of the two models, with K = 3 parameters and n = 27 observations.
n_obs = length(titre_data$titre)
k_models = c(normal = 3, gamma = 3)
nll_models = c(normal = normal_fit$value, gamma = gamma_fit$value)
aic = 2 * k_models + 2 * nll_models
aicc = aic + 2 * k_models * (k_models + 1) / (n_obs - k_models - 1)
bic = k_models * log(n_obs) + 2 * nll_models
rbind(aic = aic, aicc = aicc, bic = bic)

       normal    gamma
aic  60.99968 65.01829
aicc 62.04316 66.06176
bic  64.88719 68.90580


All three criteria prefer the Normal model, by 4.0 units. The difference is the same for the three criteria because the two models have the same number of parameters and are fitted to the same observations: the penalty is the same for both models within each criterion, and the difference between the models is twice the difference between their maximum log-likelihoods. So the comparison says that the titres are more probable under a spread that is the same on every day than under a spread that grows with the mean. This is plausible, because the titre is already a logarithm: variation by a constant factor in the number of infectious doses becomes a constant spread on the logarithmic scale. With 27 observations, however, the evidence is moderate. The curve itself hardly depends on the choice: the estimates of \(a\) and \(b\) differ by a few percent between the two models.

title: Chapter 6: Fitting ecological response curves — solutions
text:
2.1 Solution

2.1.1 Question 1
Let \(Y_i\) be the rate of the reaction in observation \(i\) and \(x_i\) the concentration of the substrate. With one curve for both states, the model is
\[
Y_i \sim \operatorname{Normal}\left(f(x_i),\,\sigma^2\right),
\qquad
f(x)=\frac{ax}{b+x},
\qquad i=1,\ldots,23,
\]
where \(a\) is the asymptote, the maximum rate of the reaction (counts/min/min), \(b\) is the half-maximum, the concentration at which the rate is \(a/2\) (ppm), and \(\sigma\) is the standard deviation of the rates around the curve (counts/min/min). The mean of a Normal distribution can take any value, and the curve is positive anyway for positive \(a\) and \(b\). All three parameters are positive, so we optimise their logarithms.
The list of data holds the concentration, the rate and the number of the state of each observation, which question 2 needs. as.numeric() of a factor returns the position of each level, so 1 is a treated cell and 2 an untreated cell. Question 6 checks the model that the criteria prefer, which we do not know yet, so we mark the rates with OBS() in both NLLs:

# Load the data and put the concentration (ppm), the rate (counts/min/min) and the number
# of the state of each observation (1 treated, 2 untreated) in a list of data.
data(Puromycin, package = "datasets")
levels(Puromycin$state)

[1] "treated"   "untreated"

enzyme_data = list(
  conc = Puromycin$conc,
  rate = Puromycin$rate,
  state = as.numeric(Puromycin$state)
)

# Negative log-likelihood of one Michaelis–Menten curve for both states.
pooled_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  rate = OBS(rate)
  a = exp(log_a)
  b = exp(log_b)
  sigma = exp(log_sigma)
  mu = a * conc / (b + conc)
  -sum(dnorm(x = rate, mean = mu, sd = sigma, log = TRUE))
}
