As starting values we take an asymptote of 190 counts/min/min, between the two values read by eye, the half-maximum of 0.06 ppm read by eye and a standard deviation of 10 counts/min/min:

# Starting values, process the NLL and fit it.
pooled_start = list(log_a = log(190), log_b = log(0.06), log_sigma = log(10))
pooled_obj = MakeADFun(cmb(pooled_nll, enzyme_data), pooled_start, silent = TRUE)
pooled_fit = optim(
  par = pooled_obj$par,
  fn = pooled_obj$fn,
  gr = pooled_obj$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)
pooled_fit$convergence

[1] 0

# Estimates on the original scale: a and sigma in counts/min/min, b in ppm.
c(a = exp(pooled_fit$par[["log_a"]]), b = exp(pooled_fit$par[["log_b"]]),
  sigma = exp(pooled_fit$par[["log_sigma"]]))

           a            b        sigma 
190.80642383   0.06038898  17.78683790 


The fit converged, with \(\hat a\approx191\) counts/min/min, \(\hat b\approx0.060\) ppm and \(\hat\sigma\approx17.8\) counts/min/min. We draw the curve over the data (Figure 4):

# Michaelis–Menten function: asymptote a and half-maximum b.
michaelis_menten = function(x, a = 1, b = 1) {
  a * x / (b + x)
}

# Observations, with a filled symbol for the treated cells, and the fitted curve.
plot(rate ~ conc, data = Puromycin,
     pch = ifelse(Puromycin$state == "treated", 16, 1),
     xlab = "Concentration of substrate (ppm)", ylab = "Rate (counts/min/min)")
curve(michaelis_menten(x, a = exp(pooled_fit$par[["log_a"]]),
                       b = exp(pooled_fit$par[["log_b"]])),
      add = TRUE, col = "#D55E00")
legend("bottomright", legend = c("treated", "untreated"), pch = c(16, 1), bty = "n")







Figure 4: Rate of an enzymatic reaction against the concentration of the substrate in cells treated with puromycin (filled circles) and in untreated cells (open circles), with one Michaelis–Menten curve for both states fitted by maximum likelihood.





The curve passes between the two groups: above 0.1 ppm, most treated cells lie above it and most untreated cells below it.


2.1.2 Question 2
In the second model the parameter log_a is a vector with the logarithms of the two asymptotes, and a[state] selects the asymptote of the state of each observation. The NLL also asks for the difference between the two asymptotes with ADREPORT(), which we use in question 3. We start from the two asymptotes read by eye:

# Negative log-likelihood with one asymptote for each state and a common b and sigma.
state_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  rate = OBS(rate)
  a = exp(log_a)
  b = exp(log_b)
  sigma = exp(log_sigma)
  # Difference between the asymptotes of the treated and the untreated cells.
  difference = a[1] - a[2]
  ADREPORT(difference)
  # a[state] is the asymptote of the state of each observation.
  mu = a[state] * conc / (b + conc)
  -sum(dnorm(x = rate, mean = mu, sd = sigma, log = TRUE))
}

# Starting values: the asymptotes read by eye (treated, untreated), b and sigma as before.
state_start = list(log_a = log(c(210, 165)), log_b = log(0.06), log_sigma = log(10))
state_obj = MakeADFun(cmb(state_nll, enzyme_data), state_start, silent = TRUE)
state_fit = optim(
  par = state_obj$par,
  fn = state_obj$fn,
  gr = state_obj$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)
state_fit$convergence

[1] 0

# Estimates on the original scale. The first two elements of par are the two values of
# log_a (treated, untreated); unname() drops their names.
a_state = unname(exp(state_fit$par[1:2]))
b_state = exp(state_fit$par[["log_b"]])
sigma_state = exp(state_fit$par[["log_sigma"]])
c(a_treated = a_state[1], a_untreated = a_state[2], b = b_state, sigma = sigma_state)

   a_treated  a_untreated            b        sigma 
208.63009736 166.60417627   0.05797186   9.87065784 


The fit converged. The asymptote is about 209 counts/min/min for the treated cells and 167 for the untreated cells, the half-maximum is 0.058 ppm, and \(\hat\sigma\) has fallen from 17.8 to 9.9 counts/min/min (Figure 5). With one curve for both states, the difference between the states is part of the spread of the rates around the curve. With one asymptote for each state the curves describe that difference, and the spread that remains is about half as large.

# Observations and one fitted curve for each state.
plot(rate ~ conc, data = Puromycin,
     pch = ifelse(Puromycin$state == "treated", 16, 1),
     xlab = "Concentration of substrate (ppm)", ylab = "Rate (counts/min/min)")
curve(michaelis_menten(x, a = a_state[1], b = b_state), add = TRUE, lty = 1, col = "#D55E00")
curve(michaelis_menten(x, a = a_state[2], b = b_state), add = TRUE, lty = 2, col = "#D55E00")
legend("bottomright", legend = c("treated", "untreated"),
       pch = c(16, 1), lty = c(1, 2), bty = "n")







Figure 5: The same observations with a Michaelis–Menten curve for each state, with separate asymptotes and a common half-maximum, fitted by maximum likelihood: treated cells (filled circles, solid line) and untreated cells (open circles, dashed line).







2.1.3 Question 3
The row difference of the summary of sdreport() holds the estimate and the standard error of the difference. A difference between two asymptotes can be positive or negative and has no bound, so we calculate the Wald interval on the original scale, as for the difference between two probabilities in the Chapter 4 practical:

# Standard errors, and the 95% Wald interval of the difference between the asymptotes.
state_sd = sdreport(state_obj)
state_summary = summary(state_sd)
state_summary

            Estimate Std. Error
log_a       5.340563 0.02687868
log_a       5.115621 0.03300880
log_b      -2.847798 0.10104611
log_sigma   2.289567 0.14744177
difference 42.025921 5.85998423

state_summary["difference", "Estimate"] +
  c(-1, 1) * critical_value * state_summary["difference", "Std. Error"]

[1] 30.54056 53.51128


The asymptote of the treated cells is higher by 42 counts/min/min, with a 95% Wald interval from 31 to 54 counts/min/min. So in this model the treatment with puromycin raises the maximum rate of the reaction by about a quarter (\(208.6/166.6\approx1.25\)), while the concentration at which the reaction reaches half of its maximum rate is the same in both states. That the half-maximum is shared is an assumption of the model; a model with one \(b\) for each state could be fitted and compared with it in the same way as in question 5.


2.1.4 Question 4
We profile \(\log(b)\) and transform the endpoints back with exp(), and we calculate the Wald interval from the row log_b, on the log scale, with its endpoints transformed back:

# Profile of log(b) and its 95% interval, transformed back (ppm). confint() warns about
# repeated values, as in Exercise 1.
state_profile_b = TMB::tmbprofile(state_obj, name = "log_b", trace = FALSE)
exp(confint(state_profile_b))

           lower      upper
log_b 0.04693476 0.07100063

# Wald interval of b (ppm): calculated on the log scale, endpoints transformed back.
exp(state_summary["log_b", "Estimate"] +
      c(-1, 1) * critical_value * state_summary["log_b", "Std. Error"])

[1] 0.04755614 0.07066882


The likelihood profile interval goes from 0.047 to 0.071 ppm and the Wald interval from 0.048 to 0.071 ppm: their endpoints differ by less than 0.001 ppm. The difference from the reed frogs is in the design. The concentrations of the experiment go from 0.02 to 1.1 ppm, about 19 times the half-maximum, so the observations cover the rise of the curve and also the part where it levels off. Both parameters are then well determined, and the log-likelihood is close to a parabola on the log scale, which is the approximation behind the Wald interval. In the reed frog experiment the densities stopped below the half-maximum, so the tanks said little about the asymptote, and the profile of the handling time was strongly asymmetric.


2.1.5 Question 5
The first model has \(K=3\) parameters and the second \(K=4\), and both are fitted to the same 23 observations, so \(n=23\) in AICc and BIC:

# AIC, AICc and BIC of the two models, with n = 23 observations.
n_enzyme = length(enzyme_data$rate)
k_enzyme = c(pooled = 3, state = 4)
nll_enzyme = c(pooled = pooled_fit$value, state = state_fit$value)
aic_enzyme = 2 * k_enzyme + 2 * nll_enzyme
aicc_enzyme = aic_enzyme + 2 * k_enzyme * (k_enzyme + 1) / (n_enzyme - k_enzyme - 1)
bic_enzyme = k_enzyme * log(n_enzyme) + 2 * nll_enzyme
rbind(aic = aic_enzyme, aicc = aicc_enzyme, bic = bic_enzyme)

       pooled    state
aic  203.6803 178.5913
aicc 204.9434 180.8135
bic  207.0868 183.1333


Here is the code for leave-one-out cross-validation with its two gaps filled in. Gap 1 fits model m to the other 22 observations: a negative index, -i, removes observation i from the list of data. Gap 2 processes the NLL for observation i alone, so that its function fn(), evaluated at the estimates of the fit, is the NLL of the held-out observation, that is, minus its log density under the model fitted to the other 22. Unlike as.list(), fn() takes the vector of estimates as it is:

# Fit one model to one list of data, from the given starting values.
fit_model = function(nll, start, data) {
  obj = MakeADFun(cmb(nll, data), start, silent = TRUE)
  optim(par = obj$par, fn = obj$fn, gr = obj$gr, method = "BFGS")
}

# Keep only the given observations in the list of data.
subset_observations = function(data, rows) {
  data$conc = data$conc[rows]
  data$rate = data$rate[rows]
  data$state = data$state[rows]
  data
}

# The NLL and the starting values of each model.
enzyme_models = list(
  pooled = list(nll = pooled_nll, start = pooled_start),
  state = list(nll = state_nll, start = state_start)
)

# Leave-one-out log score of each model: fit to 22 observations, score the one held out.
n_enzyme = length(enzyme_data$rate)
loo_enzyme = c(pooled = NA, state = NA)
n_failed = 0
for (m in seq_along(enzyme_models)) {
  score = 0
  for (i in seq_len(n_enzyme)) {
    # Gap 1: fit model m to every observation except observation i.
    fit = fit_model(
      enzyme_models[[m]]$nll,
      enzyme_models[[m]]$start,
      subset_observations(enzyme_data, -i)
    )
    n_failed = n_failed + (fit$convergence != 0)

    # Gap 2: the NLL of model m for observation i alone.
    heldout_obj = MakeADFun(
      cmb(enzyme_models[[m]]$nll, subset_observations(enzyme_data, i)),
      enzyme_models[[m]]$start,
      silent = TRUE
    )
    score = score - heldout_obj$fn(fit$par)
  }
  loo_enzyme[m] = score
}
n_failed

[1] 0

loo_enzyme

    pooled      state 
-102.16712  -90.31907 


All 46 fits converged. Every criterion prefers the model with one asymptote for each state: by 25.1 units of AIC, 24.1 of AICc and 24.0 of BIC, and by 11.8 units of log score, which corresponds to about 24 units on the scale of AIC. The criteria agree, and by a wide margin: the extra parameter improves the fit far more than any of the penalties, and the model with one asymptote for each state also predicts held-out observations better. This agrees with the halving of \(\hat\sigma\) in question 2.


2.1.6 Question 6
We simulate from the model with one asymptote for each state, as in Exercise 1 (the rates were marked with OBS() in question 1). The expected rate of each observation is the curve of its state at its concentration. DHARMa::plotQQunif() draws only the left panel of plot(), the quantile–quantile plot; we use it because the residuals against the concentration, which DHARMa::plotResiduals() draws, replace the right panel:

# 1,000 hypothetical samples of the 23 rates at the estimates.
state_simulations = matrix(NA, nrow = n_enzyme, ncol = n_sim)
set.seed(seed = 621)
for (j in seq_len(n_sim)) {
  state_simulations[, j] = state_obj$simulate(state_fit$par)$rate
}

# Expected rate of each observation, and the scaled quantile residuals.
state_expected = michaelis_menten(enzyme_data$conc, a = a_state[enzyme_data$state],
                                  b = b_state)
state_residuals = DHARMa::createDHARMa(
  simulatedResponse = state_simulations,
  observedResponse = enzyme_data$rate,
  fittedPredictedResponse = state_expected,
  integerResponse = FALSE
)

# Quantile–quantile plot, and residuals against the concentration of the substrate.
DHARMa::plotQQunif(state_residuals)







DHARMa::plotResiduals(state_residuals, form = enzyme_data$conc)








The quantile–quantile plot follows the line, so the residuals as a whole are close to uniform. Against the concentration they show a pattern: they tend to lie above 0.5 at the lowest concentration and at the two highest, and below 0.5 at the intermediate concentrations. That is, the observed rates lie above the curves at both ends and below them in the middle, as if the rate bent towards its maximum more gradually than a Michaelis–Menten curve can. However, there are only three or four observations at each concentration, and a pattern of this size can arise by chance with 23 observations (DHARMa draws one quartile in red, but its combined test does not flag the pattern), so the plot is a hint and not a conclusion. A curve with a third parameter that changes how gradually the curve bends could be fitted and compared with the criteria of question 5.

title: Chapter 6: Fitting ecological response curves — solutions
text:
3.1 Solution

3.1.1 Question 1
We count the missing values in each column with is.na(), keep the trees for which both are known, and look for fecundities that are not whole numbers:

# Load the fir data and count the missing diameters and fecundities.
data(FirDBHFec_sum, package = "emdbook")
nrow(FirDBHFec_sum)

[1] 333

colSums(is.na(FirDBHFec_sum[, c("DBH", "fecundity")]))

      DBH fecundity 
       22         0 

# Keep the trees with both a diameter and a fecundity.
complete = !is.na(FirDBHFec_sum$DBH) & !is.na(FirDBHFec_sum$fecundity)
fir = FirDBHFec_sum[complete, ]
nrow(fir)

[1] 311

# Fecundities that are not whole numbers.
fir$fecundity[fir$fecundity != round(fir$fecundity)]

[1] 206.5  63.5 107.5 129.5 227.7 114.5


The diameter is missing for 22 trees and the fecundity for none, so 311 trees remain. A missing value means that the quantity was not recorded. Replacing it by zero would add observations that were never made (a tree with a diameter of zero, or without any cones) and would pull the curve towards them. Removing the incomplete rows assumes instead that whether a value was recorded does not depend on the fecundity of the tree.
Six fecundities are not whole numbers, for example 206.5. The help page does not explain them, but in the full data set FirDBHFec of the same package the yearly counts of these six trees include fractions (such as 32.5 cones in one year). The Poisson and Negative Binomial distributions describe whole numbers, so we round the six values to the nearest whole number, which changes each of them by at most half a rachis (removing the six trees would be the alternative, at the cost of six observations). The list of data holds the diameter (cm) and the number of rachises:

# Diameter (cm) and fecundity, rounded to whole numbers of rachises.
fir_data = list(dbh = fir$DBH, cones = round(fir$fecundity))



3.1.2 Question 2
Let \(Y_i\) be the number of rachises of tree \(i\) and \(x_i\) its diameter. The model is
\[
Y_i \sim \operatorname{Poisson}\left(\mu(x_i)\right),
\qquad
\mu(x)=a\,x^b,
\qquad i=1,\ldots,311.
\]
The mean of a Poisson distribution must be positive, and the power law is positive for any \(b\) when \(a\) and \(x\) are positive, so we optimise \(\log(a)\) and leave the exponent \(b\) untransformed: it can take any real value. The units of \(a\) follow from the curve: \(ax^b\) is a number of rachises and \(x^b\) is in cm\(^b\), so \(a\) is in rachises/cm\(^b\), units that depend on the estimate of the exponent (rachises/cm² for \(b=2\)). This makes \(a\) hard to interpret on its own, and we will interpret \(b\) and quantities calculated from it. We mark the counts with OBS() for the residuals and start from the values read by eye:

# Negative log-likelihood of the power law with a Poisson observation model.
poisson_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  cones = OBS(cones)
  a = exp(log_a)
  # Mean number of rachises of a tree of each diameter.
  mu = a * dbh^b
  -sum(dpois(x = cones, lambda = mu, log = TRUE))
}

# Process the NLL from the values read by eye in the Chapter 5 practical, and fit it.
poisson_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(poisson_nll, fir_data),
  list(log_a = log(0.5), b = 2),
  silent = TRUE
)
poisson_fit = optim(
  par = poisson_obj$par,
  fn = poisson_obj$fn,
  gr = poisson_obj$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)
poisson_fit$convergence

[1] 0

c(a = exp(poisson_fit$par[["log_a"]]), b = poisson_fit$par[["b"]])

        a         b 
0.6826788 1.9775730 


The fit converged, with \(\hat b\approx1.98\), close to the exponent of 2 read by eye. We simulate 1,000 hypothetical samples of the 311 trees and calculate the residuals. The counts are whole numbers, so integerResponse = TRUE. The element scaledResiduals of the result holds the residuals, and a residual of exactly 0 or 1 marks a tree whose count lies outside the range of all its simulated values, so we also count those trees:

# Power law: a is the value at x = 1 and b is the exponent.
power_law = function(x, a = 1, b = 1) {
  a * x^b
}

# 1,000 hypothetical samples of the 311 trees at the estimates.
n_trees = length(fir_data$cones)
poisson_simulations = matrix(NA, nrow = n_trees, ncol = n_sim)
set.seed(seed = 631)
for (j in seq_len(n_sim)) {
  poisson_simulations[, j] = poisson_obj$simulate(poisson_fit$par)$cones
}

# Scaled quantile residuals and the two standard panels.
poisson_residuals = DHARMa::createDHARMa(
  simulatedResponse = poisson_simulations,
  observedResponse = fir_data$cones,
  fittedPredictedResponse = power_law(fir_data$dbh, a = exp(poisson_fit$par[["log_a"]]),
                                      b = poisson_fit$par[["b"]]),
  integerResponse = TRUE
)
plot(poisson_residuals)

# Trees outside the range of their simulations, and the dispersion statistic.
sum(poisson_residuals$scaledResiduals %in% c(0, 1))

[1] 147

DHARMa::testDispersion(poisson_residuals, plot = FALSE)$statistic

dispersion 
  22.90786 








Figure 6: Scaled quantile residuals of the Poisson model with a power law for the fecundity of 311 fir trees, from 1,000 hypothetical samples. Stars mark trees whose counts lie outside the range of their simulated values.





The Poisson model does not describe these data. The residuals are far from uniform: most of them are close to 0 or 1, and 147 of the 311 trees have counts outside the range of all their 1,000 simulated values. The dispersion statistic is about 23, so the counts vary around the curve about 23 times as much (as a variance) as the Poisson distribution allows. Trees of the same diameter differ in fecundity for many reasons that the curve does not contain, and the Poisson model, whose variance equals its mean, leaves no room for them.


3.1.3 Question 3
The Negative Binomial model keeps the curve for the mean and adds the shape \(k\), which is positive, so we optimise \(\log(k)\). dnbinom2() of RTMBdist takes the mean in mu and the shape in size. We start from the values by eye and a shape of 1:

# Negative log-likelihood of the power law with a Negative Binomial observation model.
nbinom_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  cones = OBS(cones)
  a = exp(log_a)
  k = exp(log_k)
  mu = a * dbh^b
  -sum(dnbinom2(x = cones, mu = mu, size = k, log = TRUE))
}

# Process the NLL from the values read by eye and a shape of 1, and fit it.
nbinom_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(nbinom_nll, fir_data),
  list(log_a = log(0.5), b = 2, log_k = log(1)),
  silent = TRUE
)
nbinom_fit = optim(
  par = nbinom_obj$par,
  fn = nbinom_obj$fn,
  gr = nbinom_obj$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)
nbinom_fit$convergence

[1] 0

c(a = exp(nbinom_fit$par[["log_a"]]), b = nbinom_fit$par[["b"]],
  k = exp(nbinom_fit$par[["log_k"]]))

        a         b         k 
0.9966442 1.8014395 1.8386925 


The fit converged, with \(\hat b\approx1.80\) and \(\hat k\approx1.84\). We check the residuals as for the Poisson model:

# 1,000 hypothetical samples of the 311 trees at the estimates.
nbinom_simulations = matrix(NA, nrow = n_trees, ncol = n_sim)
set.seed(seed = 632)
for (j in seq_len(n_sim)) {
  nbinom_simulations[, j] = nbinom_obj$simulate(nbinom_fit$par)$cones
}

# Scaled quantile residuals, the two standard panels and the dispersion statistic.
nbinom_residuals = DHARMa::createDHARMa(
  simulatedResponse = nbinom_simulations,
  observedResponse = fir_data$cones,
  fittedPredictedResponse = power_law(fir_data$dbh, a = exp(nbinom_fit$par[["log_a"]]),
                                      b = nbinom_fit$par[["b"]]),
  integerResponse = TRUE
)
plot(nbinom_residuals)
DHARMa::testDispersion(nbinom_residuals, plot = FALSE)$statistic

dispersion 
 0.6573872 








Figure 7: Scaled quantile residuals of the Negative Binomial model with a power law for the fecundity of 311 fir trees, from 1,000 hypothetical samples.





The Negative Binomial model describes the variation among trees far better. The quantile–quantile plot follows the line, and only one tree (the star) lies outside the range of its simulations. A smaller disagreement remains. The dispersion statistic is below one, so the counts vary around the curve somewhat less than the model allows, and in the right panel the lower quartile of the residuals rises from below 0.25 for the trees with the smallest expected fecundity to above 0.25 for the largest: large trees seldom have the very low counts that the model expects for some of them. Under a Negative Binomial model with one shape the variance, \(\mu+\mu^2/k\), grows with the square of the mean, and the residuals suggest that the variation among the largest trees grows less than that. A possible revision would let the shape depend on the diameter. For the questions of this exercise, which concern the curve, the remaining disagreement is small compared with that of the Poisson model.
Both curves are drawn over the data in Figure 8:

# Observations and the two fitted curves.
plot(fecundity ~ DBH, data = fir,
     xlab = "Diameter at breast height (cm)", ylab = "Fecundity (cone rachises)")
curve(power_law(x, a = exp(nbinom_fit$par[["log_a"]]), b = nbinom_fit$par[["b"]]),
      add = TRUE, lty = 1, col = "#D55E00")
curve(power_law(x, a = exp(poisson_fit$par[["log_a"]]), b = poisson_fit$par[["b"]]),
      add = TRUE, lty = 2)
legend("topleft", legend = c("Negative Binomial", "Poisson"),
       lty = c(1, 2), col = c("#D55E00", "black"), bty = "n")







Figure 8: Fecundity of 311 balsam fir trees against their diameter at breast height, with the power law fitted by maximum likelihood under a Negative Binomial model (solid line) and under a Poisson model (dashed line).





The two curves are almost the same for trees up to about 10 cm, and above that the Negative Binomial curve lies below the Poisson curve. The two models weight the trees differently. Under the Negative Binomial model the variance grows with the square of the mean, so the large counts of the largest trees are less informative about the curve than under the Poisson model, whose variance grows only in proportion to the mean.


3.1.4 Question 4
The Poisson model has \(K=2\) parameters and the Negative Binomial model \(K=3\), and \(n\) is the number of trees, 311:

# AIC, AICc and BIC of the two models, with n = 311 trees.
k_fir = c(poisson = 2, nbinom = 3)
nll_fir = c(poisson = poisson_fit$value, nbinom = nbinom_fit$value)
aic_fir = 2 * k_fir + 2 * nll_fir
aicc_fir = aic_fir + 2 * k_fir * (k_fir + 1) / (n_trees - k_fir - 1)
bic_fir = k_fir * log(n_trees) + 2 * nll_fir
rbind(aic = aic_fir, aicc = aicc_fir, bic = bic_fir)

      poisson   nbinom
aic  7918.190 2897.062
aicc 7918.229 2897.140
bic  7925.669 2908.281


All three criteria prefer the Negative Binomial model by about 5,000 units. With 311 trees the correction of AICc is negligible, and the extra cost of the shape in BIC (\(\log(311)\) instead of 2) is tiny compared with the difference in log-likelihood. The comparison agrees with the residuals of questions 2 and 3.


3.1.5 Question 5
The exponent is not transformed in the NLL, so confint() of its profile gives the interval of \(b\) directly. The function \(2^b\) increases with \(b\), so the endpoints of the interval of \(b\) give an interval for \(2^b\) in the same order:

# Profile of b and its 95% interval (confint() warns about repeated values, as before).
nbinom_profile_b = TMB::tmbprofile(nbinom_obj, name = "b", trace = FALSE)
b_interval_fir = confint(nbinom_profile_b)
b_interval_fir

     lower    upper
b 1.547824 2.054513

# 95% interval for the factor 2^b, from the endpoints of the interval of b.
2^b_interval_fir

     lower    upper
b 2.923757 4.154033


The exponent is estimated at 1.80, with a likelihood profile interval from 1.55 to 2.05. When the diameter doubles, the mean fecundity is multiplied by \(2^{1.80}\approx3.5\), with an interval from 2.9 to 4.2.
The value \(b=2\), for which the fecundity would be proportional to the cross-sectional area of the trunk, lies inside the interval of \(b\), close to its upper end. So the data do not rule out this proportionality, but they favour a smaller exponent, for which the mean fecundity increases by a factor of about 3.5 and not 4 when the diameter doubles. Note that the Poisson model, with \(\hat b\approx1.98\), would have suggested an exponent of 2 with an interval that is much too narrow, because it treats the trees as far less variable than they are.


3.1.6 Question 6
As in the theory, we add a grid of diameters to the list of data, as dbh_grid, and calculate the curve on the grid inside the NLL. The mean fecundity is positive, so we ask for its logarithm with ADREPORT(), a scale on which it is unbounded. We process the new NLL, fit it again (the estimates do not change) and call sdreport():

# A grid of diameters (cm), added to the list of data.
dbh_grid = seq(from = 3, to = 18, by = 0.1)
fir_data$dbh_grid = dbh_grid

# The Negative Binomial NLL with three more lines.
nbinom_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  cones = OBS(cones)
  a = exp(log_a)
  k = exp(log_k)
  mu = a * dbh^b
  # The logarithm of the mean fecundity at every diameter of the grid.
  mu_grid = a * dbh_grid^b
  log_mu_grid = log(mu_grid)
  ADREPORT(log_mu_grid)
  -sum(dnbinom2(x = cones, mu = mu, size = k, log = TRUE))
}

# Process the new NLL, fit it again and calculate the standard errors.
nbinom_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(nbinom_nll, fir_data),
  list(log_a = log(0.5), b = 2, log_k = log(1)),
  silent = TRUE
)
nbinom_fit = optim(
  par = nbinom_obj$par,
  fn = nbinom_obj$fn,
  gr = nbinom_obj$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)
nbinom_fit$convergence

[1] 0

nbinom_sd = sdreport(nbinom_obj)

With select = "report", summary() returns one row per diameter of the grid. We calculate the Wald interval of each row on the log scale, and transform the curve and the endpoints back with exp() to draw them over the data (Figure 9):

# Rows of log_mu_grid: one per diameter of the grid.
band_summary = summary(nbinom_sd, select = "report")

# Wald intervals on the log scale.
log_lower = band_summary[, "Estimate"] - critical_value * band_summary[, "Std. Error"]
log_upper = band_summary[, "Estimate"] + critical_value * band_summary[, "Std. Error"]

# Observations, and the curve and its band transformed back to numbers of rachises.
plot(fecundity ~ DBH, data = fir,
     xlab = "Diameter at breast height (cm)", ylab = "Fecundity (cone rachises)")
lines(dbh_grid, exp(band_summary[, "Estimate"]), col = "#D55E00")
lines(dbh_grid, exp(log_lower), lty = 2, col = "#D55E00")
lines(dbh_grid, exp(log_upper), lty = 2, col = "#D55E00")
legend("topleft", legend = c("Fitted curve", "95% confidence band"),
       lty = c(1, 2), col = "#D55E00", bty = "n")







Figure 9: Fecundity of 311 balsam fir trees against their diameter at breast height, with the power law fitted by maximum likelihood under a Negative Binomial model (solid line) and its pointwise 95% confidence band (dashed lines), calculated from Wald intervals on the log scale.





The band is pointwise: at each diameter, the interval contains the mean fecundity of the data generating process at that diameter in approximately 95% of hypothetical samples. On the log scale it is narrowest at about 8 cm, where the standard error of the logarithm of the mean is 0.043, so the interval extends about 8% on either side of the curve. It widens towards both ends, to standard errors of 0.13 at 3 cm and 0.11 at 17.4 cm, the largest tree. On the log scale the curve is a straight line in \(\log(x)\), \(\log(\mu(x))=\log(a)+b\log(x)\), and a line fitted to data is best determined in the middle of the observations, here around the geometric mean of the diameters, 7.9 cm. Half of the trees have diameters between 6.5 and 9.8 cm, and only six are larger than 15 cm, so away from the middle a change in the exponent moves the curve more and fewer trees hold it in place. On the original scale the band also widens because it is multiplied by the mean: at 8 cm it runs from about 39 to 46 rachises, and at 17.4 cm from about 138 to 212. The band describes the uncertainty of the mean fecundity; the fecundities of single trees vary much more around the curve, as the cloud of points shows.

title: Chapter 6: Fitting ecological response curves — solutions
text:
4.1 Solution

4.1.1 Question 1
Here is the function with its two gaps filled in. For each sample, gap 1 fits the model to the simulated titres exactly as Exercise 1 fitted it to the data, with cmb(), MakeADFun() and optim() from the values read by eye. Gap 2 takes the estimate and the standard error of the time of the peak from the row of ADREPORT() and calculates the Wald interval on the original scale, as in question 3 of Exercise 1:

# Hypothetical samples of the 27 titres from the Normal model fitted in Exercise 1. For
# each sample: the estimate of the time of the peak, its 95% Wald interval, and whether
# the fit converged.
simulate_peak_time = function(n_samples) {
  results = data.frame(
    estimate = rep(NA, times = n_samples),
    lower = rep(NA, times = n_samples),
    upper = rep(NA, times = n_samples),
    converged = rep(NA, times = n_samples)
  )
  for (i in seq_len(n_samples)) {
    # One hypothetical sample: titres on the same days, simulated at the estimates.
    titre_sim = normal_obj$simulate(normal_fit$par)$titre

    # Gap 1: fit the model to the simulated titres from the values read by eye.
    sim_obj = MakeADFun(
      cmb(normal_nll, list(day = titre_data$day, titre = titre_sim)),
      titre_start,
      silent = TRUE
    )
    sim_fit = optim(par = sim_obj$par, fn = sim_obj$fn, gr = sim_obj$gr, method = "BFGS")

    # Gap 2: estimate and 95% Wald interval of the time of the peak, on the original scale.
    sim_report = summary(sdreport(sim_obj), select = "report")
    estimate = sim_report["peak_time", "Estimate"]
    lower = estimate - critical_value * sim_report["peak_time", "Std. Error"]
    upper = estimate + critical_value * sim_report["peak_time", "Std. Error"]

    results$estimate[i] = estimate
    results$lower[i] = lower
    results$upper[i] = upper
    results$converged[i] = sim_fit$convergence == 0
  }
  results
}

The time of the peak that the samples are simulated from is \(1/\hat b\) of Exercise 1. We run the simulation (about half a minute) and count the failed fits, both those with a convergence code other than zero and those for which sdreport() could not calculate a standard error:

# 2,000 hypothetical samples from the model fitted in Exercise 1.
set.seed(seed = 641)
n_samples = 2000
peak_samples = simulate_peak_time(n_samples)

# Time of the peak used to simulate (days), and the number of failed fits.
peak_time_sim = 1 / b_mle
peak_time_sim

[1] 6.052262

sum(!peak_samples$converged | is.na(peak_samples$lower))

[1] 0


No fit failed. Had some failed, we would report how many and count them in the coverage (for example as intervals that miss), because leaving them out silently would hide the samples in which the method breaks down. The bias is the mean of the estimates minus the time of the peak used to simulate. Its Monte Carlo standard error, the standard error of a mean of 2,000 values, is the standard deviation of the estimates divided by \(\sqrt{2000}\):

# Bias of the estimator of the time of the peak, its Monte Carlo standard error, and the
# standard deviation of the estimates next to the standard error of Exercise 1.
c(
  bias = mean(peak_samples$estimate) - peak_time_sim,
  mc_se_bias = sd(peak_samples$estimate) / sqrt(n_samples),
  sd_estimates = sd(peak_samples$estimate),
  se_exercise_1 = summary(normal_sd, select = "report")["peak_time", "Std. Error"]
)

         bias    mc_se_bias  sd_estimates se_exercise_1 
  0.019098432   0.008529676   0.381458716   0.382950133 


The bias is 0.019 days, about two Monte Carlo standard errors (0.0085 days) from zero. So the estimator may be slightly biased upwards, but by about 0.3% of the time of the peak, which is negligible compared with its standard error. The standard deviation of the estimates across the hypothetical samples, 0.381 days, agrees with the standard error that sdreport() calculated from the curvature of the log-likelihood of the data, 0.383 days. With 27 observations the standard error describes the spread of the estimator well.


4.1.2 Question 2
The interval contains the time of the peak used to simulate when its lower endpoint is below that value and its upper endpoint above it. The coverage is the fraction of samples in which this is the case, and its Monte Carlo standard error is that of a proportion:

# Coverage of the Wald interval, and its Monte Carlo standard error.
covered = peak_samples$lower <= peak_time_sim & peak_time_sim <= peak_samples$upper
coverage = mean(covered)
c(coverage = coverage, mc_se = sqrt(coverage * (1 - coverage) / n_samples))

   coverage       mc_se 
0.926500000 0.005835141 


The coverage is 0.927, with a Monte Carlo standard error of 0.006, so it lies about four standard errors below the nominal 0.95. The Wald interval of the time of the peak contains the value used to simulate slightly less often than its confidence level states: with 27 observations it is an approximation.


4.1.3 Question 3
An interval lies entirely below the value used to simulate when its upper endpoint is below that value, and entirely above it when its lower endpoint is above it:

# Intervals that miss on each side of the time of the peak used to simulate.
c(
  below = sum(peak_samples$upper < peak_time_sim),
  above = sum(peak_samples$lower > peak_time_sim)
)

below above 
  104    43 


Of the 147 intervals that miss, 104 lie below the time of the peak used to simulate and 43 above it. A good interval would miss about equally often on both sides (about 50 times on each side in 2,000 samples). The Wald interval is symmetric around the estimate, whereas in question 3 of Exercise 1 the likelihood profile interval extended further above the estimate than below it, which is what an interval needs in order to miss less often on the low side. This suggests that the profile interval would have a coverage closer to 95% and that it would miss more evenly on both sides. Only a simulation that calculates the profile interval in every sample could show this.


4.1.4 Question 4
The simulation describes the behaviour of the interval when the data generating process is the fitted model: titres that follow a Ricker curve exactly, with the estimates of Exercise 1 as its parameters, and that vary around it according to a Normal distribution with the same standard deviation on every day, independently of each other. The parameters of the process that generated the real titres are unknown and differ from the estimates, and the coverage would be somewhat different with other parameter values. The model is also an approximation: the residuals of Exercise 1 suggested that the titre levels off after its peak, which a Ricker curve cannot do, and the titres of the real rabbits need not be independent or Normal. With a misspecified model the properties of estimators and intervals change (see Misspecified models), which this simulation does not explore. So the results approximate the behaviour of the interval for the real rabbits, and the approximation is better the closer the fitted model is to the data generating process.

title: Chapter 7: Grouped ecological response curves
text:
The exercises fit models with random effects to four data sets in which the observations come in groups: repeated measurements of the height of pine trees (Exercise 1), tanks of tadpoles (Exercise 2), visits to the nests of barn owls (Exercise 3) and visits to stream sites where salamanders were counted (Exercise 4). Three of these data sets were used in earlier chapters, where the observations were treated as independent; here a grouped model describes the groups. Exercise 5 simulates hypothetical samples to compare the estimates of a variance among groups by maximum likelihood and by REML. Exercises 1 to 4 are the core of the practical and Exercise 5 is extra practice. Work through the first exercise, which is worked in full on this page, before trying the remaining ones. The ideas and notation are introduced in the Chapter 7 theory, and the hints of each question point to the section that you need. Work through the exercises in one R session: later exercises reuse the helper cmb() and the object n_sim of Exercise 1.
As in the theory, every model is written and fitted with the packages RTMB and RTMBdist, which you installed in the Chapter 1 practical together with emdbook and glmmTMB, where the data of Exercises 2 to 4 are. The scaled quantile residuals are calculated with the package DHARMa, which you installed for the Chapter 6 practical. Load RTMB first and RTMBdist second:
# Load RTMB first and RTMBdist second.
library(RTMB)
library(RTMBdist)

title: Chapter 7: Grouped ecological response curves
text:
1.1 Solution

1.1.1 Question 1
The observational unit is one measurement of the height of one tree at one age, and the group is the tree: the six measurements of a tree share its genotype and its growing conditions, so they tend to resemble each other more than measurements of different trees. The data have 14 trees with six measurements each. The asymptote \(A\) is a height, so it is in feet. The rate \(k\) multiplies an age in the exponent, which has no units, so \(k\) is in 1/year, and \(t_0\) is an age in years. We plot the measurements and join those of each tree with a line in a for loop over the trees:

# Measurements, then one line for each tree.
plot(height ~ age, data = pine_data, xlab = "Age (years)", ylab = "Height (ft)")
for (j in seq_along(tree_names)) {
  in_tree = pine_data$tree == j
  lines(pine_data$age[in_tree], pine_data$height[in_tree])
}







Figure 1: Height of 14 loblolly pines against age. Lines join the measurements of the same tree.





The trees grow almost in parallel (Figure 1). Their growth slows down with age, but none of them has stopped growing at 25 years, when the tallest tree measures 64.1 ft. The differences among trees are small at 3 years and grow with age, which is what a tree with a higher asymptote does under the curve above: its curve is the typical curve multiplied by a factor.


1.1.2 Question 2
Let \(H_{ij}\) be the height of tree \(j\) at its \(i\)-th measurement, at the age \(t_{ij}\). With complete pooling all the trees share one curve, and the heights vary around it with a Normal distribution:
\[
H_{ij}\sim\operatorname{Normal}\left(h(t_{ij}),\,\sigma^2_{\mathrm{obs}}\right),
\qquad
h(t)=A\left(1-e^{-k(t-t_0)}\right),
\]
where \(\sigma_{\mathrm{obs}}\) is the standard deviation of the heights around the curve, in feet (\(\sigma^2_{\mathrm{obs}}\) is the variance of the model). The asymptote, the rate and the standard deviation are positive, so we optimise their logarithms, and \(t_0\) is not transformed:

# Negative log-likelihood with one growth curve for all the trees (complete pooling).
pooled_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  A = exp(log_A)
  k = exp(log_k)
  sd_obs = exp(log_sd_obs)
  # Expected height at the age of each measurement.
  mu = A * (1 - exp(-k * (age - t0)))
  -sum(dnorm(x = height, mean = mu, sd = sd_obs, log = TRUE))
}

We read the starting values from Figure 1. The trees are still growing at 60 ft, so we take an asymptote of 80 ft. The heights would reach zero shortly before the age of 3 years, so \(t_0=2\) years. A curve of this kind reaches 63% of its asymptote, here about 50 ft, at the age \(t_0+1/k\); the trees reach 50 ft at about 20 years, so \(1/k\approx20\) years and \(k=0.05\)/year. For the standard deviation we take 2 ft:

# Connect a likelihood to a data set.
cmb = function(f, d) function(p) f(p, d)

# Starting values read from the plot.
pine_start = list(log_A = log(80), log_k = log(0.05), t0 = 2, log_sd_obs = log(2))

# Process the NLL, minimise it with BFGS and check the convergence code.
pooled_obj = MakeADFun(cmb(pooled_nll, pine_data), pine_start, silent = TRUE)
pooled_fit = optim(
  par = pooled_obj$par,
  fn = pooled_obj$fn,
  gr = pooled_obj$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)
pooled_fit$convergence

[1] 0

# Estimates on the original scale: A and sd_obs in ft, k in 1/year, t0 in years.
c(
  A = exp(pooled_fit$par[["log_A"]]),
  k = exp(pooled_fit$par[["log_k"]]),
  t0 = pooled_fit$par[["t0"]],
  sd_obs = exp(pooled_fit$par[["log_sd_obs"]])
)

           A            k           t0       sd_obs 
102.26211027   0.03892454   2.05895634   1.68095025 


The fit converged, with an asymptote of 102 ft, a rate of 0.039/year and \(t_0=2.06\) years. The heights vary around the common curve with a standard deviation of 1.68 ft, which includes the differences among trees.


1.1.3 Question 3
The mixed model has two levels, as the model of the theory:
\[
u_j\sim\operatorname{Normal}\left(0,\sigma^2_{\mathrm{tree}}\right),
\qquad
H_{ij}\mid u_j\sim\operatorname{Normal}\left(h_j(t_{ij}),\,\sigma^2_{\mathrm{obs}}\right),
\qquad
h_j(t)=A\,e^{u_j}\left(1-e^{-k(t-t_0)}\right),
\]
where \(u_j\) is the deviation of tree \(j\) on the log scale of the asymptote and \(\sigma^2_{\mathrm{tree}}\) is the variance of these deviations among trees. The joint NLL adds minus the log density of the deviations, before they are used, to minus the log density of the heights for given deviations. Question 5 simulates from this model, so we mark the heights with OBS() now:

# Joint negative log-likelihood with a random asymptote. The heights are marked as
# observations for the simulations of question 5.
mixed_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  height = OBS(height)
  sd_tree = exp(log_sd_tree)
  # Minus the log density of the deviations of the trees, before they are used.
  nll = -sum(dnorm(x = u, mean = 0, sd = sd_tree, log = TRUE))
  # Asymptote of each tree, and minus the log density of the heights for given u.
  A = exp(log_A + u)
  k = exp(log_k)
  sd_obs = exp(log_sd_obs)
  mu = A[tree] * (1 - exp(-k * (age - t0)))
  nll - sum(dnorm(x = height, mean = mu, sd = sd_obs, log = TRUE))
}

The list of parameters adds log_sd_tree, which starts at \(\log(0.1)\) (trees whose asymptotes differ by about 10%), and one deviation per tree, which start at zero. With random = "u", MakeADFun() integrates the deviations out of the likelihood, and optim() minimises the marginal NLL over the other five parameters:

# Process the joint NLL; random = "u" integrates the deviations of the trees out.
mixed_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(mixed_nll, pine_data),
  c(pine_start, list(log_sd_tree = log(0.1), u = rep(0, 14))),
  random = "u",
  silent = TRUE
)
mixed_fit = optim(
  par = mixed_obj$par,
  fn = mixed_obj$fn,
  gr = mixed_obj$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)
mixed_fit$convergence

[1] 0

# Standard errors on the optimised scales.
mixed_sd = sdreport(mixed_obj)
summary(mixed_sd, select = "fixed")

              Estimate Std. Error
log_A        4.6252117 0.02501142
log_k       -3.2439427 0.03491620
t0           2.0581649 0.05093953
log_sd_obs  -0.3006573 0.08450276
log_sd_tree -3.2374592 0.19658686

# Estimates on the original scale.
A_mle = exp(mixed_fit$par[["log_A"]])
k_mle = exp(mixed_fit$par[["log_k"]])
t0_mle = mixed_fit$par[["t0"]]
sd_tree_mle = exp(mixed_fit$par[["log_sd_tree"]])
sd_obs_mle = exp(mixed_fit$par[["log_sd_obs"]])
c(A = A_mle, k = k_mle, t0 = t0_mle, sd_tree = sd_tree_mle, sd_obs = sd_obs_mle)

           A            k           t0      sd_tree       sd_obs 
102.02436795   0.03900979   2.05816486   0.03926353   0.74033142 


The fit converged. The curve hardly changes compared with complete pooling, but the variation is now split into two components. \(\hat\sigma_{\mathrm{obs}}\approx0.74\) ft is the standard deviation of the measurements around the curve of their own tree, less than half of the 1.68 ft of complete pooling, which counted the differences among trees as variation of the measurements. \(\hat\sigma_{\mathrm{tree}}\approx0.039\) is a standard deviation on the log scale of the asymptote, so it has no units: the asymptotes of the trees differ from the median asymptote by roughly 4%. As in the theory, we calculate its interval from the likelihood profile of its logarithm and transform the endpoints back:

# Profile of log(sd_tree), and the 95% interval of sd_tree.
mixed_profile_sd = TMB::tmbprofile(mixed_obj, name = "log_sd_tree", trace = FALSE)
exp(confint(mixed_profile_sd))

                 lower      upper
log_sd_tree 0.02769282 0.06057868


The trees differ by between about 3% and 6% in their asymptotes. Because the deviation of a tree multiplies its whole curve, the standard deviation of the typical height among trees at a given age is roughly \(\sigma_{\mathrm{tree}}\) times the typical height at that age. At 25 years the typical height is:

# Growth curve: asymptote A, rate k and age t0 at which the height is zero.
growth = function(t, A = 1, k = 1, t0 = 0) {
  A * (1 - exp(-k * (t - t0)))
}

# Typical height at 25 years (ft), and roughly the standard deviation among trees.
height_25 = growth(25, A = A_mle, k = k_mle, t0 = t0_mle)
c(typical = height_25, sd_among_trees = sd_tree_mle * height_25)

       typical sd_among_trees 
      60.33461        2.36895 


At 25 years the typical height of the trees varies by about 2.4 ft among trees, three times the 0.74 ft by which the measurements vary around the curve of their tree. At 3 years, with a typical height of less than 4 ft, the differences among trees are much smaller than the variation of the measurements. So which source of variation dominates depends on the age.


1.1.4 Question 4
summary() of the result of sdreport() with select = "random" returns the predicted deviation of each tree with its standard error:

# Predicted tree effects (log scale of the asymptote) and their standard errors.
tree_effects = summary(mixed_sd, select = "random")
rownames(tree_effects) = tree_names
round(tree_effects, 3)

    Estimate Std. Error
301    0.022      0.013
303    0.050      0.013
305    0.075      0.013
307   -0.024      0.013
309    0.039      0.013
311   -0.013      0.013
315   -0.001      0.013
319    0.013      0.013
321   -0.024      0.013
323    0.032      0.013
325   -0.019      0.013
327   -0.056      0.013
329   -0.061      0.013
331   -0.031      0.013


The predicted effects range from \(-0.061\) (tree 329) to \(0.075\) (tree 305), so the asymptotes of the trees lie between about 6% below and 8% above the median, with a standard error of 0.013 for every tree (all the trees have the same six ages). The curve of an observed tree uses its predicted asymptote \(\hat A\,e^{\hat u_j}\); the typical curve has \(u_j=0\); and 95% of new trees have asymptotes between \(\hat A\,e^{-1.96\,\hat\sigma_{\mathrm{tree}}}\) and \(\hat A\,e^{1.96\,\hat\sigma_{\mathrm{tree}}}\) (Figure 2):

# Predicted asymptote of each tree, and the range of the asymptotes of 95% of new trees
# (ft).
tree_asym = A_mle * exp(tree_effects[, "Estimate"])
new_tree_asym = A_mle * exp(qnorm(p = c(0.025, 0.975)) * sd_tree_mle)
new_tree_asym

[1]  94.46757 110.18566

# Measurements, the curves of the 14 trees, the typical curve and the range of new trees.
plot(height ~ age, data = pine_data, xlab = "Age (years)", ylab = "Height (ft)")
for (j in seq_along(tree_asym)) {
  curve(growth(x, A = tree_asym[j], k = k_mle, t0 = t0_mle), add = TRUE, col = "grey60")
}
curve(growth(x, A = A_mle, k = k_mle, t0 = t0_mle), add = TRUE, col = "#D55E00")
curve(growth(x, A = new_tree_asym[1], k = k_mle, t0 = t0_mle), add = TRUE,
      col = "#D55E00", lty = 2)
curve(growth(x, A = new_tree_asym[2], k = k_mle, t0 = t0_mle), add = TRUE,
      col = "#D55E00", lty = 2)
legend("topleft", legend = c("Observed trees", "Typical tree", "95% of new trees"),
       col = c("grey60", "#D55E00", "#D55E00"), lty = c(1, 1, 2), bty = "n")







Figure 2: Height of 14 loblolly pines against age, with the curve of each tree from its predicted deviation (grey lines), the typical curve (u = 0, solid line) and the range that contains the curves of 95% of new trees at the estimates (dashed lines), under the model with a random asymptote.





The asymptotes of 95% of new trees lie between 94 and 110 ft, so at 25 years their heights lie between about 56 and 65 ft, and the curves of the 14 trees fill this range. The range describes the variation among trees at the estimates and leaves out the uncertainty of the estimates themselves.
The estimated asymptote, 102 ft, lies far above the tallest tree in the data, 64.1 ft. The curve reaches 63% of its asymptote at the age of \(\hat t_0+1/\hat k\):

# Age at which the typical curve reaches 63% of its asymptote (years).
t0_mle + 1 / k_mle

[1] 27.69276


This is about 28 years, after the last measurement at 25 years. So the measurements cover only the part of the curve in which the trees grow fast, and the asymptote is an extrapolation: it is the height that the trees would approach if they kept growing as the saturating exponential says. Its standard error on the log scale, 0.025, measures its uncertainty only under this assumption, which the data cannot check. The asymptote is therefore better read as a parameter of the curve than as a prediction of the final height of a pine.


1.1.5 Question 5
The heights are marked with OBS(), so simulate() of the fitted object draws new deviations for the 14 trees and then new heights for these deviations (unconditional simulation). We keep 1,000 hypothetical samples in a matrix with one row per measurement:

# 1,000 hypothetical samples: new tree deviations, then new heights for them.
n_sim = 1000
mixed_simulations = matrix(NA, nrow = length(pine_data$height), ncol = n_sim)
set.seed(seed = 711)
for (j in seq_len(n_sim)) {
  mixed_simulations[, j] = mixed_obj$simulate(mixed_fit$par)$height
}

The expected height of a measurement before the deviation of its tree is known is the typical curve at its age, so that is the fittedPredictedResponse of DHARMa. plot() draws the two standard panels and DHARMa::plotResiduals() the residuals against age, which has only six values, so DHARMa draws a box for each age (rank = FALSE labels the boxes with the ages):

# Expected height of each measurement on the typical curve (u = 0).
mixed_expected = growth(pine_data$age, A = A_mle, k = k_mle, t0 = t0_mle)

# Scaled quantile residuals and the two standard panels.
mixed_residuals = DHARMa::createDHARMa(
  simulatedResponse = mixed_simulations,
  observedResponse = pine_data$height,
  fittedPredictedResponse = mixed_expected
)
plot(mixed_residuals)







Figure 3: Scaled quantile residuals of the 84 heights under the model with a random asymptote, from 1,000 hypothetical samples with new tree deviations. Left: quantile–quantile plot against a uniform distribution. Right: residuals for each value of the typical curve, which has one value for each age.






# Residuals against the age of the measurement.
DHARMa::plotResiduals(mixed_residuals, form = pine_data$age, rank = FALSE)







Figure 4: Scaled quantile residuals of the 84 heights against age.





The quantile–quantile plot follows the line, so the residuals as a whole are close to uniform. Against age they show a pattern (Figure 4): at 3 years most residuals lie above 0.5, with a median of about 0.8, and at 5 years most lie below it, with a median of about 0.25. So the heights lie above the curve at 3 years and below it at 5 years. To see why, we calculate the mean height at each age with tapply(), which applies a function (here mean()) to the values of its first argument within each group given by its second argument, and from it the mean growth rate in the first two intervals:

# Mean height at each of the six ages (ft).
mean_height = tapply(pine_data$height, pine_data$age, mean)
mean_height

The mean heights grow by 3.0 ft/year between 3 and 5 years and by 3.4 ft/year between 5 and 10 years, so the young pines first accelerate their growth before it slows down, an S-shaped start that the saturating exponential cannot follow, because its slope is largest at \(t_0\). DHARMa also flags that the spread of the residuals differs among the ages: at 3 years the heights vary less around the curves than \(\hat\sigma_{\mathrm{obs}}\) allows, whereas the model has one \(\sigma_{\mathrm{obs}}\) for all ages. As in the theory, we read the plots as exploratory evidence and not the tests that DHARMa prints with them. Both points concern the youngest trees; a curve with an inflection, such as the logistic or the Gompertz function, could be fitted and compared with this one.
The residuals of the trees come from the sums of the six heights of each tree:

tree_scaled = residuals(tree_residuals)

They are spread between 0.04 (tree 329) and 0.98 (tree 305), with no tree far outside its simulations; with 14 trees this is what we expect if the distribution of tree effects describes the trees. The residuals of the trees cannot show the problem at young ages, because each of them adds up the heights of all ages of a tree; the residuals of the measurements show it. This is the point of the warning in the theory: each level of residuals can hide what the other one shows.


1.1.6 Question 6
Complete pooling has \(K=4\) parameters (\(A\), \(k\), \(t_0\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{obs}}\)), and the mixed model \(K=5\), because the 14 deviations of the trees are integrated out and cost one parameter, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{tree}}\). Both are fitted to the same 84 heights in the same units, and the minimum of each NLL is minus its maximum log-likelihood (the marginal one for the mixed model):

# AIC of the two models: K = 4 and K = 5 estimated parameters.
K_pines = c(pooled = length(pooled_fit$par), mixed = length(mixed_fit$par))
nll_pines = c(pooled = pooled_fit$value, mixed = mixed_fit$value)
2 * K_pines + 2 * nll_pines

  pooled    mixed 
333.6340 243.3372 


The mixed model has an AIC about 90 units lower. Complete pooling is the mixed model with \(\sigma_{\mathrm{tree}}=0\), which lies at the boundary of the range of the parameter, where the large-sample theory behind AIC does not hold, so the comparison is only an approximate guide. A difference of 90 units leaves no doubt here, but for a smaller difference leave-one-tree-out cross-validation, as in the theory, would be the better guide. AICc and BIC need the number of independent observations, which is ambiguous for grouped data: the 84 heights are not independent, but they are not only 14 observations either, because each height adds information about the curve of its tree.

title: Numerical optimisation
text:
In this chapter, we learn how to find the maximum of a likelihood when the optimiser does not find it by itself, and how to tell whether it has. Since Chapter 4 every fit has minimised a negative log-likelihood (NLL) with optim(), the BFGS method and the gradient that RTMB supplies, and from the starting values that we chose this has usually worked. An optimiser can, however, stop somewhere other than the maximum and still report a convergence code of zero. The practical of this chapter shows this with a Gamma model of penguin body masses whose fit stops after a single step, and the practical of Chapter 7 met it with fits that stopped at a practically zero variance among sites although the maximum lay at a positive one.
The chapter is organised by problem. Each section states a difficulty in general terms, shows it on a fit from an earlier chapter that goes wrong, explains as much of the mechanism as we need to understand it, and gives the remedy; there are no new data. What is new is how a gradient method searches, the difference between exact and approximate gradients, the stopping rules of an optimiser, how to diagnose a fit, multiple starting values, identifiability, estimates at a boundary, scaling and parameterisation, the local optimisers nlminb(), Nelder–Mead and optimize(), and global search with differential evolution. BFGS with the gradient of RTMB remains the method of the course; the other optimisers are the next tool when it fails. This is the last chapter, and it completes the line on estimation that started in Chapter 3.

title: Numerical optimisation
text:
3.1 How a gradient method searches
A gradient method moves downhill. The negative gradient, \(-\mathbf g(\boldsymbol\theta)\), points in the direction in which the NLL falls fastest, so the simplest method takes a step in that direction, evaluates the NLL and the gradient at the new point, and repeats. How far to step is decided by a line search: the method tries a step of some length along the chosen direction and shortens it until the NLL falls by enough. Following the steepest slope alone is slow in a narrow, tilted valley, such as the surface of correlated estimates in Chapter 4, because the steepest direction points across the valley rather than along it.
Newton’s method also uses the curvature. Near a minimum the NLL is close to a parabola, the quadratic approximation of Chapter 4, and Newton’s method jumps to the minimum of the parabola that has the gradient and the Hessian of the current point. Close to the minimum this is fast, because the parabola describes the NLL well there. Far from it the parabola can be a poor description: the jump can be far too long, and where the curvature is negative in some direction, the parabola has no minimum and the step can go uphill. BFGS, the method that we have used since Chapter 4, is a quasi-Newton method: it takes steps like those of Newton’s method, but with an approximation of the curvature that it builds from the gradients of successive steps (two nearby gradients that differ show how the slope changes, which is what the curvature measures). So it needs only fn and gr, and it becomes about as fast as Newton’s method once it is close to a minimum. The method is named after Broyden, Fletcher, Goldfarb and Shanno, who published it independently in 1970.1






CautionStatistical detail: Newton’s method and BFGS





Let \(\boldsymbol\theta_t\) be the parameter values after \(t\) steps. Newton’s method takes the step
\[
\boldsymbol\theta_{t+1}=\boldsymbol\theta_t-\mathbf H(\boldsymbol\theta_t)^{-1}\,
\mathbf g(\boldsymbol\theta_t),
\]
where \(\mathbf g(\boldsymbol\theta_t)\) is the gradient and \(\mathbf H(\boldsymbol\theta_t)\) the Hessian of the NLL at \(\boldsymbol\theta_t\). This is the minimum of the parabola \(-\ell(\boldsymbol\theta_t)+\mathbf g^{\top}\mathbf d+\tfrac12\mathbf d^{\top}\mathbf H\,\mathbf d\) in the step \(\mathbf d=\boldsymbol\theta_{t+1}-\boldsymbol\theta_t\), which exists when \(\mathbf H\) is positive definite (see the box in Section 3.4). With one parameter the step is \(-g/H\): the slope divided by the curvature.
BFGS replaces \(\mathbf H^{-1}\) by a matrix \(\mathbf B_t\) and takes the step \(\boldsymbol\theta_{t+1}=\boldsymbol\theta_t-\lambda_t\mathbf B_t\,\mathbf g(\boldsymbol\theta_t)\), where the step length \(\lambda_t\) comes from a line search. After each step, with the change in the parameters \(\mathbf s_t=\boldsymbol\theta_{t+1}-\boldsymbol\theta_t\) and the change in the gradient \(\mathbf y_t=\mathbf g(\boldsymbol\theta_{t+1})-\mathbf g(\boldsymbol\theta_t)\), the matrix is updated as
\[
\mathbf B_{t+1}=\left(\mathbf I-\rho_t\,\mathbf s_t\mathbf y_t^{\top}\right)\mathbf B_t
\left(\mathbf I-\rho_t\,\mathbf y_t\mathbf s_t^{\top}\right)+\rho_t\,\mathbf s_t\mathbf s_t^{\top},
\qquad
\rho_t=\frac{1}{\mathbf y_t^{\top}\mathbf s_t},
\]
where \(\mathbf I\) is the identity matrix. The update makes \(\mathbf B_{t+1}\mathbf y_t=\mathbf s_t\): the new matrix turns the observed change of the gradient into the observed change of the parameters, as the inverse of the Hessian would for a parabola. In optim(), \(\mathbf B_0\) is the identity matrix, so the first step goes along the negative gradient with a length set by the size of the gradient, and the line search starts with \(\lambda_t=1\) and divides it by 5 until the NLL falls by at least a small fraction of the decrease that the slope predicts. In plain English, BFGS learns the curvature of the surface from how the slope changes along its path, and uses it as Newton’s method would.



Newton’s method still has a place in this book: RTMB uses it for the inner optimisation of a model with random effects (Chapter 7), where automatic differentiation supplies the exact second derivatives that it needs and the search starts close to the minimum.
Whatever the method, the consequence is the same: a gradient method follows the slope from wherever it starts, so it ends at the minimum, ridge or boundary to which the slope leads. Figure 2 shows three searches on the likelihood surface of the reed frog functional response of Chapter 6, a Binomial model with the Holling type II curve and two parameters, the attack rate \(\alpha\) and the handling time \(H\). BFGS works with \(\operatorname{logit}(\alpha)\) and \(\log(H)\), so the edges of the figure, \(\alpha=1\) and \(H=0\), lie at \(+\infty\) and \(-\infty\) on the scales that it searches. From the starting values of Chapter 6 it reaches the maximum in five steps. From a small attack rate, the first step goes along the steep gradient and is so long that \(\alpha\) jumps to practically 1, and the search ends there, on the edge, at an NLL of 59.77 against 46.72 at the maximum. From a third start the search first runs close to the same edge and then jumps to \(H\) practically 0, where it ends at 52.22. We return to these two fits in Section 5.3.








Figure 2: Contours of the relative log-likelihood of the reed frog model of Chapter 6, with the attack rate and the handling time on their original scales, and the paths of three BFGS searches. The points are the points at which BFGS evaluated the gradient (the start and the end of each accepted step), and the lines join them in order. From the starting values of Chapter 6 (α = 0.5, H = 1/60) the search reaches the maximum likelihood estimate (circle); from α = 0.01, H = 1/60 it ends at α practically 1, and from α = 0.05, H = 0.03 at H practically 0.

title: Numerical optimisation
text:
3.2 Exact and approximate gradients
When optim() is not given gr, it approximates the gradient. Each partial derivative is replaced by a finite difference, the change in the NLL between two nearby values of one parameter divided by the distance between them, as in Chapter 5. optim() uses two evaluations of the NLL for each parameter, one on each side of the current value, so each approximate gradient of a model with \(p\) parameters costs \(2p\) extra evaluations. The distance between the two values is a compromise. A large distance makes the straight line between the two points a poor approximation of the slope at the point, and a very small one makes the difference of two nearly equal numbers inaccurate, because the computer rounds every number it stores. The gradient that RTMB calculates by automatic differentiation (Chapter 6) has neither problem: it is exact up to rounding error, and it costs about as much as a few evaluations of the NLL, whatever the number of parameters.






CautionTechnical detail: finite differences





For a function \(f\) of the parameters \(\boldsymbol\theta\), the forward difference and the central difference approximate the partial derivative with respect to \(\theta_j\) by
\[
\frac{\partial f}{\partial\theta_j}\approx
\frac{f(\boldsymbol\theta+h\,\mathbf e_j)-f(\boldsymbol\theta)}{h}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\frac{\partial f}{\partial\theta_j}\approx
\frac{f(\boldsymbol\theta+h\,\mathbf e_j)-f(\boldsymbol\theta-h\,\mathbf e_j)}{2h},
\]
where \(h\) is the step and \(\mathbf e_j\) is a vector with 1 in position \(j\) and 0 elsewhere, so that \(\boldsymbol\theta+h\,\mathbf e_j\) changes only \(\theta_j\). The error of the forward difference is roughly proportional to \(h\) and that of the central difference to \(h^2\), so the central difference is more accurate for the same step. Both suffer from rounding: \(f\) is stored with a relative precision of about \(2.2\times10^{-16}\) (.Machine$double.eps), and this error is divided by \(h\), so it grows as the step shrinks. optim() uses central differences with the step set by the control argument ndeps, \(10^{-3}\) for every parameter by default (on the scale of the parameters divided by parscale). In plain English, the step must be small enough for the line between the two points to follow the curve, and large enough for the difference of the two values to be more than rounding noise.



For the CO₂ model, we fit again from the starting values of Chapter 7 without gr:

# The fit from the starting values of Chapter 7 without the gradient of RTMB.
pooled_fd_fit = optim(par = pooled_obj$par, fn = pooled_obj$fn, method = "BFGS")

# Minimum of the NLL and the counts of evaluations of fn and gr, with and without gr.
c(with_gr = pooled_fit$value, without_gr = pooled_fd_fit$value)

   with_gr without_gr 
  296.2557   296.2565 

rbind(with_gr = pooled_fit$counts, without_gr = pooled_fd_fit$counts)

           function gradient
with_gr         104       33
without_gr       83       32


Both fits report code 0, and without gr the search ends at an NLL slightly above the minimum (296.2565 against 296.2557). The element counts gives the number of calls to fn and to gr, but, as the help page of optim() says, it does not include the evaluations of fn for the finite differences. With four parameters each approximate gradient costs eight of them, so the fit without gr called fn \(83+8\times32=339\) times, against 104 calls to fn and 33 to gr with the exact gradient. Here the approximation costs time and a little precision; in a model with many parameters, or in a narrow valley, it can stop the search well before the minimum. From the three other starting values of Section 3, BFGS without gr stops in the same wrong places as with it, so the exact gradient does not cure those failures.

title: Numerical optimisation
text:
3.3 Stopping rules and convergence codes
A stopping rule decides when an optimiser ends its search. The rule of BFGS in optim() looks at the value of the NLL. A step that lowers the NLL by less than a relative tolerance, \(\texttt{reltol}\times\left(|{-\ell(\boldsymbol\theta)}|+\texttt{reltol}\right)\), counts as no progress. BFGS then discards its approximation of the curvature and tries a step along the negative gradient; when that step makes no progress either, the search stops and optim() returns convergence code 0. The tolerance is the control argument reltol, by default \(\sqrt{\epsilon}\approx1.5\times10^{-8}\), where \(\epsilon\approx2.2\times10^{-16}\) is the precision of numbers in R. For the CO₂ model, whose NLL is about 300, a step must lower the NLL by more than about \(4.4\times10^{-6}\) to count as progress. The search also stops after maxit iterations, 100 by default for BFGS, and then the convergence code is 1. The help page of optim() lists other codes, which belong to other methods.
In plain English, BFGS stops when it can no longer lower the NLL, and it does not check the gradient at all. At a minimum this is what we want. The same thing happens, however, on a ridge, where the NLL hardly changes in any direction that the search tries; near a saddle point, where the gradient is close to zero; at a boundary on the optimised scale, where the NLL keeps falling by ever smaller amounts as a parameter runs towards \(\pm\infty\); and on a surface that is nearly flat compared with the size of the NLL, because the tolerance is relative to the value of the NLL. The last case explains the penguin fit of the practical of this chapter: with the masses in grams, the NLL is large, and a step that still lowered it was too small to count as progress. The note “When a fit fails” in Chapter 4 dealt with a code other than zero and with an NLL that cannot be calculated; this chapter deals with a code of zero that hides a failure.






WarningA convergence code of zero



A convergence code of 0 says that the stopping rule was met. It does not say that the search reached the maximum of the likelihood: the rule is also met on a ridge, near a saddle point, at a boundary and on a nearly flat surface, as the CO₂ fits of Section 3 show. Whether a fit found the maximum is decided by the checks of Section 3.4.

title: Numerical optimisation
text:
3.4 Diagnosing a fit
Diagnosing a fit means checking whether the point where the optimiser stopped is the maximum of the likelihood. Each check looks at the fit from a different side, and none of them is sufficient alone:

The estimates on the original scale. Are they sensible values in their units? Is a parameter very large or very small on the optimised scale (a logarithm of 27 or of \(-245\)), which means that it ran towards a boundary or along a ridge?
The gradient at the solution, obj$gr(fit$par), whose elements should be close to zero. A large element shows that the search stopped on a slope. A small one is necessary but not enough, because the gradient is also close to zero on a ridge and near a saddle point.
The curvature, from sdreport(). At a minimum the Hessian is positive definite (box below), and sdreport() returns the element pdHess, which is TRUE when it is. When it is not, the standard errors are NaN, and printing the result gives the warning “Hessian of fixed effects was not positive definite”. Huge standard errors are a warning sign as well (Section 5). By default sdreport() uses the parameter values with the lowest NLL that the object has evaluated, so after several fits of the same object we pass the values of the fit to check with the argument par.fixed.
A refit, from the solution and from other starting values. A refit that starts where the fit stopped and moves on shows that the search stopped too early; fits from other starting values that end lower show that it stopped at the wrong minimum.
A slice through the solution along a suspicious parameter, with the other parameters fixed at the solution: the likelihood slice of Chapter 4, now used as a diagnostic. It shows how the NLL behaves beyond the point where the optimiser stopped.







CautionStatistical detail: the Hessian at a minimum





The Hessian \(\mathbf H\) of the NLL at a point describes its curvature in every direction: for a direction \(\mathbf d\) (a vector of changes in the parameters), the curvature of the NLL along the straight line through the point in that direction is proportional to \(\mathbf d^{\top}\mathbf H\,\mathbf d\). The Hessian is positive definite when \(\mathbf d^{\top}\mathbf H\,\mathbf d>0\) for every direction \(\mathbf d\neq\mathbf 0\), that is, when the NLL curves upwards in every direction. A stationary point with a positive definite Hessian is a local minimum.
The eigenvalues of \(\mathbf H\) are the curvatures along a set of perpendicular directions, its eigenvectors, and the Hessian is positive definite when all of them are positive. An eigenvalue of zero is a flat direction: the NLL does not change to second order along it, as on a ridge, and \(\mathbf H\) has no inverse, so the covariance matrix \(\mathbf H^{-1}\) of Chapter 4 and the standard errors cannot be calculated. A negative eigenvalue is a direction in which the NLL curves downwards, so the point is not a minimum; if the gradient is also zero there, the point is a saddle point. In plain English, sdreport() checks that the NLL rises in every direction from the solution, which is what a minimum requires, and it can only calculate standard errors when it does.



For the four CO₂ fits, we calculate the largest element of the gradient (in absolute value), the check of the Hessian and the minimum that BFGS reaches when it starts again where each fit stopped:

# Largest absolute gradient, check of the Hessian and refit from the solution, per fit.
max_gradient = rep(NA, length(co2_fits))
pd_hess = rep(NA, length(co2_fits))
refit_nll = rep(NA, length(co2_fits))
for (i in seq_along(co2_fits)) {
  fit = co2_fits[[i]]
  max_gradient[i] = max(abs(pooled_obj$gr(fit$par)))
  # sdreport() at the values of this fit.
  pd_hess[i] = sdreport(pooled_obj, par.fixed = fit$par)$pdHess
  # A new search that starts where this fit stopped.
  refit_nll[i] = optim(
    par = fit$par,
    fn = pooled_obj$fn,
    gr = pooled_obj$gr,
    method = "BFGS"
  )$value
}
data.frame(
  nll = stop_table$nll,
  max_gradient = signif(max_gradient, 2),
  pd_hess = pd_hess,
  refit_nll = refit_nll
)

       nll max_gradient pd_hess refit_nll
1 296.2557      2.5e-03    TRUE  296.2557
2 318.6817      5.2e-06   FALSE  318.6817
3 402.7917      7.4e-06   FALSE  402.7917
4 302.3233      1.9e-02   FALSE  302.3233


The fit from the starting values of Chapter 7 passes every check: its gradient is small, its Hessian is positive definite and a refit stays where it is. The fits that ended at the constant curve and at zero have even smaller gradients, so the gradient does not reveal them, but sdreport() does. For the constant curve, for example:

# sdreport() at the end of the fit from the slow rise.
pooled_ridge_sd = sdreport(pooled_obj, par.fixed = stop_fits$slow_rise$par)
pooled_ridge_sd

sdreport(.) result

Warning:
Hessian of fixed effects was not positive definite.

None of the standard errors can be calculated. At this point the rate is so large that the curve is flat over all the measured concentrations, and changing the rate or the location no longer changes the NLL: these are flat directions, which have no curvature. The fit at zero is flat in three directions for the same reason, because a curve that is practically zero stays practically zero when the asymptote, the rate or the location change a little. The fit with \(c\) at 90.3 µL/L is a different case. Its gradient is larger, but still small, and a refit stays where it is. The Hessian, however, has a negative curvature in one direction, a combination of the location and the rate, so the NLL falls if both change together, and the point is not a minimum. A slice along \(c\) alone would show a minimum at 90.3 µL/L, because the direction in which the NLL falls is not along one parameter; the Hessian looks in every direction at once.
A slice shows what the optimiser could not see from where it stopped. We fix the asymptote, the location and the standard deviation at the end of the fit from the slow rise, and vary the rate from 0.001 to 10 L/µL, with a for loop over pooled_obj$fn() as in Chapter 4:

# Slice through the end of the fit from the slow rise along the log rate; the other
# parameters stay where the fit stopped.
ridge_par = stop_fits$slow_rise$par
log_rate_grid = seq(from = log(0.001), to = log(10), length.out = 101)
ridge_slice = rep(NA, times = length(log_rate_grid))
for (i in seq_along(log_rate_grid)) {
  slice_par = ridge_par
  slice_par[["log_rate"]] = log_rate_grid[i]
  ridge_slice[i] = -pooled_obj$fn(slice_par)
}

# Relative log-likelihood: the difference from the log-likelihood where the fit stopped.
ridge_relative = ridge_slice - (-stop_fits$slow_rise$value)









Figure 3: Slice of the relative log-likelihood of the complete-pooling CO₂ model along the rate, through the point where the fit from the slow rise stopped (the other parameters fixed there). The fit stopped at a rate of about 5 × 10¹¹ L/µL, far to the right, where the slice is flat at zero. The dashed line marks zero.





Figure 3 shows a plateau: for rates above about 0.2 L/µL the curve is already flat over the measured concentrations, and the log-likelihood hardly changes. The fit stopped far out on this plateau, where the slope is zero and BFGS has no direction in which to move. At a rate of about 0.015 L/µL the slice rises about 12 units above the plateau, so the point where the fit stopped is not the maximum, even along this one line. The slice also shows how the search got there: once a step took the rate onto the plateau, nothing led it back.
