Which fits found the maximum? What happened in the others, and what would you check next?






TipSolution





Fit A is the best candidate: it has the lowest NLL, a convergence code of 0, a small gradient, a positive definite Hessian and sensible estimates (a maximum of about 41 eggs per patch, half of it reached at about 19 hosts). Three fits are few, so a refit from A and a few more starting values would confirm it.
Fit B reached the limit of iterations (code 1). Its NLL is only 0.03 above that of A and its estimates are close, but its gradient is not small: the search was still moving when it was stopped. A restart from where B stopped would most likely end at A.
Fit C reports code 0 and has a tiny gradient, but its NLL is 16.6 units higher than that of A, both parameters are enormous and the Hessian is not positive definite. The ratio \(a/b\) is about 2.1 eggs per host, and when \(b\) is much larger than every \(x\), the curve \(ax/(b+x)\) is practically the straight line \((a/b)\,x\). So C stopped on a ridge that leads to the linear model without saturation, where \(a\) and \(b\) can grow together without changing the NLL. It is not the maximum, because A is lower; it is reported as a failed fit, not as estimates.

title: Numerical optimisation
text:
5.1 Structural non-identifiability
Chapter 7 gave each of the 12 plants its own asymptote in two ways: as 12 separate parameters (no pooling), and as a common log asymptote plus a deviation for each plant, with a Normal distribution for the deviations (partial pooling). A model between the two, a common log asymptote log_asym plus 12 deviations dev without a distribution, has 13 parameters for 12 asymptotes. Adding any number to log_asym and subtracting it from every deviation gives the same 12 asymptotes, and so exactly the same likelihood. We write its NLL with the plant of each measurement in the list of data, as in Chapter 7:

# List of data with the index (1 to 12) of the plant of each measurement.
co2_data_plant = list(
  conc = co2$conc,
  uptake = co2$uptake,
  plant = match(as.character(co2$Plant), unique(as.character(co2$Plant)))
)

# NLL with a common log asymptote and a free deviation for each plant.
deviation_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  a = exp(log_asym + dev)
  b = exp(log_rate)
  sd_obs = exp(log_sd_obs)
  mu = a[plant] * (1 - exp(-b * (conc - c0)))
  -sum(dnorm(x = uptake, mean = mu, sd = sd_obs, log = TRUE))
}

We fit it from three starting values of the common asymptote, 10, 20 and 40 µmol/m²/s, with every deviation at zero and the other parameters as in Chapter 7, except for a standard deviation of 8 µmol/m²/s, which avoids the failures of Section 3. For each fit we record the NLL, the check of the Hessian, the common asymptote and the asymptotes of the first and the last plant:

# Process the NLL once; the three fits differ only in the starting common asymptote.
deviation_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(deviation_nll, co2_data_plant),
  list(
    log_asym = log(10), dev = rep(0, 12), log_rate = log(0.01), c0 = 50,
    log_sd_obs = log(8)
  ),
  silent = TRUE
)
deviation_table = NULL
deviation_plants = NULL
for (start_asym in c(10, 20, 40)) {
  start = deviation_obj$par
  start[["log_asym"]] = log(start_asym)
  fit = optim(par = start, fn = deviation_obj$fn, gr = deviation_obj$gr, method = "BFGS")
  fit_sd = sdreport(deviation_obj, par.fixed = fit$par)
  # Asymptote of each plant (µmol/m²/s): the common one times exp(deviation).
  plant_asym = unname(exp(fit$par[["log_asym"]] + fit$par[names(fit$par) == "dev"]))
  deviation_plants = rbind(deviation_plants, plant_asym)
  deviation_table = rbind(
    deviation_table,
    data.frame(
      start = start_asym,
      convergence = fit$convergence,
      nll = fit$value,
      pd_hess = fit_sd$pdHess,
      # Number of the 16 standard errors that cannot be calculated.
      nan_se = sum(is.nan(summary(fit_sd)[, "Std. Error"])),
      common_asym = exp(fit$par[["log_asym"]]),
      first_plant = plant_asym[1],
      last_plant = plant_asym[12]
    )
  )
}
print(deviation_table, digits = 5)

  start convergence    nll pd_hess nan_se common_asym first_plant last_plant
1    10           0 171.44    TRUE     16      28.341       39.43     20.149
2    20           0 171.44    TRUE     16      29.893       39.43     20.150
3    40           0 171.44   FALSE     16      31.530       39.43     20.150


The three fits reach the same minimum, 171.44, which is the minimum of the model without pooling of Chapter 7, and they agree on the asymptote of every plant. The common asymptote, however, ends at a different value in each fit, in the order of the starting values, because nothing in the data pulls it in either direction: BFGS moves it only as far as the steps that bring the plant asymptotes to their values happen to take it. None of the 16 standard errors can be calculated in any of the fits (nan_se). One fit nevertheless passes the check of the Hessian, because the curvature along the flat direction is zero only up to rounding error, and rounding can make it slightly positive. So pdHess is not a reliable symptom here; the agreement of the NLL and of the plant asymptotes, with a common asymptote that depends on the start, is.
The remedy is to change the model. Removing log_asym gives the model without pooling of Chapter 7, with one parameter per asymptote. Giving the deviations a Normal distribution with mean zero, as the mixed model of Chapter 7 does, also makes the common asymptote identifiable: the distribution ties it to the centre of the plant asymptotes, where it is the typical asymptote around which the plants vary.

title: Numerical optimisation
text:
5.2 Practical non-identifiability
In the CO₂ data, the observations that tell us about the location \(c\) are those at low concentrations: the partial derivative of the curve with respect to \(c\), \(-ab\,e^{-b(x-c)}\), is largest in size at \(x=c\) and falls towards zero as the concentration grows. To see what happens without them, we fit the model with complete pooling only to the 60 measurements at 250 µL/L and above, from the starting values of Chapter 7:

# The measurements at 250 µL/L and above.
high = co2$conc >= 250
co2_high_data = list(conc = co2$conc[high], uptake = co2$uptake[high])

# The NLL with complete pooling, connected to these data, and its fit.
high_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(pooled_nll, co2_high_data),
  list(log_asym = log(30), log_rate = log(0.01), c0 = 50, log_sd_obs = log(2)),
  silent = TRUE
)
high_fit = optim(par = high_obj$par, fn = high_obj$fn, gr = high_obj$gr, method = "BFGS")
high_fit$convergence

[1] 0


The fit reports code 0. Its standard errors and correlations show what the data leave undetermined:

# Standard errors on the optimised scales, and the correlations between the estimates.
high_sd = sdreport(high_obj)
summary(high_sd)

            Estimate   Std. Error
log_asym    3.472909   0.07864105
log_rate   -4.524665   3.14370703
c0         49.981980 578.75078858
log_sd_obs  2.227487   0.09164010

round(cov2cor(high_sd$cov.fixed), 3)

           log_asym log_rate     c0 log_sd_obs
log_asym      1.000   -0.812 -0.764     -0.067
log_rate     -0.812    1.000  0.992      0.087
c0           -0.764    0.992  1.000      0.088
log_sd_obs   -0.067    0.087  0.088      1.000

high_sd$pdHess

[1] TRUE


The Hessian is positive definite, so sdreport() gives no warning, but the location has stayed at its starting value of 50 µL/L with a standard error of 579 µL/L, against 21.7 µL/L with all 84 measurements (Section 4), and the standard error of the log rate is 3.1, ten times that of the full data. The estimates of the log rate and of the location have a correlation of 0.992 (0.84 with all the data): over the concentrations from 250 to 1000 µL/L, a curve that reaches zero far to the left and rises slowly looks like one that reaches zero at 50 µL/L and rises faster. A likelihood profile of the location shows how little the data say about it. We calculate it with TMB::tmbprofile() for both data sets, limiting the range of the location with the argument parm.range (the profile of the reduced data would otherwise continue to enormous negative values), and the interval of the full data with confint():

# Likelihood profiles of the location for all the data and for the high concentrations.
# ytol = 6 continues each profile to 6 units below its start, within parm.range; the
# smaller ystep gives more points on the flat profile. confint() warns that it collapses
# repeated values, as in Chapter 6.
pooled_profile_c0 = TMB::tmbprofile(
  pooled_obj, name = "c0", parm.range = c(-1000, 260), ytol = 6, trace = FALSE
)
high_profile_c0 = TMB::tmbprofile(
  high_obj, name = "c0", parm.range = c(-1000, 260), ytol = 6, ystep = 0.01,
  trace = FALSE
)
confint(pooled_profile_c0)

       lower    upper
c0 -26.57884 75.01537










Figure 4: Likelihood profiles of the location c of the complete-pooling CO₂ model, fitted to all 84 measurements and to the 60 measurements at 250 µL/L and above. Each profile is drawn relative to its highest value in the range shown. The dashed line is the cutoff of 1.92 below the maximum for a 95% interval.





With all 84 measurements the profile has a clear maximum, and the 95% interval of the location runs from \(-26.6\) to 75.0 µL/L (Figure 4). Without the low concentrations the profile stays within 0.4 units of its highest value over the whole range from \(-1000\) to 245 µL/L, far less than the cutoff of 1.92, so the 95% interval contains all these values and has no lower end: the data cannot tell us at which concentration the uptake reaches zero. The profile even rises slightly towards very negative values, so BFGS did not stop at the maximum either, but a difference of a few tenths of a unit in the log-likelihood is far below what the data can distinguish, and a location far below zero has no meaning for the plants. The remedy is a design with measurements at low concentrations, which the full data set has; with the reduced data we would report that the location is not determined. The ridge of Section 3 is a different case: with all 84 measurements the location is determined, and the ridge leads towards the constant curve, whose NLL is 22.4 units above the minimum. It is a direction that the data do not favour, on which a search can stop.

title: Numerical optimisation
text:
5.3 Estimates at a boundary
The maximum of a likelihood, or a point to which an optimiser is drawn, can lie at the boundary of the range of a parameter: a probability of 0 or 1, or a variance or a handling time of zero. On the scale that is optimised, the logarithm of a positive parameter or the logit of a probability, the boundary lies at \(-\infty\) or \(+\infty\). The optimiser then walks towards it with ever smaller decreases of the NLL, and stops with code 0 when the decreases fall below the tolerance of Section 3.3. The estimate on the optimised scale is a large number that depends on where the search happened to stop, and its standard error cannot be calculated, because the NLL is flat out there. Such an estimate is reported as being at the boundary (an attack rate of 1, a handling time of 0), or the model is changed.
The reed frog searches of Figure 2 are stored in frog_fits, a list with the three results of optim(). Their estimates on both scales, and the check of the Hessian:

# NLL, convergence code, estimates on the optimised and original scales, and the check of
# the Hessian, for the three searches of the figure of the reed frog surface.
frog_table = NULL
for (start_name in names(frog_fits)) {
  fit = frog_fits[[start_name]]
  frog_table = rbind(
    frog_table,
    data.frame(
      convergence = fit$convergence,
      nll = fit$value,
      logit_alpha = fit$par[["logit_alpha"]],
      log_H = fit$par[["log_H"]],
      alpha = plogis(fit$par[["logit_alpha"]]),
      H = exp(fit$par[["log_H"]]),
      pd_hess = sdreport(binomial_obj, par.fixed = fit$par)$pdHess,
      row.names = start_name
    )
  )
}
print(frog_table, digits = 4)

                                convergence   nll logit_alpha   log_H  alpha
From Chapter 6: maximum                   0 46.72      0.1035  -4.098 0.5259
From α = 0.01: α to 1                     0 59.77    203.8161  -3.304 1.0000
From α = 0.05, H = 0.03: H to 0           0 52.22     -0.6299 -16.229 0.3475
                                        H pd_hess
From Chapter 6: maximum         1.660e-02    TRUE
From α = 0.01: α to 1           3.674e-02   FALSE
From α = 0.05, H = 0.03: H to 0 8.948e-08   FALSE


The search from a small attack rate stopped with \(\operatorname{logit}(\alpha)\) at about 204, which is an attack rate of 1 to the precision of the computer, and the search from the third start with \(\log(H)\) at about \(-16\), a handling time of \(9\times10^{-8}\) (in units of the length of the experiment per tadpole killed), practically zero. Both report code 0, and neither passes the check of the Hessian. Neither is the maximum, because the NLL at the maximum is lower (46.72 against 59.77 and 52.22): these are boundaries towards which the searches were drawn from poor starting values, and multiple starts would reveal them as failures.
A boundary can also be where the maximum lies. A variance among groups whose maximum likelihood estimate is zero is the common case in grouped models: it happens when the groups differ less than the variation within groups would make them differ by chance. On the scale of the log standard deviation the maximum then lies at \(-\infty\), and BFGS stops on its way there with code 0. The estimate is reported as zero, which means that the model reduces to complete pooling, and the likelihood profile of the standard deviation (Chapter 7) shows which values the data allow. A fit that stops at a practically zero variance can also be a failure, with the maximum at a positive variance; the practical of Chapter 7 met such fits, and the practical of this chapter tells the two cases apart.
Some optimisers accept bounds on the parameters: optim(method = "L-BFGS-B") and nlminb() take the arguments lower and upper on the scale of the parameters, so that a search can reach a boundary exactly instead of walking towards infinity. This book keeps the transformations of Chapter 4 instead, because then every value on the optimised scale is allowed, and the standard errors, likelihood profiles and ADREPORT() all work on a scale without edges. An estimate at a boundary is recognised, as above, by a parameter that runs towards \(\pm\infty\) on the optimised scale.






Practice 2: identifiability of seed predation



Rodents are offered trays with 5 to 40 seeds for one night, and the number of seeds removed from each tray is counted. Two colleagues propose models for the expected number removed, with a Poisson distribution of the counts:

\(\lambda = a\,p\,x\), where \(x\) is the number of seeds in the tray, \(a\) the proportion of seeds that rodents find in one night and \(p\) the probability that a seed that is found is removed;
the Michaelis–Menten function \(\lambda = ax/(b+x)\), where earlier studies suggest that the half-maximum \(b\) is about 500 seeds per tray.

For each model, which parameters can the data determine, which symptoms would a fit show, and what would you change?






TipSolution





In the first model \(a\) and \(p\) enter the mean only through their product \(ap\), the proportion of the seeds that are removed. Any pair with the same product gives the same distribution of the counts, so the model is structurally non-identifiable. A fit would reach the same NLL from different starting values with different estimates of \(a\) and \(p\), with NaN standard errors and, usually, the warning that the Hessian is not positive definite. The remedy is to estimate the product as one parameter, or to add data that measure one of the two separately (for example, observations of how many of the seeds that rodents find they remove).
In the second model both parameters are identifiable in principle, but all the trays have far fewer seeds than the half-maximum, where the curve is practically the straight line \((a/b)\,x\). The data determine the initial slope \(a/b\), and not \(a\) and \(b\) separately: the model is practically non-identifiable. A fit would show very large standard errors, a correlation of the estimates of \(\log(a)\) and \(\log(b)\) close to 1, flat likelihood profiles, or a search that runs along the ridge towards the straight line, as fit C of Practice 1. The remedy is a design with trays around and above 500 seeds, or the linear model with the slope \(a/b\) as its only parameter of the curve.

title: Numerical optimisation
text:
6.1 Scaling
An optimiser works best when a change of about one unit in each parameter changes the NLL by similar amounts. Its steps must suit every parameter at once, and the first step of BFGS goes along the negative gradient, with the same step length for all of them; a step that is right for an asymptote of 30 is far too large for a rate of 0.01. There are three remedies. The first is a transformation: on the log scale a change of one unit multiplies a parameter by \(e\), whatever its size, so a rate of 0.01 and an asymptote of 30 become \(-4.6\) and \(3.4\). The second is the choice of units for the data and for untransformed parameters. The units also set the size of the NLL, which matters for the relative tolerance of Section 3.3; the penguin masses in grams of the practical of this chapter are an example. The third is the control argument parscale of optim(), which gives the typical size of each parameter: optim() then searches over the parameters divided by these sizes, so that every parameter it works with is of about one unit.
For the CO₂ model, we write the NLL with the rate on its original scale, as rate, and fit it from the starting values of Chapter 7:

# The NLL with complete pooling, with the rate (L/µL) on its original scale.
rate_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  a = exp(log_asym)
  sd_obs = exp(log_sd_obs)
  mu = a * (1 - exp(-rate * (conc - c0)))
  -sum(dnorm(x = uptake, mean = mu, sd = sd_obs, log = TRUE))
}

# Process it with the starting values of Chapter 7, and fit it.
rate_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(rate_nll, co2_data),
  list(log_asym = log(30), rate = 0.01, c0 = 50, log_sd_obs = log(2)),
  silent = TRUE
)
rate_fit = optim(par = rate_obj$par, fn = rate_obj$fn, gr = rate_obj$gr, method = "BFGS")
c(convergence = rate_fit$convergence, nll = rate_fit$value, rate = rate_fit$par[["rate"]])

convergence         nll        rate 
   0.000000  318.681733    1.270452 


The search ends on the ridge of the constant curve, with code 0, an NLL of 318.68 and a rate of 1.27 L/µL, far out on the plateau of Figure 3. The gradients at the starting values show why:

# Gradient at the starting values with the rate (second element) and with the log rate.
rbind(rate = rate_obj$gr(rate_obj$par), log_rate = pooled_obj$gr(pooled_obj$par))

         [,1]        [,2]     [,3]      [,4]
[1,] -1125.38 -17252.1917 1.492677 -1428.527
[2,] -1125.38   -172.5219 1.492677 -1428.527


The other three elements are the same, but the element for the rate is 100 times that for the log rate. By the chain rule, the derivative with respect to \(\log(b)\) is \(b\) times the derivative with respect to \(b\), and \(b=0.01\) L/µL. So the first step changes the rate far more, relative to its size, than the log rate would change, and it takes the rate onto the plateau, from which nothing leads back. With parscale, the rate is measured in units of 0.01 L/µL and the location in units of 10 µL/L:

# The same fit, with the typical size of each parameter given to optim().
rate_scaled_fit = optim(
  par = rate_obj$par,
  fn = rate_obj$fn,
  gr = rate_obj$gr,
  method = "BFGS",
  control = list(parscale = c(1, 0.01, 10, 1))
)
c(convergence = rate_scaled_fit$convergence, nll = rate_scaled_fit$value)

convergence         nll 
     0.0000    296.2557 


Now BFGS reaches the minimum of 296.26, as it does with the log rate of Chapter 7. A transformation is the usual remedy in this book, because it also deals with the constraint that the rate is positive; parscale is the tool for a parameter that cannot be transformed, such as the location \(c\), whose scale is set by its units.

title: Numerical optimisation
text:
6.2 Parameterisation
A parameterisation changes the shape of the surface and, with it, the correlation of the estimates (Chapter 4). Strongly correlated estimates mean a narrow valley that is tilted with respect to the axes of the parameters, along which the NLL changes slowly and across which it changes fast. Such a valley is harder to search, because the steepest direction points across it, and the approximation of the curvature that BFGS builds must learn its tilt before the steps can follow it. This is one reason why the course writes distributions with their mean where possible (Chapter 4): the data usually determine the mean well, and its estimate is often nearly uncorrelated with those of the other parameters.
For the owl calls of Chapter 4, the Negative Binomial model can be written with the mean \(\mu\) and the shape \(k\), or with the shape and the probability \(p\) (size and prob of dnbinom()). We set up the data and the two NLLs as in Chapter 4:

# Calls at the visits of the female parent to nests with satiated nestlings (Chapter 4).
data(Owls, package = "glmmTMB")
satiated_female = Owls[Owls$FoodTreatment == "Satiated" & Owls$SexParent == "Female", ]
call_counts = satiated_female$SiblingNegotiation

# Method-of-moments estimates, used as starting values in Chapter 4.
mu_mom = mean(call_counts)
var_mom = mean((call_counts - mu_mom)^2)
k_mom = mu_mom^2 / (var_mom - mu_mom)

# Negative Binomial NLLs with the mean and the shape, and with the shape and probability.
nb_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  mu = exp(log_mu)
  k = exp(log_k)
  -sum(dnbinom2(x = calls, mu = mu, size = k, log = TRUE))
}
nb_prob_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  k = exp(log_k)
  p = plogis(logit_p)
  -sum(dnbinom(x = calls, size = k, prob = p, log = TRUE))
}

We fit both from the method-of-moments estimates, and compare the minimum, the number of evaluations of fn and gr and the correlation of the estimates:

# Fit both parameterisations from the same starting values.
owl_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(nb_nll, list(calls = call_counts)),
  list(log_mu = log(mu_mom), log_k = log(k_mom)),
  silent = TRUE
)
owl_fit = optim(par = owl_obj$par, fn = owl_obj$fn, gr = owl_obj$gr, method = "BFGS")
owl_prob_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(nb_prob_nll, list(calls = call_counts)),
  list(log_k = log(k_mom), logit_p = qlogis(k_mom / (k_mom + mu_mom))),
  silent = TRUE
)
owl_prob_fit = optim(
  par = owl_prob_obj$par,
  fn = owl_prob_obj$fn,
  gr = owl_prob_obj$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)

# Minimum, evaluations of fn and gr, and the correlation of the two estimates.
rbind(
  mu_k = c(nll = owl_fit$value, owl_fit$counts,
           correlation = cov2cor(sdreport(owl_obj)$cov.fixed)[1, 2]),
  k_p = c(nll = owl_prob_fit$value, owl_prob_fit$counts,
          correlation = cov2cor(sdreport(owl_prob_obj)$cov.fixed)[1, 2])
)

          nll function gradient  correlation
mu_k 299.4419       16        5 6.196508e-08
k_p  299.4419       14        6 7.111355e-01


Both fits reach the same minimum, as invariance requires, and the correlation is practically zero with \(\mu\) and \(k\) and 0.71 with \(k\) and \(p\). Here the tilt does not hurt BFGS, which needs a similar number of evaluations in both cases. A correlation of 0.71 is a mild tilt; a narrower valley can stop the search early. The reed frog model of Chapter 6 has a correlation of 0.82 with \(\operatorname{logit}(\alpha)\) and \(\log(H)\), and of 0.98 in the Michaelis–Menten form with \(\log(a)\) and \(\log(b)\), and the Gamma model of the penguin masses, with a correlation of 0.996 between the estimates of the log shape and the log rate, is the case that the practical of this chapter examines. The remedy is a parameterisation in which the estimates are less correlated, often the one with the mean.






Practice 3: scaling a growth curve



The length of a fish (mm) is described as a function of its age \(x\) in days by the saturating exponential \(a\left(1-e^{-b(x-c)}\right)\), with a Normal distribution of the lengths around the curve. From a plot of the data, a colleague reads starting values of \(a=600\) mm, \(b=0.0005\)/day, \(c=-100\) days and a standard deviation of 20 mm. The asymptote, the rate and the standard deviation are optimised on the log scale, and the location \(c\) untransformed. Calculate the starting values on the optimised scale. Which parameter is poorly scaled, and what change of units would bring all four to comparable scales? Does a change of the units of length help?






TipSolution





On the optimised scale, with age in days and then in years (the rate is multiplied by 365 and the location divided by 365):

# Starting values on the optimised scale with age in days, and with age in years.
c(log_a = log(600), log_b = log(0.0005), c = -100, log_sd = log(20))

      log_a       log_b           c      log_sd 
   6.396930   -7.600902 -100.000000    2.995732 

c(log_a = log(600), log_b = log(0.0005 * 365), c = -100 / 365, log_sd = log(20))

     log_a      log_b          c     log_sd 
 6.3969297 -1.7010051 -0.2739726  2.9957323 


With age in days the location is \(-100\), while the other three lie between \(-8\) and 7; a step of one unit is a change of one day in \(c\), which hardly changes the curve, but a factor of \(e\) in \(a\), \(b\) or \(\sigma\). With age in years the location is \(-0.27\) and all four values are of comparable size. The units of length do not help: a log-transformed parameter only shifts by a constant when its units change (by \(\log(10)\) from millimetres to centimetres), so its scale stays the same. They change only the size of the NLL.

title: Numerical optimisation
text:
7.1 Other local optimisers
The function nlminb() calls the optimisers of the PORT library (see ?nlminb). Like BFGS, it uses the gradient and an approximation of the curvature (or the Hessian itself, if it is given), but it controls its steps differently: it trusts the local parabola only within a certain distance of the current point, and adjusts that distance as the search goes. It is the optimiser of the examples in the documentation of RTMB and TMB, and glmmTMB, which the supplement on formula-based methods introduces, uses it by default. Its arguments are:

start, the starting values (obj$par);
objective, the NLL (obj$fn);
gradient, its gradient (obj$gr).

It returns a list whose elements correspond to those of optim(), with other names:

par, the estimates;
objective, the minimum of the NLL;
convergence, 0 when the search stopped normally;
message, the reason why it stopped;
evaluations, the numbers of evaluations of the NLL and of the gradient.

From the three starting values of Section 3 at which BFGS stopped in the wrong place:

# nlminb() from the three other sets of starting values of the CO2 model.
nlminb_table = NULL
for (start_name in rownames(other_starts)) {
  s = other_starts[start_name, ]
  start = c(
    log_asym = log(s[["a"]]),
    log_rate = log(s[["b"]]),
    c0 = s[["c"]],
    log_sd_obs = log(s[["sd_obs"]])
  )
  fit = nlminb(start = start, objective = pooled_obj$fn, gradient = pooled_obj$gr)
  nlminb_table = rbind(
    nlminb_table,
    data.frame(
      convergence = fit$convergence,
      nll = fit$objective,
      fn_evaluations = fit$evaluations[["function"]],
      message = fit$message,
      row.names = start_name
    )
  )
}
nlminb_table

               convergence      nll fn_evaluations                  message
slow_rise                0 296.2557             31 relative convergence (4)
high_asymptote           0 296.2557             28 relative convergence (4)
early_plateau            0 296.2557             55 relative convergence (4)


nlminb() reaches the minimum of 296.2557 from all three: a search that controls its steps differently avoids the ridge, the curve at zero and the early plateau from these starts.
The Nelder–Mead method, optim(method = "Nelder-Mead"), which is the default of optim(), uses no gradient at all. With \(p\) parameters it keeps a simplex of \(p+1\) points (a triangle for two parameters) and the NLL at each of them. At each step it replaces the worst point by its reflection through the centre of the others; if the reflected point is much better it tries a point further out (an expansion), and if it is worse it tries one closer in (a contraction); when nothing helps, the whole simplex shrinks towards its best point. The search stops when the values of the NLL at the points of the simplex agree within the relative tolerance reltol. Because it needs no gradient, it suits an NLL that cannot be differentiated, but it needs many evaluations, and it stops less precisely than a gradient method. In one dimension optim() warns that Nelder–Mead is unreliable and recommends optimize(), which we use below.
Comparing optimisers fairly means giving them the same NLL and the same starting values, comparing the minimum of the NLL that each reaches and not only the estimates, and counting the evaluations. Even then, one model is not a ranking: another model, or another set of starting values, can reverse the order. For the CO₂ model we fit nlminb() and Nelder–Mead from the 50 random starting values of Section 4, drawn again with the same seed in the same order, and count the fits that end within 0.01 and within 2 units of the lowest NLL:

# The 50 starting values of the multiple starts, drawn again with the same seed, fitted with
# nlminb() and with Nelder-Mead. nlminb() warns when the NLL is NaN at a trial point.
other_results = data.frame(bfgs = multi_results$nll, nlminb = NA, nelder_mead = NA)
set.seed(801)
for (i in 1:n_starts) {
  start = runif(4, min = start_lower, max = start_upper)
  names(start) = names(pooled_obj$par)
  other_results$nlminb[i] =
    nlminb(start = start, objective = pooled_obj$fn, gradient = pooled_obj$gr)$objective
  other_results$nelder_mead[i] =
    optim(par = start, fn = pooled_obj$fn, method = "Nelder-Mead")$value
}

# Number of fits that end close to the lowest NLL, for each optimiser.
best_nll = min(other_results)
rbind(
  within_0.01 = colSums(other_results < best_nll + 0.01),
  within_2 = colSums(other_results < best_nll + 2)
)

            bfgs nlminb nelder_mead
within_0.01   17     42          12
within_2      17     42          34


In this example nlminb() reaches the minimum from 42 of the 50 starts and stops at the ridge from the other 8, against 17 starts for BFGS. Nelder–Mead ends close to the minimum from many starts but reaches it exactly from fewer: it stops when the points of its simplex have similar values, which can happen a few tenths of a unit above the minimum (three of the 50 fits also stopped at its limit of 500 iterations, with code 1). Each of these fits would be recognised in a diagnosis, and a restart of BFGS from the best of them would end at the minimum.

title: Numerical optimisation
text:
7.2 One parameter in an interval
For a single parameter, optimize() searches an interval that we give it. It combines golden-section search, which shrinks the interval around the minimum by a fixed fraction at each step, with parabolic interpolation through three points, which jumps to the minimum of the parabola when the NLL is smooth. It needs no gradient and no starting value, only the interval. Its arguments are f, the NLL as a function of one number, and interval, the lower and upper ends of the search; it returns minimum, the estimate, and objective, the minimum of the NLL. For the fir seedlings of Chapter 4, with the Poisson NLL on the log scale:

# Counts of balsam fir seedlings in 50 quadrats and the Poisson NLL of Chapter 4.
data(fir, package = "boot")
seedling_counts = fir$count
poisson_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  lambda = exp(log_lambda)
  -sum(dpois(x = counts, lambda = lambda, log = TRUE))
}
fir_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(poisson_nll, list(counts = seedling_counts)),
  list(log_lambda = log(1)),
  silent = TRUE
)

# Search log(lambda) between -3 and 3 (0.05 to 20 seedlings per quadrat).
fir_fit = optimize(f = fir_obj$fn, interval = c(-3, 3))
c(lambda = exp(fir_fit$minimum), nll = fir_fit$objective, mean = mean(seedling_counts))

   lambda       nll      mean 
 2.139962 89.285287  2.140000 


The estimate is 2.14 seedlings per quadrat, the mean of the counts, as Chapter 4 showed for the Poisson model, and the search needed no starting value.

title: Numerical optimisation
text:
7.3 Global search
Every method so far is local: it follows one path from its starting values. A global method explores a whole box of parameter values instead. Differential evolution keeps a population of parameter vectors, drawn at random within the box, and improves it over many generations. In each generation, every member of the population gets a challenger. The challenger is made by adding a scaled difference of two other members to a third member (mutation), and by taking each of its parameters either from this mutant or from the current member (crossover). The challenger replaces the member if its NLL is lower (selection). Differences between members are large while the population is spread over the box and shrink as it gathers around a minimum, so the steps adapt to the surface without a gradient.2 It needs a box, thousands of evaluations and a seed. It can find a minimum that local searches miss, but it proves nothing: the population can gather around a local minimum as well, and it approaches the minimum it finds only slowly. Other global methods, such as simulated annealing and genetic algorithms, work on similar principles; we do not use them.






CautionTechnical detail: differential evolution





Let \(\mathbf x_1,\ldots,\mathbf x_{NP}\) be the \(NP\) members of the population, each a vector of the \(p\) parameters. In the classical scheme, the mutant for member \(i\) is
\[
\mathbf v_i=\mathbf x_{r_0}+F\left(\mathbf x_{r_1}-\mathbf x_{r_2}\right),
\]
where \(r_0\), \(r_1\) and \(r_2\) are three other members chosen at random and \(F\) is a weight, usually between 0 and 1. In the crossover, each element of the challenger is taken from \(\mathbf v_i\) with probability \(CR\) and from \(\mathbf x_i\) otherwise (with at least one element from \(\mathbf v_i\)). The challenger replaces \(\mathbf x_i\) if its NLL is not higher. DEoptim() uses \(F=0.8\) and \(CR=0.5\) by default, and its default strategy also moves each mutant part of the way from the current member towards the best member of the population. Elements that fall outside the box are brought back inside it. With \(NP\) members and \(G\) generations, the search evaluates the NLL \(NP\times(G+1)\) times. In plain English, the population learns the scale and direction of useful steps from the differences between its own members.



DEoptim::DEoptim() (we call it with the prefix, without attaching the package) takes:

fn, the NLL (obj$fn);
lower and upper, the box on the optimised scale, which the method needs;
control, made with DEoptim::DEoptim.control(), with the size of the population NP, the number of generations itermax and trace = FALSE to stop it printing its progress.

The elements of its result that we use are in its element optim:

bestmem, the best member of the final population;
bestval, its NLL;
nfeval, the number of evaluations of the NLL.

For the CO₂ model we use the box of Section 4, 40 members and 200 generations, with a seed:

# Differential evolution within the box of the multiple starts.
set.seed(802)
pooled_de = DEoptim::DEoptim(
  fn = pooled_obj$fn,
  lower = start_lower,
  upper = start_upper,
  control = DEoptim::DEoptim.control(NP = 40, itermax = 200, trace = FALSE)
)
c(nll = pooled_de$optim$bestval, evaluations = pooled_de$optim$nfeval)

        nll evaluations 
   296.2557   8040.0000 


The best member reaches the minimum of 296.26, after 8,040 evaluations of the NLL, against about 100 for one fit with BFGS from good starting values. Global, then local: a global search finds the region of the minimum, and a local search finds the minimum precisely and starts the diagnosis. We start BFGS from the best member (whose elements DEoptim() names par1 to par4, so we give them the names of pooled_obj$par):

# Refine the best member with BFGS.
de_start = pooled_de$optim$bestmem
names(de_start) = names(pooled_obj$par)
pooled_de_fit = optim(par = de_start, fn = pooled_obj$fn, gr = pooled_obj$gr, method = "BFGS")
c(convergence = pooled_de_fit$convergence, nll = pooled_de_fit$value)

convergence         nll 
     0.0000    296.2557 

sdreport(pooled_obj, par.fixed = pooled_de_fit$par)$pdHess

[1] TRUE


BFGS confirms the minimum, with a positive definite Hessian, and its estimates agree with those of the fit from the starting values of Chapter 7. Here differential evolution found the maximum likelihood estimates without any starting values, at the cost of many evaluations. For a model with random effects, in which every evaluation contains an inner optimisation, that cost grows quickly, and multiple starts of BFGS, or of nlminb(), are usually cheaper.

title: Numerical optimisation
text:
Footnotes

title: Chapter 8: Numerical optimisation — solutions
text:
The fully worked first exercise is on the student practical page. These solutions use the same data, tasks and seeds as Exercises 2 and 3 on that page. All three exercises are the core of the practical, and each follows the four steps of a diagnosis: the symptom, the diagnosis, the remedy and the confirmation.
As on that page, we load RTMB first and RTMBdist second, and define the helper cmb() that connects a likelihood to a data set:
# Load RTMB first and RTMBdist second.
library(RTMB)
library(RTMBdist)

# Connect a likelihood to a data set.
cmb = function(f, d) function(p) f(p, d)

title: Chapter 8: Numerical optimisation — solutions
text:
1.1 Solution

1.1.1 Question 1
We select the Adelie penguins, remove the missing mass and write the NLL of the Gamma model as in Chapter 4, with the data in the element x:

# Load the penguin data (in R 4.5.0 and later) and keep the Adelie penguins.
data(penguins, package = "datasets")
adelie = penguins[penguins$species == "Adelie", ]

# One body mass is missing; remove it and keep the masses in grams.
mass_g = adelie$body_mass[!is.na(adelie$body_mass)]
length(mass_g)

[1] 151

# Negative log-likelihood of the Gamma model with shape k and rate r.
gamma_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  shape = exp(log_shape)
  rate = exp(log_rate)
  -sum(dgamma(x = x, shape = shape, rate = rate, log = TRUE))
}

The method-of-moments estimates come from \(E[X]=k/r\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=k/r^2\), which give \(k=\bar x^2/s^2\) and \(r=\bar x/s^2\). Question 3 needs them again for the masses in kilograms, so we calculate them with a small function that returns them as starting values on the log scale:

# Method-of-moments estimates of the shape and the rate, as starting values on the log
# scale; the variance has divisor n.
gamma_mom_start = function(x) {
  mu_mom = mean(x)
  var_mom = mean((x - mu_mom)^2)
  list(log_shape = log(mu_mom^2 / var_mom), log_rate = log(mu_mom / var_mom))
}

We fit the model from these values and look at the counts of evaluations and at the shape before and after the search:

# Process the NLL of the masses in grams with the method-of-moments estimates, and fit it.
penguin_obj_g = MakeADFun(
  cmb(gamma_nll, list(x = mass_g)),
  gamma_mom_start(mass_g),
  silent = TRUE
)
penguin_fit_g = optim(
  par = penguin_obj_g$par,
  fn = penguin_obj_g$fn,
  gr = penguin_obj_g$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)

# Convergence code, evaluations of fn and gr, and the shape at the start and at the end.
c(
  convergence = penguin_fit_g$convergence,
  penguin_fit_g$counts,
  shape_start = exp(penguin_obj_g$par[["log_shape"]]),
  shape_end = exp(penguin_fit_g$par[["log_shape"]])
)

convergence    function    gradient shape_start   shape_end 
    0.00000     8.00000     1.00000    65.56026    65.56283 


The fit reports code 0, with 8 evaluations of fn and a single one of gr. BFGS evaluates the gradient at its starting values and again after every step that counts as progress, so a single evaluation of gr means that no step counted as progress: the 8 evaluations of fn are the starting values and the trial points of one line search. The shape changed only from 65.560 to 65.563. So the search took one tiny step and stopped.


1.1.2 Question 2
The gradient at the solution, and a refit that starts where the fit stopped:

# Gradient at the solution.
penguin_obj_g$gr(penguin_fit_g$par)

           [,1]       [,2]
[1,] -0.2219675 -0.3889439

# A refit from the solution, and how much lower its NLL is.
penguin_restart_g = optim(
  par = penguin_fit_g$par,
  fn = penguin_obj_g$fn,
  gr = penguin_obj_g$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)
c(
  convergence = penguin_restart_g$convergence,
  shape = exp(penguin_restart_g$par[["log_shape"]]),
  nll_above_minimum = penguin_fit_g$value - penguin_restart_g$value
)

      convergence             shape nll_above_minimum 
       0.00000000       66.09495532        0.00248012 


The gradient, \(-0.22\) and \(-0.39\), is far from zero, so the search stopped on a slope. The refit moves on to a shape of 66.09, and its NLL is 0.0025 lower. The difference is small, but it shows that the first fit stopped before the minimum.
The stopping rule of BFGS in optim() counts a step as no progress when it lowers the NLL by less than \(\texttt{reltol}\times\left(|{-\ell(\boldsymbol\theta)}|+\texttt{reltol}\right)\), with the NLL at the start of the step and \(\texttt{reltol}=\sqrt{\epsilon}\) by default. We compare the decrease of the NLL in the single step with this threshold:

# Decrease of the NLL in the single step, and the smallest decrease that counts as
# progress, with the default reltol of optim().
reltol = sqrt(.Machine$double.eps)
nll_start_g = penguin_obj_g$fn(penguin_obj_g$par)
c(
  decrease = nll_start_g - penguin_fit_g$value,
  threshold = reltol * (abs(nll_start_g) + reltol)
)

    decrease    threshold 
1.641945e-05 1.695345e-05 


The step lowered the NLL by \(1.64\times10^{-5}\), just below the threshold of \(1.70\times10^{-5}\), so it counted as no progress. After a step without progress BFGS discards its approximation of the curvature and tries a step along the negative gradient. This was the first step, which already went along the negative gradient, so the search stopped at once and returned code 0. The threshold is proportional to the NLL, which is about 1138 with the masses in grams.


1.1.3 Question 3
For remedy (a) we divide the masses by 1000 and calculate the method-of-moments estimates again from them:

# (a) The masses in kilograms, from the method-of-moments estimates in these units.
mass_kg = mass_g / 1000
penguin_obj_kg = MakeADFun(
  cmb(gamma_nll, list(x = mass_kg)),
  gamma_mom_start(mass_kg),
  silent = TRUE
)
penguin_fit_kg = optim(
  par = penguin_obj_kg$par,
  fn = penguin_obj_kg$fn,
  gr = penguin_obj_kg$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)

For remedy (b) the NLL takes the mean and the shape, and calculates the rate from them as \(k/\mu\). We call it gamma_mean_nll() and start at the mean of the masses and the method-of-moments estimate of the shape, which are the same starting values as before, written with other parameters:

# (b) Negative log-likelihood of the Gamma model with the mean mu (g) and the shape k.
gamma_mean_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  mu = exp(log_mu)
  shape = exp(log_shape)
  # The rate that gives the mean mu: E[X] = shape / rate.
  -sum(dgamma(x = x, shape = shape, rate = shape / mu, log = TRUE))
}
penguin_mean_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(gamma_mean_nll, list(x = mass_g)),
  list(log_mu = log(mean(mass_g)), log_shape = gamma_mom_start(mass_g)$log_shape),
  silent = TRUE
)
penguin_mean_fit = optim(
  par = penguin_mean_obj$par,
  fn = penguin_mean_obj$fn,
  gr = penguin_mean_obj$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)

Remedy (c), nlminb(), takes the object of question 1, with the masses in grams:

# (c) nlminb() from the method-of-moments estimates, with the masses in grams.
penguin_nlminb_g = nlminb(
  start = penguin_obj_g$par,
  objective = penguin_obj_g$fn,
  gradient = penguin_obj_g$gr
)

We compare the convergence code and the estimate of the shape of each search with those of the refit of question 2:

# Convergence code and estimate of the shape of each search.
rbind(
  refit_grams = c(convergence = penguin_restart_g$convergence,
                  shape = exp(penguin_restart_g$par[["log_shape"]])),
  kilograms = c(convergence = penguin_fit_kg$convergence,
                shape = exp(penguin_fit_kg$par[["log_shape"]])),
  mean_shape = c(convergence = penguin_mean_fit$convergence,
                 shape = exp(penguin_mean_fit$par[["log_shape"]])),
  nlminb = c(convergence = penguin_nlminb_g$convergence,
             shape = exp(penguin_nlminb_g$par[["log_shape"]]))
)

            convergence    shape
refit_grams           0 66.09496
kilograms             0 66.09495
mean_shape            0 66.09526
nlminb                0 66.09475


All three remedies reach the maximum: each reports code 0 and a shape of 66.09, the estimate of the refit of question 2.


1.1.4 Question 4
For the masses in kilograms we calculate the threshold of the stopping rule at the starting values, as in question 2:

# Smallest decrease that counts as progress at the starting values, in kilograms.
nll_start_kg = penguin_obj_kg$fn(penguin_obj_kg$par)
c(nll_start = nll_start_kg, threshold = reltol * (abs(nll_start_kg) + reltol))

   nll_start    threshold 
9.465560e+01 1.410478e-06 


In kilograms the NLL at the starting values is about 95, against 1138 in grams. A density is a probability per unit of the measurement, so the density of each mass in kilograms is 1000 times larger than in grams, and the log-likelihood rises by \(\log(1000)\) for each penguin, \(151\times\log(1000)\approx1043\) in all. The threshold falls with the NLL, to \(1.4\times10^{-6}\). The surface in kilograms is that in grams moved by \(\log(1000)\) along the log rate and lowered by this constant, so the gradient and the first step are the same as in grams, and so is its decrease of \(1.64\times10^{-5}\). In kilograms this decrease counts as progress, and BFGS goes on to the maximum.
For the parameterisation we compare the correlations of the estimates at the maximum, with the refit of question 2 for the shape and the rate:

# Correlation of the estimates of log(k) and log(r) at the maximum.
cov2cor(sdreport(penguin_obj_g, par.fixed = penguin_restart_g$par)$cov.fixed)

          log_shape  log_rate
log_shape 1.0000000 0.9962198
log_rate  0.9962198 1.0000000

# Correlation of the estimates of log(mu) and log(k) at the maximum.
cov2cor(sdreport(penguin_mean_obj, par.fixed = penguin_mean_fit$par)$cov.fixed)

                 log_mu     log_shape
log_mu     1.000000e+00 -1.281074e-06
log_shape -1.281074e-06  1.000000e+00


With the shape and the rate the correlation is 0.996. The NLL is a narrow valley, tilted with respect to the axes, along which the shape and the rate change together and keep the mean \(k/r\) close to the mean of the masses. The steepest direction points across this valley, so a step along it soon goes uphill, and the line search had to shorten the first step to a change of the shape of about 0.003 before the NLL fell at all. With the mean and the shape the correlation is practically zero: the valley is not tilted, and the steps of BFGS can follow it.
The change of units and the change of parameterisation change the problem that the optimiser solves. In kilograms the surface has the same shape, but the NLL is smaller and so is the threshold of the stopping rule. With the mean and the shape the surface has another shape, a valley that is not tilted. The refit of question 2 and nlminb() search the same problem again: the refit continues from where the first search stopped, and nlminb() controls its steps differently and follows another path on the same surface. Here all of them work, but a change of units or of parameterisation changes the surface for every later fit of the model, whereas a new search repairs only this fit.

title: Chapter 8: Numerical optimisation — solutions
text:
2.1 Solution

2.1.1 Question 1

# Samples with a practically zero REML estimate of the variance among sites, and their
# convergence codes.
zero_samples = which(reml_results$var_site < 0.001)
length(zero_samples)

[1] 28

table(convergence = reml_results$convergence[zero_samples])

convergence
 0 
28 


In 28 of the 500 samples the REML estimate of \(\sigma^2_{\mathrm{site}}\) is below 0.001, and all of these fits report code 0. To check a fit we need its object again. Question 2 needs the objects as well, so a small function processes the NLL of sample i as in the simulation:

# The REML object of sample i, processed again with its data.
reml_object = function(i) {
  MakeADFun(
    cmb(site_nll, list(log_biomass = reml_samples[, i], site = site_index)),
    site_start,
    random = c("u", "mu"),
    silent = TRUE
  )
}

A loop calculates the two checks at the estimates of each of these samples, passing the estimates to sdreport() with par.fixed:

# Largest absolute gradient and the check of the Hessian at the estimates of each sample.
zero_checks = data.frame(
  sample = zero_samples,
  max_gradient = NA,
  pd_hess = NA
)
for (j in seq_along(zero_samples)) {
  obj = reml_object(zero_samples[j])
  estimates = unlist(reml_results[zero_samples[j], c("log_sd_site", "log_sd_obs")])
  zero_checks$max_gradient[j] = max(abs(obj$gr(estimates)))
  zero_checks$pd_hess[j] = sdreport(obj, par.fixed = estimates)$pdHess
}
range(zero_checks$max_gradient)

[1] 3.585182e-05 1.797653e-02

table(pd_hess = zero_checks$pd_hess)

pd_hess
FALSE  TRUE 
    9    19 


Every gradient is small (at most 0.018), so the gradient does not tell these fits apart. The check of the Hessian does: in 9 samples the Hessian is not positive definite, so these fits did not stop at a minimum, and in the other 19 it is positive definite.


2.1.2 Question 2
The box of starting values is the same for both standard deviations, from \(\log(0.1)\) to \(\log(10)\) on the optimised scale. For each sample we fit the model from 10 starting values drawn in this box, store the NLL and the estimate of \(\log(\sigma_{\mathrm{site}})\) of each fit, and keep the fit with the lowest NLL. The seed is set once, before the loop over the samples:

# Refits of each sample from 10 random starting values: the lowest NLL and its variance
# among sites.
refits = data.frame(
  sample = zero_samples,
  nll_simulation = reml_results$nll[zero_samples],
  nll_best = NA,
  var_best = NA
)
set.seed(831)
for (j in seq_along(zero_samples)) {
  obj = reml_object(zero_samples[j])
  start_nll = rep(NA, 10)
  start_log_sd_site = rep(NA, 10)
  for (r in 1:10) {
    # Both log standard deviations drawn between log(0.1) and log(10).
    start = runif(2, min = log(0.1), max = log(10))
    names(start) = names(obj$par)
    fit = optim(par = start, fn = obj$fn, gr = obj$gr, method = "BFGS")
    start_nll[r] = fit$value
    start_log_sd_site[r] = fit$par[["log_sd_site"]]
  }
  # Keep the fit with the lowest NLL.
  best = which.min(start_nll)
  refits$nll_best[j] = start_nll[best]
  refits$var_best[j] = exp(2 * start_log_sd_site[best])
}

A sample has moved when its best refit ends at a variance above 0.001 with a lower NLL than the fit of the simulation. We count these samples and compare them with the check of the Hessian:

# Samples whose best refit moved to a positive variance with a lower NLL.
moved = refits$var_best > 0.001 & refits$nll_best < refits$nll_simulation
sum(moved)

[1] 9

table(moved = moved, pd_hess = zero_checks$pd_hess)

       pd_hess
moved   FALSE TRUE
  FALSE     0   19
  TRUE      9    0


In 9 of the 28 samples the best refit moves to a positive variance with a lower NLL, and these are exactly the 9 samples whose Hessian was not positive definite. In the other 19 the best refit also ends below 0.001.


2.1.3 Question 3
The standard deviation among sites is optimised as \(\log(\sigma_{\mathrm{site}})\), and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{site}}=e^{\log(\sigma_{\mathrm{site}})}\) is positive for every finite value of its logarithm. A variance of zero is reached only in the limit \(\log(\sigma_{\mathrm{site}})\to-\infty\), so it is a boundary that lies at \(-\infty\) on the optimised scale. As \(\log(\sigma_{\mathrm{site}})\) falls, the variance shrinks towards zero and the NLL approaches the value of the model without site effects ever more slowly. Far enough out, a step changes the NLL by less than the relative tolerance, and BFGS stops with code 0, at a variance that is practically zero and depends on where the search happened to stop.
The same plateau explains the two kinds of fits of question 1. When the maximum lies at zero, the NLL falls all the way towards the plateau, so it curves upwards where the fit stopped, and the Hessian is positive definite although the fit is still on its way to the maximum. When the maximum lies at a positive variance, the NLL rises from that minimum towards the plateau. A search that a long step took past the minimum finds no slope on the plateau to lead it back, and there the NLL curves downwards as it levels off, so the Hessian is not positive definite.
The maximum lies at zero when the sites differ less than the quadrats alone would make them differ. Each site mean is the mean of five quadrats, so even without site effects the site means vary with a variance of \(\sigma^2_{\mathrm{obs}}/5\); when the six observed means vary less than that, no positive variance among sites makes the data more probable. The closed form of this balanced design makes the comparison exact:

# Closed form of the REML estimate for this balanced Normal design (a special case): the
# variance of the six site means minus the variance within sites divided by five.
closed_form = rep(NA, length(zero_samples))
for (j in seq_along(zero_samples)) {
  y = reml_samples[, zero_samples[j]]
  site_means = tapply(y, site_index, mean)
  var_means = var(site_means)
  var_within = sum((y - site_means[site_index])^2) / (5 * n_sites - n_sites)
  closed_form[j] = max(0, var_means - var_within / 5)
}

# Closed form against the best refit of question 2, with the check of the Hessian.
data.frame(
  sample = zero_samples,
  closed_form = signif(closed_form, 3),
  var_best = signif(refits$var_best, 3),
  pd_hess = zero_checks$pd_hess
)
